The same scale and scope metrics and likelihood are used for positive impacts. Financial effects of risks/opportunities were assessed qualitatively in 2024.
- Describes prioritization: a materiality threshold of ≥4, calibrated using DNB’s existing risk frameworks and climate risk tolerance, with Group Risk Management and internal experts consulted.
- Outlines portfolio approach and aggregation: separate analyses for lending/facilitation and for the investment portfolio, then aggregated with higher weighting to the loan book due to its larger size, greater impact potential and DNB’s direct exposure to borrowers.
- Covers Step 4 governance: internal stakeholder engagement and approvals by Group Management and the Board. Identified material ESRS topics: E1 (Climate), E3 (Water/Marine), S1 (Own workforce), S4 (Consumers/End-users), G1 (Business conduct), plus three company-specific topics (Cyber security; Financial crime; Financial infrastructure and financial stability). New material topics will be operationalized with action plans and objectives in 2025.
- Provides an index mapping ESRS 2 and topical disclosure requirements to report pages, with applicability/comments (including items not applicable or phased-in/not reported per ESRS 1 Appendix C).
- Includes a cross-reference list linking ESRS data points to other EU legislation (SFDR, CRR/Pillar 3 Article 449a, Benchmark Regulation, EU Climate Law) and indicates where items are applicable.

structure.title: The EU taxonomy
structure.heading: 2 The EU taxonomy
structure.start_phrase: Regulation (EU) 2020/852 (the EU taxonomy) is a classification system designed to facilitate sustainable investments.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Explains the EU Taxonomy framework under Regulation (EU) 2020/852, its six environmental objectives, and the conditions for taxonomy-eligibility and taxonomy-alignment (substantial contribution, DNSH, minimum safeguards, technical screening criteria).
- Reporting basis: DNB Bank ASA reports at consolidated group level under Article 8 and Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178, Commission Notice C/2024/6691, and CRR (EU) 575/2013.
- Strategy and governance: Sustainability is integrated into DNB’s strategy, including an ambition to mobilise NOK 1,500 billion for sustainable transition; development of a Sustainable Product Framework aligned with market principles (LMA) and partially harmonised with the EU Taxonomy (focused on substantial contribution for climate mitigation and adaptation due to DNSH/minimum safeguard uncertainties).
- Asset management and SFDR: DNB Asset Management integrates SFDR, managing Article 8 and Article 9 products with exclusions and sustainability objectives.
- Ongoing regulatory development: DNB participates in EU Taxonomy interpretation forums, prepares for expanded disclosures; will add KPIs for Fees and commission and Trading book in 2025.
- Mixed-group KPI reporting (second statutory year): Uses weighted KPIs across banks, asset managers, insurers, and non-financial undertakings following Notice C/2024/6691. 2024 average Group KPIs: 4.82% (turnover-based) and 4.84% (Capex-based). No historical comparatives due to stricter 2024 scope and limited 2023 data.
- Segment contributions (turnover-based, weighted): Banking 4.64%, Asset management 0.06%, Insurance 0.12%, Non-financial undertakings 0% (data not available in 2024). Group revenue: NOK 86,537 million.
- Composition of environmentally sustainable assets: 95% from activities 7.1 Construction of new buildings and 7.7 Acquisition and ownership of buildings within households (NOK 137,584 million), slightly reduced due to adding DNSH (climate adaptation) assessment and portfolio mix; remaining 5% (NOK 7,272 million) from counterparties’ reported data (latest available 2023).
- Methodology for banks: Three-step process (identify, classify, calculate). GAR excludes exposures to central governments/central banks/supranationals and certain instruments; includes municipal funding. Household loans use use-of-proceeds approach; issuer KPIs used for bonds; SPVs mapped to closest reporting parent. Flow vs stock KPIs defined; household collateral data enhanced via Eiendomsverdi (year built, EPC, climate risk, collateral values).
- Methodology for asset management and insurance: Portfolio holdings mapped to company-reported taxonomy KPIs via Bloomberg; excludes governments/supranationals/derivatives and non-disclosing undertakings from numerator; avoids double counting between DAM and DNB Livsforsikring; KPIs presented per Annexes IV and X.
- Data sources and limitations: Bloomberg (company taxonomy data), Eiendomsverdi (real estate EPC and physical risk), Multiconsult (NZEB-10% and top-15% evidence). Real estate numerator coverage limited to Norway. Car loans alignment reported as zero due to inability to assess DNSH tyre criteria for activity 6.5.
- Technical screening details:
  - 7.1 Construction: Substantial contribution via PED at least NZEB-10% (proxy: post-2020 EPC A per Multiconsult). DNSH for climate adaptation via Eiendomsverdi physical risk scores; high risk (5–6) excluded. Minimum safeguards not applicable to households/public authorities.
  - 7.7 Acquisition/ownership: Substantial contribution via EPC/PED and top 15% threshold (TEK10 standard or EPC A–B depending on building standard); DNSH approach mirrors 7.1.
- Property treatment: Investment properties (mostly through DNB Livsforsikring) shown under Other assets for taxonomy purposes; further DNSH assessments planned in 2025.
- Trading book: Defined per CRR; 2024 mapping and integration work initiated; aligned with Group net-zero ambition; reporting to be expanded in 2025.
- Nuclear and fossil gas: Discloses taxonomy-aligned exposures to activities 4.27 (new nuclear) and 4.28 (existing nuclear) primarily via financial undertakings within Total GAR assets; no exposures under Financial guarantees KPI.
- Exclusions and scope notes: DNB Markets Inc. (US) not in EU taxonomy scope; no investment companies per (EU) 2021/2178; non-financial undertakings’ taxonomy KPIs reported as zero in 2024 pending data integration.

structure.title: ESRS E1 Climate change
structure.heading: 3 ESRS E1 Climate change
structure.start_phrase: The role of the Board and the Group Management team, and how sustainability-related results are integrated into the incentive schemes for the Group Management team, is described under Incentive schemes (ESRS 2 GOV-3) in sub-chapter ESRS 2 General disclosures.
structure.summary:
- Scope and governance: ESRS E1 Climate change section detailing DNB’s climate governance, with Board and Group Management oversight of the transition plan; climate targets embedded in management incentive schemes (ESRS 2 GOV-3).

- Transition plan overview (ESRS E1-1): Net‑zero by 2050 ambition across lending, investments, and own operations; transition plan launched in 2023 as a core strategic tool. Current plan does not fully align with ESRS E1‑1 format (e.g., use of intensity vs absolute targets). The plan is dynamic, subject to periodic reviews and a comprehensive reassessment in 2025; not all sector targets are 1.5°C‑aligned yet.

- Coverage and prioritization: Targets for loan portfolio currently cover ~70% of financed emissions (2019 drawn exposure), prioritizing high‑emitting and influenceable sectors per NZBA guidance and materiality; remaining sectors under review pending data/method maturity and credible 1.5°C pathways.

- Methodologies and scenarios: Use of science‑based pathways where available, including CRREM (real estate), SBTi/SDA tools (mortgages, motor vehicles, power generation), IEA NZE2050 (steel), Poseidon Principles/IMO (shipping), NGFS Net Zero 2050 (oil & gas). Baselines: generally 2019 for lending/real estate; 2022 for DAM, DNB Livsforsikring and own operations. 2030 as first interim target year per NZBA.

- Data, scopes, and quality: Predominantly intensity‑based targets; Scope 3 often excluded due to inconsistent/low‑quality data. PCAF data quality scores disclosed by sector; mix of actual and estimated data, with rationale and limitations explained.

- Key decarbonisation levers (ESRS E1-3): Customer and company engagement and assessments; capital allocation and investment integration; formal climate transition expectations for clients/suppliers/investees; expanded sustainable finance products/services; enhanced internal climate competence. Integration into group processes (sector expectations, ESG risk tools), with a near‑term focus on commercial real estate energy efficiency and EPC coverage.

- External dependencies: Achievement relies on client transition readiness and supportive public policy/regulation to enable an orderly transition; active stakeholder engagement emphasized.

- Sector targets and metrics (ESRS E1-4):
  - Commercial real estate: −29% emissions intensity by 2030 vs 2019; CRREM‑based; Norway focus initially; Scope 1–2; baseline below CRREM due to Norwegian energy mix; PCAF ~4.4.
  - Mortgages: −47% intensity by 2030 vs 2019; SDA/CRREM; Scope 1–2; EPCs and national energy factors; PCAF ~3.95. 2019 baseline updated to include Sbanken; biofuel factor updated (ESRS 2 BP‑2).
  - Housing cooperatives: −50% intensity by 2030 vs 2019; SDA/CRREM; Scope 1–2; EPC‑based approach; PCAF ~3.7.
  - Shipping: −33% AER by 2030 vs 2019; Poseidon Principles v4.2/IMO; Scope 1 for vessels ≥5,000 GT; coverage ~94%; PCAF 1.0.
  - Motor vehicles: −32% intensity (g CO2e/pkm) by 2030 vs 2019; SBTi SDA using IEA ETP B2DS; well‑to‑wheel, Scope 1–2; baseline from national averages; PCAF ~4.0; 100% estimated.
  - Steel: −30% intensity by 2030 vs 2019; IEA NZE2050; Scope 1–2; Nordic production context; 100% actual data; PCAF 1.0.
  - Oil and gas (upstream): −18% absolute committed lending by 2030 vs 2019; NGFS NZ2050 supply curve alignment; excludes trade finance/guarantees; not an exit strategy. Baseline currency switched from NOK to USD; portfolio reclassification noted; ambition unchanged (ESRS 2 BP‑2).
  - Power generation: No reduction target set; monitoring intensity only (2019 baseline 29.3 kg CO2e/MWh), already well below 2030 pathway due to renewables focus; Scope 1; PCAF ~2.6; 27% estimates.
  - Salmon farming: No target due to lack of suitable 1.5°C pathway; monitoring Scope 1–3 financed emissions intensity; main drivers are feed and air freight; 100% actual data; PCAF ~2.81. 2019 baseline recalculated using a unified SINTEF factor (ESRS 2 BP‑2).

- Investment portfolios:
  - DNB Asset Management (listed equities and corporate bonds): Target 58% of AUM with SBTs by 2030 using SBTi Portfolio Coverage; proprietary framework to assess science‑based targets; baseline 2022; in 2024 all counted targets were SBTi‑approved.
  - DNB Livsforsikring:
    - WACI: −55% by 2030 vs 2019 across listed equities and corporate bonds (~65% of AUM); 68% actual data overall.
    - AUM with SBTs: 53% by 2030 (baseline 2022), within covered universe (~62% of total AUM); 100% actual data.
    - Engagement: Targeted engagement with 15 highest emitters to set SBTs/net‑zero; execution via DAM leveraging stewardship capabilities.

- Real assets:
  - DNB Næringseiendom: −35% carbon intensity by 2030 (84% portfolio coverage); CRREM‑aligned. 2019 baseline corrected to Scope 1–2 only (7.2), after prior misreporting included Scope 3 (ESRS 2 BP‑2).

- Reporting clarifications and updates (ESRS 2 BP‑2): Multiple methodological/data updates disclosed, including mortgage baseline integration of Sbanken, biofuel emissions factor change, oil & gas baseline currency change and client reclassification, salmon farming factor consolidation, and correction of DNB Næringseiendom baseline scopes.

nodes.title: ESRS E1 Climate change - Introduction
nodes.heading: 3 ESRS E1 Climate change
nodes.start_phrase: The role of the Board and the Group Management team, and how sustainability-related results are integrated into the incentive schemes for the Group Management team, is described under Incentive schemes (ESRS 2 GOV-3) in sub-chapter ESRS 2 General disclosures.
nodes.summary: Overview of DNB Group’s ESRS E1 climate change approach, governance, strategy, and transition plan: Board and Group Management oversight with sustainability results integrated into incentives (ESRS 2 GOV-3); net‑zero by 2050 across loans, investments, and own operations; 2023 transition plan is integral to Group strategy but not fully ESRS E1‑1 compliant (intensity- vs absolute-based targets; partial 1.5°C coverage), dynamic and to be reviewed in 2025. Decarbonisation levers include customer/company engagement, capital allocation, expectations, products/services, and climate competence, with integration into ESG risk tools and sector expectations; dependence on client action and policy support noted. Methodology and scenarios: SBT/SDA with 1.5°C where available (2°C where not), NZBA guidance, baselines 2019 (loans) and 2022 (DAM, Liv, own ops), interim 2030 targets, non-linear pathways; PCAF data quality scores disclosed; Scope 3 often excluded due to data limits. Sector targets and metrics (ESRS E1‑4, ESRS 2 BP‑2): Commercial real estate −29% intensity by 2030 (CRREM; Norway focus; Scope 1–2; EPC-based; PCAF 4.4; fluorinated gases excluded); Mortgages −47% intensity (CRREM; Scope 1–2; PCAF 3.95; baseline updated to include Sbanken; biofuel factor change); Housing cooperatives −50% intensity (CRREM; Scope 1–2; PCAF 3.7); Shipping −33% AER by 2030 (Poseidon Principles v4.2/IMO; Scope 1; ≥5,000 GT; ~94% coverage; PCAF 1.0); Motor vehicles −32% gCO2e/pkm (SBTi SDA B2DS; well‑to‑wheel; PCAF 4.0; 100% estimates); Steel −30% tCO2e/t (IEA NZE2050; Scope 1–2; 100% actual; PCAF 1.0; 2019 baseline 0.22); Oil & gas −18% absolute committed lending to upstream by 2030 (NGFS NZ2050 supply curve; currency for baseline changed to USD; reclassification of one customer; not an exit strategy); Power generation: no reduction target, monitoring intensity (2019: 29.3 kg CO2e/MWh; Scope 1; PCAF 2.6; 27% estimates); Salmon farming: no reduction target, monitoring Scope 1–3 intensity (2019 baseline 4.59 kg CO2e/kg HOG using SINTEF; PCAF 2.81; Scope 3 ~80% of sector emissions). Investments: DNB Asset Management targets 58% of AUM with SBTs by 2030 via SBTi Portfolio Coverage, using a 2022 baseline and a quality framework referencing CA100+, CDP, IIGCC, TCFD, SBTi.

nodes.title: DNB Livsforsikring: listed shares and corporate bonds – weighted average carbon intensity (WACI)
nodes.heading: 3.1 DNB Livsforsikring: listed shares and corporate bonds – weighted average carbon intensity (WACI)
nodes.start_phrase: DNB Livsforsikring has set a WACI 4 reduction target across the portfolio of 55 per cent by 2030, compared with the 2019 baseline.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines DNB’s climate-related target-setting and reporting aligned with TCFD, SBTi, and ESRS standards, noting that DAM’s approach can credit transition efforts in sectors lacking SBTi methodologies, though all companies counted toward 2024 target attainment had approved SBTi targets.
- DNB Livsforsikring set a portfolio-level WACI reduction target of 55% by 2030 versus a 2019 baseline, covering listed equities and corporate bonds (about 65% of total AUM).
- WACI methodology and data quality: 85% portfolio coverage; within that, 80% actual data and 20% estimates, resulting in 68% overall actual data and 32% estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2).
- DNB Livsforsikring target for science-based targets: 53% of AUM in listed shares and corporate bonds to have SBTs by 2030, based on a linear path to 100% by 2040; calculations are based entirely on actual data (coverage represents 62% of total AUM in the baseline year) (ESRS E1-4).
- Engagement strategy: DNB Livsforsikring will engage the 15 highest-emitting portfolio companies to encourage adoption of SBTs or net‑zero targets, prioritizing dialogues; DAM will conduct engagements and exercise ownership rights on DNB Livsforsikring’s behalf (ESRS E1-4).
- Real estate decarbonization: DNB Næringseiendom targets a 35% reduction in carbon intensity by 2030, covering 84% of the property portfolio, and benchmarks against CRREM 1.5°C pathways aligned with SBTi and IEA NZE2050 to enhance comparability.
- Baseline correction disclosure (ESRS 2 BP-2): The 2019 real estate baseline was corrected from 11.3 to 7.2 because Scope 3 emissions had been mistakenly included; the target covers Scope 1 and 2 using the location-based method.

nodes.title: DNB Livsforsikring: listed shares and corporate bonds, proportion of AUM with SBTs
nodes.heading: 3.2 DNB Livsforsikring: listed shares and corporate bonds, proportion of AUM with SBTs
nodes.start_phrase: DNB Livsforsikring has set a target that 53 per cent of the company’s AUM must have SBTs for emissions reduction by 2030.
nodes.summary:
- Alignment and methodology: The text references TCFD and SBTi, noting DAM’s approach to give credit to companies in sectors lacking SBTi-approved methods if they meet internal criteria; for 2024, all companies counted toward target attainment had approved SBTi targets.
- DNB Livsforsikring WACI target: A 55% reduction in weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) by 2030 versus 2019 for listed equities and corporate bonds, covering about 65% of total AUM. WACI methodology and data quality are detailed: 85% portfolio coverage (within which 80% is actual data and 20% estimates), with the remaining 15% imputed at the portfolio average; overall 68% actual data and 32% estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2).
- DNB Livsforsikring SBT coverage target: By 2030, 53% of AUM (shares and corporate bonds) to be invested in companies with science-based targets, following a linear path to 100% by 2040. For the baseline year, the covered AUM equals 62% of total AUM; calculations use only actual data (no estimates) (ESRS E1-4).
- Engagement with high emitters: Target to engage 15 highest-emitting portfolio companies to encourage adoption of SBTs or net-zero targets, prioritizing dialogues. Specialized external managers, including DAM, conduct engagements and exercise ownership rights on DNB Livsforsikring’s behalf (ESRS E1-4).
- DNB Næringseiendom real estate target: A 35% reduction in carbon intensity by 2030, covering 84% of the portfolio. The target was assessed against CRREM 1.5°C pathways, aligned with SBTi and IEA NZE2050, chosen for market comparability.
- Baseline correction (ESRS 2 BP-2): The 2019 carbon intensity baseline for the real estate portfolio was corrected from 11.3 (which mistakenly included Scope 3) to 7.2 (Scope 1 and 2 only), calculated using the location-based method.

nodes.title: DNB Livsforsikring: external asset managers with net-zero targets
nodes.heading: 3.3 DNB Livsforsikring: external asset managers with net-zero targets
nodes.start_phrase: DNB Livsforsikring has set a target of engaging 15 of the companies with the highest annual emissions in the portfolio, and encouraging them to set SBTs or net-zero targets.
nodes.summary:
- Context and frameworks: The section sits within ESRS E1 (Climate change) of DNB Group’s 2024 annual report and references TCFD, SBTi, CRREM and IEA NZE2050 frameworks. DAM’s approach can recognize credible transition efforts in sectors lacking SBTi methodologies; nevertheless, in 2024 all companies counted toward target attainment had approved SBTi targets.

- DNB Livsforsikring — WACI target and methodology:
  - Target: Reduce weighted average carbon intensity (WACI) of listed equities and corporate bonds by 55% by 2030 versus 2019, covering ~65% of total AUM.
  - Metric: WACI is portfolio-weighted carbon-to-revenue intensity (tCO2e per USD million revenue).
  - Data coverage and quality: 85% holding coverage; of that, 80% based on actual data and 20% estimates. Remaining 15% imputed using the average WACI of covered companies. Overall WACI is 68% actual data and 32% estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2).

- DNB Livsforsikring — AUM with SBTs target:
  - Target: 53% of AUM (shares and corporate bonds) to have science-based emissions reduction targets by 2030, following a linear path from end‑2022 baseline to 100% by 2040.
  - Scope: Targeted AUM equals 62% of total AUM in the baseline year.
  - Data basis: Calculations use only actual data, no estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2).

- DNB Livsforsikring — engagement with high emitters and role of external managers:
  - Targeted stewardship: Engage 15 highest‑emitting portfolio companies to encourage adoption of SBTs or net‑zero targets, prioritizing dialogues with high emitters.
  - Execution: A significant share of investments is run by specialized managers (including DAM), which will lead company dialogues and stewardship on DNB Livsforsikring’s behalf.

- DNB Næringseiendom — real estate climate target and baseline correction:
  - Target: Reduce property portfolio carbon intensity by 35% by 2030, covering 84% of the portfolio.
  - Alignment: Benchmarked against CRREM 1.5°C pathways, consistent with SBTi and IEA NZE2050, to ensure comparability and science-based alignment.
  - Baseline revision (ESRS 2 BP-2): 2019 baseline corrected from 11.3 (which mistakenly included Scope 3) to 7.2 to reflect Scope 1 and 2 only; target uses the location-based method. Note provided on the data basis for 2019 Scope 2 values (2%).

nodes.title: DNB Næringseiendom
nodes.heading: 3.4 DNB Næringseiendom
nodes.start_phrase: In 2022, DNB Næringseiendom set a target of reducing the carbon intensity in the property portfolio by 35 per cent by 2030.
nodes.summary:
- Describes DNB Asset Management’s approach to recognizing companies’ transition efforts in line with TCFD and SBTi, noting that in 2024 all companies counted toward target attainment had approved SBTi targets.
- Sets out DNB Livsforsikring’s portfolio targets:
  - WACI reduction of 55% by 2030 versus 2019 for listed equities and corporate bonds (about 65% of total AUM). Explains WACI methodology (tonnes CO2e per USD million revenue), 85% holdings coverage, with the remaining 15% estimated using portfolio averages; within the covered share, 80% is actual data and 20% estimates, resulting in 68% actual and 32% estimated overall (ESRS 2 BP-2).
  - Increase the proportion of AUM with science-based targets to 53% by 2030 on a linear path to 100% by 2040; target covers shares and corporate bonds representing 62% of total AUM at baseline; calculations use only actual data (no estimates) (ESRS E1-4).
  - Engagement goal to approach 15 highest-emitting portfolio companies to encourage adoption of SBTs or net‑zero targets; DAM conducts these stewardship dialogues on DNB Livsforsikring’s behalf, leveraging external specialized managers (ESRS E1-4).
- Details DNB Næringseiendom’s real estate decarbonization:
  - Target to reduce carbon intensity by 35% by 2030, covering 84% of the portfolio.
  - Alignment and assessment against the CRREM 1.5°C pathways, consistent with SBTi and IEA NZE2050, to enhance comparability across the market.
  - Correction to the 2019 baseline (ESRS 2 BP-2): previously reported 11.3 included Scope 3 by mistake; corrected to 7.2 for Scope 1 and 2 using a location-based method; note on limited Scope 2 data components for 2019.
- Cross-references to ESRS E1-4 on targets for climate change mitigation and adaptation throughout.

nodes.title: DNB Næringseiendom - Introduction
nodes.heading: 3.4 DNB Næringseiendom
nodes.start_phrase: In 2022, DNB Næringseiendom set a target of reducing the carbon intensity in the property portfolio by 35 per cent by 2030.
nodes.summary:
DNB Næringseiendom 
In 2022, DNB Næringseiendom set a target of reducing 
the carbon intensity in the property portfolio by 
35 per cent by 2030. The target covers 84 per cent of 
DNB Næringseiendom’s portfolio. When DNB prepared 
the transition plan, the existing target was assessed 
against the CRREM scenario, which was chosen because 
it provides science-based pathways adapted to 
1.5°C scenarios at land and property type level, which 
is in line with the SBTi and IEA NZE2050 scenarios. It 
also increased comparability, as CRREM is the standard 
scenario in the market, and is used by several financial 
institutions for their real estate portfolios.

nodes.title: ESRS 2 BP-2 Disclosures in relation to specific circumstances: Changes to the value for the baseline year 2019
nodes.heading: 3.4.1 ESRS 2 BP-2 Disclosures in relation to specific circumstances: Changes to the value for the baseline year 2019
nodes.start_phrase: Information was given in the transition plan that the baseline value for 2019 was 11.3 and covered Scope 1 and 2 emissions.
nodes.summary:
- The document details DNB Group’s climate-related targets, methodologies, and materiality assessments under ESRS E1, with specific focus on DNB Livsforsikring and DNB Næringseiendom.
- DNB Asset Management (DAM) uses an approach aligned with TCFD and SBTi to credit transition efforts even in sectors lacking SBTi methodologies; in 2024, all companies counted toward target attainment had approved SBTi targets.
- DNB Livsforsikring targets:
  - WACI reduction: 55% by 2030 from a 2019 baseline, covering listed shares and corporate bonds (~65% of total AUM). WACI measures portfolio exposure to carbon-intensive companies; 85% coverage, with 68% of overall WACI based on actual data and 32% on estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2).
  - Proportion of AUM with SBTs: 53% by 2030 on a linear path to 100% by 2040, covering shares and corporate bonds; baseline coverage represents 62% of total AUM and is calculated entirely from actual data (ESRS 2 BP-2).
  - Engagement: target to engage 15 highest-emitting portfolio companies to set SBTs or net-zero targets; DAM conducts dialogues and exercises ownership on DNB Livsforsikring’s behalf.
- DNB Næringseiendom (real estate):
  - Target to reduce portfolio carbon intensity by 35% by 2030 (84% portfolio coverage), benchmarked against the CRREM 1.5°C pathways aligned with SBTi and IEA NZE2050.
  - Baseline correction: 2019 intensity adjusted from 11.3 to 7.2 to properly reflect Scope 1 and 2 only; location-based calculation; 98% actual data for Scope 2 and no estimates for Scope 1 (ESRS 2 BP-2).
  - Despite current performance near CRREM, DNB retains the 2030 target (above CRREM pathway) due to COVID-19-related anomalies; additional intensity reduction targets set: 40% for 2030–2040 and a further 40% for 2040–2050.
  - Exclusions: partially owned/unmanaged assets, undeveloped properties, and the DNB ECP Invest fund; the fund has separate data collection, environmental reporting, and SFDR-aligned procedures.
- Own operations are part of the net-zero 2050 plan but are reported under ESRS E1-6; DNB’s most material climate impacts, risks, and opportunities are in the downstream value chain via financed emissions (loans and investments).
- Materiality and risk:
  - Climate change adaptation, mitigation, and energy are all material across short, medium, and long term.
  - DNB’s exposures span high-emitting sectors (e.g., oil and gas, shipping, commercial real estate) reflecting its Norwegian corporate loan portfolio and international investment exposure.
  - No quantified financial impact disclosed this year; portfolio stress testing, scenario analyses, and risk management are ongoing across DAM and DNB Livsforsikring.
  - Stakeholder expectations reinforce the materiality of climate risk and the need for robust management and disclosure.

nodes.title: Own operations
nodes.heading: 3.5 Own operations
nodes.start_phrase: Own operations are important in order to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, and are included in DNB’s transition plan.
nodes.summary:
- Data quality and methodology: 98% of emissions data are based on actual measurements; no estimated values are used for Scope 1 emissions (ESRS 2 BP-2).
- Climate targets for real estate (ESRS E1-4): DNB Næringseiendom retains its 2030 emissions-intensity target set in 2022, even though it is above the updated CRREM pathway, citing Covid-19-related distortions in recent intensity trends. Longer-term targets are a 40% reduction in emissions intensity from 2030–2040 and an additional 40% reduction from 2040–2050.
- Scope and exclusions: Portions of the portfolio that are partly owned, not directly managed, undeveloped, or held in the DNB ECP Invest fund are excluded from the main target tracking. DNB ECP Invest follows separate procedures, collects environmental data against defined metrics, publishes a dedicated environmental report, and reports under the EU SFDR.
- Own operations and net zero: Own operations are part of DNB’s 2050 net-zero transition plan but, under CSRD principles, are only covered in greenhouse gas accounting (ESRS E1-6) since material impacts, risks, and opportunities are assessed as primarily downstream. References are made to the double materiality process (ESRS 1 IRO-1).
- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities (ESRS 2 SBM-3): Given DNB’s broad exposure—particularly to high-emitting sectors like oil and gas, shipping, and commercial real estate—material impacts and risks span climate change adaptation, mitigation, and energy. The primary negative impacts and risks arise in the downstream value chain via financed emissions from loans and investments, including international exposures.
- Time horizons and financial assessment: Climate-related impacts, risks, and opportunities are considered equally relevant in the short, medium, and long term. While no quantitative financial effect analysis was completed this year, DNB assesses portfolio effects through stress tests, scenario analyses, and ongoing risk management, including annual scenario analyses for DAM and DNB Livsforsikring.
- Stakeholder expectations: The materiality of climate change has been reinforced by clear stakeholder expectations for DNB to assess and manage climate-related risks.

nodes.title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 3.6 Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: DNB offers a wide range of products and services to personal and corporate customers.
nodes.summary:
- Data quality and scope: 98% of emissions figures are based on actual data; no estimated values for Scope 1 emissions (ESRS 2 BP-2).
- Climate targets (ESRS E1-4): DNB Næringseiendom retains its 2030 emissions-intensity target set in 2022, acknowledging it is above the updated CRREM pathway due to Covid-19 distortions; further targets set for 2030–2040 (-40%) and 2040–2050 (-40% additional).
- Portfolio coverage: Properties partly owned, not directly managed, undeveloped, and those in DNB ECP Invest are excluded from the main target; DNB ECP Invest follows separate procedures, gathers environmental data on defined metrics, reports under SFDR, and assesses progress against targets.
- Own operations: Included in the net-zero 2050 transition plan but, per CSRD, reported for GHG accounting under ESRS E1-6; material impacts, risks, and opportunities primarily lie in the downstream value chain.
- Materiality and strategy (ESRS 2 SBM-3, ESRS 2 IRO-1): DNB’s lending and investment exposures span high-emitting sectors (oil and gas, shipping, commercial real estate) domestically and internationally; financed emissions are the most material negative impact. Adaptation, mitigation, and energy are material across short, medium, and long term. Stakeholder expectations elevate climate materiality. Financial effects are not yet quantified; risk is assessed via stress tests, scenario analyses, and portfolio risk management.
- Risk and opportunity detail:
  - Adaptation: Physical risks to financed companies and real estate could impair borrowers’ capacity; customer insurance mitigates some real estate risk.
  - Mitigation: Transition risk is most material; reputational risk exists. DNB prioritizes engagement and financing real-economy decarbonization over exiting high-emission sectors; opportunities to fund renewable and clean technologies.
  - Energy: Positive impact and opportunities in financing renewables, energy efficiency, and advisory; regulatory risk from the EU EPBD may raise customer costs and affect property valuations, potentially weakening debt-servicing capacity in mortgage and CRE portfolios.
- Transition plan: Tool to reduce environmental impact and financial risk from GHG emissions; integrates climate considerations into strategy, processes, customer selection, and engagement, potentially reshaping future activities.
- Scenario analysis of the loan portfolio: Ongoing climate-credit risk analyses across time horizons; prior pilots with UNEP FI’s Transition Check and 2° Investing Initiative’s PACTA revealed data/coverage limits; DNB is developing an internal climate stress-testing tool and expects continuous improvements in data and scenarios.

nodes.title: Scenario analysis of the loan portfolio
nodes.heading: 3.7 Scenario analysis of the loan portfolio
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the general risk assessment, DNB performs analyses of how climate risk can cause credit loss for the bank using different scenarios for the short, medium and long term.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: ESRS E1 Climate change. Identifies impacts, risks and opportunities across climate change adaptation, climate change mitigation, and energy for DNB Group.
- Adaptation: Physical climate risks to financed companies and DNB’s real estate collateral can impair customers’ debt-servicing capacity and increase credit risk; customer insurance mitigates some financial risk.
- Mitigation: Indirect negative impact via financed emissions. Transition risk is most material (costs from regulation/resource scarcity) and reputational risk exists for high-emitting sectors. Strategy is to engage and finance real-world decarbonisation rather than exit, with clear expectations for customers; significant business opportunities in financing the energy transition.
- Energy: Positive impact and financial opportunities in renewable energy, energy efficiency and advisory services. Regulatory risk from the EU Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) may raise customer costs and affect property valuations, potentially weakening debt-servicing capacity.
- Transition plan: Tool to reduce environmental impact and financial risk from emissions by embedding climate considerations into strategy, customer selection and engagement, and broader processes, potentially reshaping future activities.
- Loan portfolio scenario analysis: Development of an in-house, flexible stress-testing tool aligned with evolving regulation and data. 2024 analysis to 2040 using NGFS Net Zero 2050, Delayed Transition and Current Policies scenarios. Assessed carbon price pass-through and abatement investment needs with sector/region differentiation. Excluded agriculture (data scarcity) and commercial real estate (assessed separately for EPBD risk). Did not include physical risk, collateral effects, broad demand shifts, or dynamic portfolio changes (static balance). Inputs from company-level emissions/financials, Statistics Norway carbon prices, and Norwegian Environment Agency abatement costs; high uncertainty acknowledged.
- Key findings: Overall limited transition-risk impact across analysed portfolios; higher potential impacts in maritime sectors (shipping/offshore) due to high Scope 1–2 emissions, prospective ETS costs, and uncertain cost pass-through. Significant uncertainty in assumptions and data quality; analyses guide prioritisation of data improvements and sector focus to mitigate climate-related credit loss risk. Confirms materiality of customer emissions to DNB’s business model.
- Risk management: Climate risks addressed through credit assessments and sectoral targets within the transition plan.
- DNB Asset Management (DAM): Regular long-term (to 2050) scenario analyses (Jan 2025) covering transition risk (NGFS: Net Zero 2050, Delayed Transition, Current Policies) and physical risk (IPCC RCP 2.6/4.5/8.5). Outcomes: Net Zero—higher transition risk for carbon-intensive, opportunities in clean tech; Delayed—elevated post-2030 transition risk; Current Policies—limited transition but severe physical risk. Insights inform engagement, risk processes and investment decisions.
- DNB Livsforsikring: Largest climate risk via investment portfolio. Uses emissions intensity metrics and MSCI Climate Value-at-Risk based on NGFS scenarios, with a primary Net Zero 2050 pathway aligned to 2050 net-zero target. Scenario features early stringent policies, high carbon prices, growing role for carbon removal/storage; high transition risk and relatively low physical risk over the long term.

nodes.title: Climate risk in DNB Asset Management (DAM)
nodes.heading: 3.8 Climate risk in DNB Asset Management (DAM)
nodes.start_phrase: In order to assess the climate risk in its investment portfolio, DAM conducts regular scenario analyses, with the most recent being conducted in January 2025.
nodes.summary:
- Highlights variability in transition costs and quota obligations for sectors like shipping (differences inside vs. outside the EU) and notes wide investment cost differences across companies, complicating emissions coverage assessments.
- Emphasizes data quality gaps and uncertainty in assumptions, limiting precise conclusions but helping identify sectors most exposed to climate risk and priorities for improving data and methodologies.
- Confirms that customers’ greenhouse gas emissions are material to DNB’s business model, aligning with the Group’s materiality analysis.
- States that DNB manages and reduces climate-related credit risk through credit assessments and sector targets in its transition plan.
- Describes DNB Asset Management’s 2025 long-term (to 2050) scenario analyses covering transition and physical risks:
  - Uses NGFS scenarios (Net Zero 2050, Delayed Transition, Current Policies) for transition risk and IPCC RCPs 2.6, 4.5, 8.5 for physical risk.
  - Finds Net Zero 2050 creates higher transition risk for carbon-intensive sectors but opportunities in clean tech; Delayed Transition heightens transition risk post-2030 due to abrupt policy shifts; Current Policies reduces transition risk but raises severe physical risks.
  - Notes increasing physical risk from extreme weather and sea-level rise under higher-warming pathways; insights guide client dialogue, risk processes, and investment decisions.
- Details DNB Livsforsikring’s climate risk:
  - Main exposure is through its investment portfolio, facing both transition and physical risks.
  - Tracks emissions intensity for equities, bonds, and real estate but supplements with forward-looking scenario analysis.
  - Applies MSCI Climate Value-at-Risk (CVaR), based on NGFS scenarios, over a long-term horizon.
  - Main scenario aligns with Net Zero 2050: early stringent climate policy, high carbon prices, growing roles for carbon removal and storage; implies relatively low physical risk but high transition risk.

nodes.title: Climate risk in DNB Livsforsikring
nodes.heading: 3.9 Climate risk in DNB Livsforsikring
nodes.start_phrase: The investment portfolio is assessed as being DNB Livsforsikring’s largest exposure to climate risk, and leads to DNB Livsforsikring being exposed to both transition risk and physical climate risk.
nodes.summary:
- Variability in shipping sector costs and emissions coverage due to differing EU/non-EU quota obligations, with investment costs differing across companies.
- Data quality limitations and uncertain assumptions hinder precise conclusions on climate risk impacts for DNB; scenario analyses are exploratory, indicating sectoral exposures and guiding data and assumption improvements to reduce climate-related credit losses.
- DNB manages climate risk through credit assessments and sector-specific targets in its transition plan, aligning with the Group’s materiality assessment.
- DNB Asset Management (DAM) conducts long-term (to 2050) scenario analyses using NGFS transition scenarios (Net Zero 2050, Delayed Transition, Current Policies) and IPCC RCPs (2.6, 4.5, 8.5) for physical risk:
  - Net Zero 2050: higher transition risk for carbon-intensive sectors, opportunities in clean tech.
  - Delayed Transition: elevated transition risk from post-2030 policy shocks.
  - Current Policies: lower transition risk but high physical risk from unchecked warming.
  - Insights inform client dialogue, risk processes, and investment decisions.
- DNB Livsforsikring’s primary climate risk arises from its investment portfolio; it applies MSCI Climate VaR (CVaR) based on NGFS scenarios to quantify long-term transition (policy, technology) and physical risks:
  - Model coverage: listed equities, corporate and government bonds; excludes alternatives, real estate, and municipal bonds due to data gaps.
  - 2024 model updates (notably coastal flooding) improved data quality and reduced estimated physical risk.
  - CVaR is negative across portfolios; for defined-contribution pensions, physical risk moved from -7.60% in 2023 (coastal flooding -3.81%, extreme heat -4.31%) to -0.9% in 2024 (extreme heat -0.5%, coastal flooding -0.3%).
  - Physical risk is less material for liquid Norwegian-focused equities/bonds, more material for commercial real estate.
  - Defined-contribution portfolio shows greater potential loss than the common/corporate portfolio due to sector mix and higher equity exposure.
  - Oil and gas exposure declined: defined-contribution from 14.8% (2023) to 12.5% (2024); common/corporate from 3.2% to 2.1%.
  - Paris alignment: ~21% (common/corporate) and 20.8% (defined-contribution) aligned with 1.5°C targets; under <2°C, alignment rises to 48% and 47% respectively.
  - Acknowledged uncertainties (e.g., impacts of extreme weather like Storm Hans) and model scope gaps; CVaR remains a useful long-horizon tool that does not affect short-term market risk metrics.
- Introduction to governance of impacts, risks, and opportunities under ESRS E1, including policies for climate change mitigation and adaptation (ESRS E1-2/ESRS 2 MDR-P).

nodes.title: Managing impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 3.10 Managing impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: How DNB will manage the material impacts, risks and opportunities associated with climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation and energy is set out in the Group’s sustainability policy.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and coverage: The MSCI CVaR model currently assesses bonds and listed equities, now including government bonds. It excludes alternative investments, real estate, and municipal bonds due to data quality constraints, so it does not capture DNB Livsforsikring’s full portfolio.
- Risk types: The model quantifies transition risk (policy/carbon cost and technology/green revenue exposure) and physical risk (losses from extreme weather at the 95th percentile under the most probable pathway to 2100).
- 2024 methodology update: Major enhancements to the physical risk module—especially coastal flooding—improved data quality and reduced estimated physical risk; extreme heat impacts were also revised down.
- Portfolio results: All portfolios exhibit negative CVaR (potential loss). Year-over-year changes from 2023 to 2024 are chiefly driven by the physical risk recalibration. Defined-contribution (DC) pensions show the largest loss due to higher climate-exposed sector weights and the shares/bonds mix.
- Key figures: In 2023, DC physical risk CVaR was -7.60% (coastal flooding -3.81%, extreme heat -4.31%). In 2024, DC physical risk fell to -0.9% (extreme heat -0.5%, coastal flooding -0.3%), minimally affecting overall CVaR. Oil & gas exposure declined: DC from 14.8% (2023) to 12.5% (2024); common/corporate from 3.2% to 2.1%.
- Materiality by asset class: Physical climate risk is less material for Norwegian liquid shares and bonds, but more material for the commercial real estate portfolio.
- Paris alignment: Using “implicit temperature increase,” about 21% of the common/corporate portfolio and 20.8% of DC are aligned with Paris targets in 2024; if warming is kept below 2°C, alignment would rise to 48% and 47% respectively.
- Limitations and uncertainty: Model gaps (alternatives, real estate, municipal bonds) and inherent uncertainty in climate/financial outcomes remain. Storm Hans (2023) causing ~NOK 2 billion in damage illustrates domestic exposure, with more frequent/severe events expected.
- Usefulness and horizon: Despite limitations, the MSCI CVaR model is a useful, long-horizon indicator for sectoral risk in the transition to a low-emission economy and does not influence short-term market risk metrics.
- Next section preview: Introduction to “Managing impacts, risks and opportunities,” including ESRS E1-2 policies on climate change mitigation and adaptation within DNB’s governing documents.

nodes.title: Governing documents
nodes.heading: 3.10.1 Governing documents
nodes.start_phrase: How DNB will manage the material impacts, risks and opportunities associated with climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation and energy is set out in the Group’s sustainability policy.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and limitations of MSCI’s CVaR model: currently covers bonds and listed shares; excludes alternative investments, real estate, and municipal bonds due to data quality constraints; newly includes government bonds.
- Risk coverage: quantifies transition risk (policy costs related to emissions and technology risk via green revenue share) and physical risk (asset losses from extreme weather at the 95th percentile), assuming an average pathway to 2100.
- Scenario analysis results: CVaR is negative across all portfolios. 2024 model updates, especially for coastal flooding and extreme heat, reduced estimated physical risk. For defined-contribution pensions, physical risk CVaR fell from -7.60% in 2023 (coastal flooding -3.81%, extreme heat -4.31%) to -0.9% in 2024 (extreme heat -0.5%, coastal flooding -0.3%), with minimal effect on overall CVaR.
- Materiality by asset class: physical climate risk seen as less material for liquid shares and bonds given high Norwegian exposure; more significant for commercial real estate.
- Portfolio sensitivities: defined-contribution pension portfolio shows the largest loss in value versus the common and corporate portfolio, driven by sector exposures and equity/bond mix. Oil and gas exposure declined in 2024 (DC: 12.5% from 14.8%; common/corporate: 2.1% from 3.2%).
- Paris alignment: uses “implicit temperature increase.” In 2024, about 21% of the common and corporate portfolio and 20.8% of defined-contribution pensions align with Paris targets; if global warming stays below 2°C, alignment would rise to 48% and 47%, respectively.
- Model caveats and uncertainty: exclusions limit completeness; future climate and financial impacts remain uncertain. Storm Hans (2023) caused ~NOK 2 billion in damages, evidencing exposure. Despite limitations, the model helps identify sectoral transition risks and informs long-term risk, without affecting short-term market risk.
- Governance and policy framework (ESRS E1-2): DNB Group sustainability policy commits to net-zero by 2050 across lending, investments, and operations; measuring, reporting, and managing climate risk; and enabling the transition via financing. Climate and environment are integrated across all activities. Policy applies Group-wide; CFO leads strategy and operations; Group EVPs ensure implementation; CEO reports metrics to the Board. Alignment with UN SDGs, UNGPs, OECD Guidelines, and UN Global Compact. Policy developed with internal expertise and stakeholder input (double materiality), publicly available, and operationalized through Group instructions for credit sustainability and responsible investments (expectations, exclusions, and formalized risk assessments). Group Risk Management holds ultimate responsibility; industry guidelines and continuous stakeholder dialogue support implementation.
- Actions and resources (ESRS E1-3): DNB has implemented a transition plan and other measures to mitigate climate change and reduce indirect impacts through financed companies, with a financial target to contribute to the sustainable transition. The Group supports customers’ transition through financing and advisory, including renewable energy and energy efficiency investments.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 3.10.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: In the last few years, DNB has worked to put in place measures and resources to mitigate climate change and the indirect negative effect the Group has on the climate through the companies it finances, in addition to meeting the purposes and goals of the Group’s sustainability policy.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines DNB Group’s sustainability policy focus on climate and environment, including integrating these considerations into all activities (product and service development, advisory, sales, credit and investment decisions, procurement, production, and operations).
- Sets strategic climate objectives: net-zero emissions by 2050 across lending and investment portfolios and own operations; ability to measure, report and manage climate risk; and acting as a financier/facilitator of the sustainable transition.
- Commits to reducing indirect environmental impacts in roles as owner, investor, lender and purchaser.
- Defines scope and governance: policy applies to all DNB Group entities and employees globally; approved by Group Management; CFO oversees strategy and operations; Group EVPs ensure implementation; CEO reports climate metrics to the Board.
- Aligns with international frameworks: UN SDGs, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises, and UN Global Compact principles.
- Describes policy development: internal expert involvement, management consultation, stakeholder expectations reflected via double materiality analysis; policy available internally and publicly on dnb.no.
- Operationalisation through Group instructions for sustainability in credit activities and responsible investments, including:
  - Expectations of investee/borrower alignment with international conventions and guidelines.
  - Defined excluded activities and formalised sustainability risk assessments before credit and investment decisions.
  - Clear roles, responsibilities, processes, and applicability across all geographies; Group Risk Management holds ultimate responsibility; sector guidelines derived from these instructions.
- Details actions and resources under ESRS E1-3: DNB’s transition plan to mitigate climate change, reduce financed emissions, manage climate risk, and meet a financial target to support the transition.
- Emphasises client enablement: financing and advisory for renewable energy and energy efficiency; reliance on clients’ willingness and capacity to transition.
- Integrates ESG risk assessments into credit processes, influencing customer selection, capital allocation and lending decisions; assessments include emissions reporting, credible transition strategies and decarbonisation targets.
- Strengthens internal capabilities: ESG training via DNB University; targeted upskilling for customer-facing roles; ESG certification introduced in 2023 and made mandatory in 2024 for corporate market-facing staff, with annual updates.
- Notes external dependencies and uncertainties: evolving regulations, methodologies, scenarios and technology timelines may affect progress toward targets.
- Presents sector-specific measures to meet portfolio targets:
  - Mortgages: green mortgage and fixed-rate products with price incentives for EPC A/B homes; renovation loans; exploration of new financing models and partnerships aligned with public support schemes; enhanced customer guidance and internal competence; dialogue with industry and authorities on standards.
  - Housing cooperatives: green financing for highly energy-efficient buildings, sustainable renovations and energy efficiency measures; advisory on public incentives and support schemes.

nodes.title: Actions - Introduction
nodes.heading: 3.10.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: In the last few years, DNB has worked to put in place measures and resources to mitigate climate change and the indirect negative effect the Group has on the climate through the companies it finances, in addition to meeting the purposes and goals of the Group’s sustainability policy.
nodes.summary: Overview of DNB’s climate actions and resources under ESRS E1, highlighting implementation of a Group transition plan aimed at reducing negative climate impact and climate risk while setting a financial target to contribute to the sustainable transition. DNB supports customer transition through financing and advisory, e.g., renewable energy and energy efficiency, with a table (below) describing measures linked to each loan and investment portfolio target. ESG risk assessments are integrated into credit decision-making based on thresholds for company size and commitment, evaluating borrowers’ sustainability risks, emissions reporting, credible transition strategies, and decarbonisation targets to guide customer selection, capital allocation, and credit decisions. The section also details employee capability building via ESG training at DNB University, targeted training for customer-facing roles, a 2023 ESG certification made mandatory in 2024 for corporate-market staff and relevant partners, with annual updates. It notes evolving regulation, guidance, methodologies, scenarios, technology, and other external factors may affect plans and progress, with further detail under Transition plan (ESRS E1-1).

nodes.title: Overview of measures associated with each target for the loan and investment portfolio that has been set in the target portfolio transition plan
nodes.heading: 3.10.2.1 Overview of measures associated with each target for the loan and investment portfolio that has been set in the target portfolio transition plan
nodes.start_phrase: In order to reach the target, DNB will actively support and encourage customers to improve the energy efficiency of their homes.
nodes.summary:
- Embedding ESG and climate considerations in lending and investment decisions: DNB conducts ESG risk assessments in credit processes based on company size/commitment thresholds, evaluating emissions reporting, credible transition strategies and decarbonisation targets to inform customer selection, capital allocation and credit approvals.
- Employee capability building: Group-wide ESG training via DNBU, targeted advanced training for customer-facing roles, and a mandatory ESG certification (from 2024) for all corporate market employees and relevant partners, with annual updates, to better integrate climate/sustainability into daily work and advisory/product development.
- Evolving external context: Recognition that changing regulation, guidance, methodologies, scenarios and technology timelines can affect measures, plans and target attainment (linked to the Transition plan under ESRS E1-1).
- Sector- and portfolio-specific transition measures and financing levers:
  - Mortgages: Green mortgage products and renovation loans with EPC-based incentives; customer guidance; collaboration with industry and authorities on standards; explore new financing models and public-scheme integration.
  - Housing cooperatives: Dialogue, green financing for energy-efficient buildings and renovations; advice on public support schemes.
  - Commercial real estate: Market, regulatory and technology drivers push energy upgrades; green and sustainability-linked loans; stronger advisory and energy focus in credit assessments; potential exclusion where no improvement plans; rising competition for low-emission assets.
  - Shipping: Emissions/efficiency assessment (incl. AER); integrated ESG/transition risk; sustainable/transition financing; support for best-available tech, flexible fuels and energy-saving retrofits.
  - Motor vehicles: Grow zero-emission vehicle share; align partners with net-zero; develop green products (e.g., Autolease Greenlease) to transition fleets.
  - Steel: Back transition leaders exceeding minimums; support innovations like hydrogen-based reduction.
  - Oil and gas: Reduce committed lending via dynamic portfolio adjustments; continue selective upstream financing while supporting operational emissions cuts and investments in renewables/clean tech.
  - Power generation: Prioritise financing renewables and grid/district heating; limited financing of gas backup (preferably with CCS) for system stability.
  - Salmon farming: Finance lower-emission technologies across traditional and emerging farming models; use sustainable financing to reduce financed emissions.
  - DNB Asset Management (listed equity/credit): Active ownership (dialogue, voting), ESG integration in active funds, forward-looking climate risk, thematic expectations for credible decarbonisation, climate-themed products, and climate expertise development.
  - DNB Livsforsikring (listed equity/credit, external managers): Active ownership via managers targeting high emitters; encourage managers’ net-zero targets; capital allocation to sustainable alternatives; Green Transition pension profile; exclusions for non-transitioning companies.
  - DNB Næringseiendom: Cut energy-related operational emissions via upgrades; invest to improve environmental standards though full CRREM alignment by 2030 may be challenging.
- Implementation horizon and resources: Measures are ongoing through 2030; require human/tech resources, new tools/systems, continuous monitoring/reporting, advanced analytics/models and external collaboration; costs not deemed significant.
- Emissions impact and use of credits: DNB cannot directly quantify achieved/expected GHG reductions due to indirect Scope 3 nature and limited control; focuses on enabling client emissions reductions; avoids near-term carbon credits but may consider them for long-term residual emissions.
- Metrics and targets (ESRS E1-4): DNB has Scope 1, 2 and 3 climate targets set with employee involvement and aligned with state ownership expectations; Scope 3 targets use exposure data (Dec 2024; shipping Dec 2023). Even without 2030 targets in some sectors (power generation, salmon farming), progress against baselines will be reported.

nodes.title: Achieved and expected reduction
nodes.heading: 3.10.3 Achieved and expected reduction
nodes.start_phrase: The measures that DNB carries out cannot be measured as a direct reduction of greenhouse gases, and DNB therefore cannot calculate expected or achieved reduction.
nodes.summary:
- The climate measures outlined are ongoing without fixed end dates and are intended to continue through the 2030 target year.
- Implementation requires human and technological resources, including new tools and systems, continuous monitoring and reporting, advanced analyses and models, and collaboration with external experts; these costs are not considered significant.
- DNB cannot directly quantify expected or achieved GHG reductions from its measures because emissions largely occur indirectly in its value chain (financed emissions), limiting direct control; instead, it aims to enable customers’ emissions reductions over time.
- To reach net-zero, DNB and its customers must accelerate emissions cuts; the Group intends not to use carbon credits in the short term but may consider them for hard-to-abate residual emissions in the long term.
- Under ESRS E1-4, DNB has set Scope 1, 2, and 3 targets for climate mitigation and adaptation, developed with employee involvement and aligned with expectations from its largest owner, the Norwegian government.
- Scope 3 sector targets are based on exposure data as of 31 December 2024 (shipping uses December 2023 data); associated expected reductions and key measures are described under ESRS E1-3.
- For power generation and salmon farming, no 2030 targets are set, but progress will be reported against the baseline per DNB’s transition plan (ESRS E1-1).

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 3.11 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: DNB has set Scope 1, 2 and 3 targets for the mitigation of and adaptation to climate change.
nodes.summary:
- The climate measures are ongoing with no fixed end date and are intended to run through 2030, aligned with target timelines.
- Execution requires human and technological resources, including new tools, systems, continuous monitoring/reporting, advanced analytics and models, and collaboration with external experts; these costs are not deemed significant.
- DNB cannot directly quantify expected or achieved GHG reductions because impacts occur through financed activities (Scope 3) outside its direct control; it aims to enable client emissions reductions, accelerate progress toward net zero, avoid short-term use of carbon credits, and consider credits only for hard-to-abate residual emissions in the long term.
- Under ESRS E1-4, DNB has set climate mitigation and adaptation targets for Scopes 1, 2, and 3, with employee involvement and oversight expectations from the Norwegian government as majority owner; methodology is referenced under ESRS E1-1.
- Scope 3 sector targets are based on exposure data as of 31 December 2024 (shipping uses December 2023 data); expected reductions and key measures are detailed under ESRS E1-3. Power generation and salmon farming lack 2030 targets but are tracked against a baseline.

nodes.title: Targets and tracking
nodes.heading: 3.11.1 Targets and tracking
nodes.start_phrase: DNB has set Scope 1, 2 and 3 targets for the mitigation of and adaptation to climate change.
nodes.summary:
- Long-term climate measures: Actions have no fixed end date and are intended to run through 2030.
- Resourcing: Delivery requires human and technological resources (new tools/systems, continuous monitoring/reporting, advanced analytics/models, and cooperation with external experts), with costs not deemed significant.
- Emissions impact and carbon credits: DNB cannot quantify direct or expected GHG reductions due to indirect value-chain emissions; focus is on enabling client decarbonisation. Preference is to avoid carbon credits in the short term, reserving them for hard-to-abate residual emissions over the long term.
- Metrics and targets (ESRS E1-4): Scope 1, 2, and 3 targets set for mitigation/adaptation; employees involved; expectations from the Norwegian government as main owner. Sector portfolio targets use recognised pathways (CRREM, Poseidon Principles v4.2, SBTi SDA B2DS, IEA NZE2050, NGFS NZ2050).
- Sector targets and 2024 status: 
  - Mortgages, housing cooperatives, commercial real estate: intensity-reduction targets; 2024 intensities improved from 2019 baselines.
  - Shipping: aligned to Poseidon Principles; 2023 AER increased due to LNG market dynamics; otherwise continued intensity reductions across most vessel types.
  - Motor vehicles: significant intensity reduction vs 2019.
  - Steel: intensity higher than 2019 baseline.
  - Oil & gas: committed lending reduced by 21% from 2019; exposures remain dynamic.
  - Power generation and salmon farming: baseline reporting without 2030 targets; power generation intensity further reduced from already low baseline.
  - Asset management and life insurance: targets for share of AUM with SBTs and portfolio-wide WACI reductions; progress reported.
  - DNB Næringseiendom: building intensity target on CRREM pathway.
  - Sustainable finance: NOK 1,500bn mobilisation target (2020 baseline) and NOK 200bn in sustainability-profile funds by 2025; progress reported.
- Reporting approach: Emphasis on emissions intensity rather than absolute emissions, consistent with ESRS phase-in for financials; absolute 2030 figures not reported. Sectoral Scope 1/2/3 splits and quantitative contributions to overall reductions are not calculated due to lack of concrete net-zero pathways per sector. Data based on exposures as of 31 Dec 2024 (shipping 2023); PCAF data quality scores and share of estimated vs actual data disclosed.
- External validation: DNV validated that most 2030 targets are science-based and consistent with 1.5°C pathways, including scenario choices, baselines, and methodologies (see Transition plan ESRS E1-1).
- Annual developments: Brief status for each target/portfolio provided, highlighting intensity movements, market drivers (e.g., LNG in shipping), and data quality.

nodes.title: Description of developments during the year for each target
nodes.heading: 3.11.2 Description of developments during the year for each target
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, the emissions intensity was 3.03 kg CO2e/m²/year for the entire home mortgage portfolio, which is somewhat down from the baseline year 2019 (3.69 kg CO2e/m²/year), and down from 2023 (3.75 kg CO2e/m²/year).
nodes.summary:
- Reporting approach and methodology
  - Transition plan targets are intensity-based; absolute 2030 figures are not reported due to ESRS E1 value-chain reporting phase-in under CSRD.
  - DNB prioritised emissions-intensity data over absolute values and has not broken down Scope 1, 2, 3 shares per sector or quantified sectoral contributions to portfolio targets, as no sector-specific net-zero pathways are set yet.
  - Methods, pathways, and assumptions are referenced under Transition plan (ESRS E1-1).

- External validation
  - DNV validated the 2030 targets, concluding most are science-based and consistent with the Paris Agreement/1.5°C, including scenario choices, baseline years, and emissions estimation methodology.

- Portfolio progress and key 2024/2023 metrics (intensity unless noted; ESRS 2 BP-2; PCAF data quality in parentheses)
  - Mortgages: 3.03 kg CO2e/m²/year in 2024 (vs 3.69 in 2019; 3.75 in 2023); 100% estimates; PCAF 3.2.
  - Housing cooperatives: 2.78 kg CO2e/m²/year in 2024 (vs 3.65 in 2019); 100% estimates; PCAF 3.6.
  - Commercial real estate: 2.97 kg CO2e/m²/year in 2024 (vs 3.68 in 2019); 100% estimates; PCAF 3.9.
  - Shipping: 2023 loan-weighted AER up 3.2%; 100% actual; PCAF 1.0. Increase driven by high LNG activity amid tight energy markets; most other vessel types improved.
  - Motor vehicles: 56 g CO2e/km in 2024 (37.1% below 2019); 100% estimates; PCAF 3.9.
  - Steel: 0.87 t CO2e/t steel in 2023, higher than 2019 baseline 0.22; 100% actual; PCAF 1.0.
  - Oil and gas: committed lending down 21% vs 2019; exposure remains dynamic due to market factors.
  - Power generation: 2019 baseline 29.3 kg CO2e/MWh; no reduction target set due to low baseline. 2024 intensity 14.1 kg CO2e/MWh; 27% estimates/73% actual; PCAF 2.8.
  - Salmon farming: Scope 1–3 intensity rose from 4.59 kg CO2e/kg HOG (2019) to 9.96 (2023); 100% actual; PCAF 1.7.
  - DNB Asset Management (listed equity and corporate bonds): share of portfolio companies with SBTs increased from 30% (2023) to 36.5% (2024); 70 engagement dialogues with top 25 emitters to drive SBT adoption toward the 2030 target (58% AUM with SBTs).
  - DNB Livsforsikring (listed equity and corporate bonds, WACI): carbon intensity at end-2024 reflects a 46% reduction since 2019 and a 3% decrease vs 2023; drivers include portfolio allocation and sector mix changes; 96% actual/4% estimates. SBT coverage rose to 23% in 2024 (behind the 53% by 2030 target but improving faster than the MSCI World).
  - DNB Næringseiendom: 4.11 kg CO2e/m² in 2024 (vs 7.2 in 2019); reductions from operations, projects, and asset sales; Scope 2 is 98% actual; no Scope 1 estimation.

- Sustainable finance mobilisation
  - Target to mobilise NOK 1,500 billion by 2030 through lending and facilitation for the sustainable transition; products and inclusion criteria are defined within the transition plan framework.

nodes.title: Mobilise NOK 1 500 billion to the sustainable transition, through lending and facilitation, by 2030
nodes.heading: 3.11.3 Mobilise NOK 1 500 billion to the sustainable transition, through lending and facilitation, by 2030
nodes.start_phrase: The target to mobilise NOK 1 500 billion to the sustainable transition, through lending and facilitation, is included in DNB’s transition plan.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from DNB Group’s 2024 Annual Report (Sustainability report, ESRS E1 Climate change) covering portfolio emissions, target progress, sustainable finance mobilization, sustainable products, and GHG accounting.
- Salmon farming portfolio: Average Scope 1–3 emissions intensity rose from 4.59 to 9.96 kg CO2e/kg HOG (2019–2023); 100% actual data (ESRS 2 BP-2); PCAF score 1.7.
- DNB Asset Management (listed shares and corporate bonds): Companies with science-based targets (SBTs) increased from 30% (end-2023) to 36.5% (end-2024), progressing toward 58% AUM with SBTs by 2030. Conducted 70 engagement dialogues in 2024 with top 25 emitters to drive realistic SBTs aligned with DAM’s transition plan.
- DNB Livsforsikring (listed shares and corporate bonds, WACI): Carbon intensity at 58.1 at end-2024, down 3% from 2023 and 46% since 2019, on track for 55% reduction by 2030. Decline driven by allocations and sector mix shifts favoring lower-emission sectors. Data quality: 96% actual, 4% estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2).
- DNB Livsforsikring SBT coverage: 23% of portfolio companies had SBTs at end-2024 (up from 15% in 2022 and 18% in 2023); slightly behind the 53% AUM-by-2030 target but improving faster than the MSCI World.
- DNB Næringseiendom: Portfolio carbon intensity reduced to 4.11 kg CO2e/m2 in 2024 from 7.2 in 2019, driven by operations, projects, and asset sales; Scope 2 data 98% actual, no estimation for Scope 1 (ESRS 2 BP-2).
- Sustainable finance mobilization: Target to mobilize NOK 1,500 billion by 2030 via lending and facilitation. Detailed inclusion criteria across:
  - Bonds (green/social/sustainability; sustainability-linked; unlabeled renewables),
  - Advisory (debt; equity and M&A for renewables-related),
  - Loans (green loans; sustainability-linked loans; unlabeled renewables),
  - Guarantees (green),
  - Environmentally friendly transport (zero-emission vehicles; excludes fossil-fuel transport).
  In 2024, NOK 190 billion mobilized; cumulative NOK 751.8 billion since 2020. Growth led by green loans (real estate, renewables), plus increases in SLLs, EV financing, and sustainable bonds.
- Mutual funds and portfolios with a sustainability profile (DAM): Strategic aim for NOK 200 billion AUM by 2025 and 50% of net flows to such products. Approaches include climate criteria, exclusions, broader E/S focus, SDG alignment; includes SFDR Articles 8 and 9. 2024 saw new launches and reclassifications, supporting AUM growth to NOK 137.8 billion (from NOK 124.3 billion in 2023). ESRS 2 BP-2 note: From Q3 2024, target expanded to include discretionary mandates (SFDR 8/9); no restatement; three Luxembourg Article 8 low-carbon funds added in Q4.
- Greenhouse gas accounting (ESRS E1-6): For financial institutions, primary emissions are financed emissions (Scope 3, category 15). DNB reports Scope 3 only for category 15; other Scope 3 categories omitted. 2024 established as the baseline year for financed emissions (pending future scope consistency). Scope 1 and 2 cover DNB’s own operations. Baseline years for some climate targets remain 2019 and 2022.

nodes.start_phrase: The reporting includes the following greenhouse gases in Scope 1 and 2, all converted to CO2 equivalents: CO2 (carbon dioxide), CH4 (methane), N2O (nitrous oxide), SF6 (sulphur hexafluoride), HFCs (hydrofluorocarbons) and PFCs (perfluorocarbons).
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines DNB’s greenhouse gas reporting boundaries and methods for Scopes 1 and 2, aligning with the GHG Protocol and an operational control (control approach) boundary. It includes CO2, CH4, N2O, SF6, HFCs, and PFCs converted to CO2e. nodes.title: Reporting limits and calculation methods - Introduction
nodes.heading: 3.12.1 Reporting limits and calculation methods
nodes.start_phrase: The reporting includes the following greenhouse gases in Scope 1 and 2, all converted to CO2 equivalents: CO2 (carbon dioxide), CH4 (methane), N2O (nitrous oxide), SF6 (sulphur hexafluoride), HFCs (hydrofluorocarbons) and PFCs (perfluorocarbons).
nodes.summary:
Reporting limits and calculation methods
The reporting includes the following greenhouse gases 
in Scope 1 and 2, all converted to CO2 equivalents: 
CO2 (carbon dioxide), CH4 (methane), N2O 
(nitrous oxide), SF6 (sulphur hexafluoride), HFCs 
(hydrofluorocarbons) and PFCs (perfluorocarbons). 
The calculations in DNB's greenhouse gas accounting 
are performed in accordance with the GHG Protocol. 
The calculations are based on a control approach, which 
means that DNB includes factors that the Group has 
operational control of. See further details below.

nodes.title: Scope 1
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.1 Scope 1
nodes.start_phrase: DNB’s Scope 1 emissions include use of fuel from rental cars used by DNB’s employees.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and standards: Reports Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, SF6, HFCs, PFCs) converted to CO2e, calculated under the GHG Protocol using an operational control (control) approach.
- Scope 1 boundary and results: Includes fuel use from rental/leased cars used by employees; 2024 emissions total 67 tCO2e.
- Scope 1 methodology: Based on total mileage in leasing agreements, converted to litres and kWh; calculations by a third party. Emission factors: petrol and diesel tailored to Nordic/Luxembourg contexts; hybrids use combined fuel and electricity factors. Sources include DEFRA 2024, Norwegian Environment Agency, and IEA 2024. Electricity use from hybrids/EVs is accounted for in Scope 2.
- Scope 2 boundary: Indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heating, and cooling; reported using both location-based and market-based methods.
- Scope 2 location-based results and methods: 2024 total 1,379 tCO2e, of which electricity accounts for 1,247 tCO2e. Primarily uses metered activity data; estimates applied for smaller Norwegian sites (based on other offices’ consumption) and international representative offices (based on Odyssee-Mure per-employee statistics). Emission factors are country/region-specific IEA 2024 values.
- Context: Extract from DNB Group Annual Report 2024, Sustainability Report, ESRS E1 Climate change.

nodes.title: Scope 2
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.2 Scope 2
nodes.start_phrase: DNB’s Scope 2 emissions include indirect emissions relating to purchased energy, heating and cooling.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt defines DNB’s greenhouse gas reporting scope, gases, and methods. It covers Scope 1 and 2 emissions converted to CO2e for CO2, CH4, N2O, SF6, HFCs, and PFCs, calculated under the GHG Protocol using an operational control (control) approach. Calculations are performed by a third party with region-appropriate emissions factors.

Scope 1 comprises emissions from fuel use in employees’ rental cars, totaling 67 t CO2e in 2024. Mileage from leasing agreements is converted to liters and kWh using average fuel/electric consumption per kilometer. Emission factors come from DEFRA (2024) and the Norwegian Environment Agency for fuels and from the IEA (2024) for electricity; hybrids use combined factors, and electricity use for hybrids/EVs is reported under Scope 2.

Scope 2 includes indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heating, and cooling, reported using both location-based and market-based methods. For 2024, location-based Scope 2 emissions were 1,379 t CO2e, dominated by electricity at 1,247 t CO2e. Most electricity data is activity-based; smaller Norwegian sites and international representative offices use estimates (other-office benchmarks and Odyssee-Mure per-employee statistics). Emission factors for electricity are country/region-specific from the IEA (2024).

nodes.heading: 3.12.1.2 Scope 2
