nodes.summary:
Scope 2
DNB’s Scope 2 emissions include indirect emissions 
relating to purchased energy, heating and cooling. The 
calculation and reporting of Scope 2 emissions are 
based on both the location-based and the market-based 
method.

nodes.title: Location-based method
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.2.1 Location-based method
nodes.start_phrase: When using the location-based method, DNB’s total Scope 2 emissions were 1 379 t CO2e in 2024.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Reporting limits and calculation methods for DNB Group’s greenhouse gas (GHG) accounting under ESRS E1.
- Gases covered: CO2, CH4, N2O, SF6, HFCs, and PFCs, all converted to CO2e across Scope 1 and Scope 2.
- Methodology: Calculations follow the GHG Protocol using a control approach (operational control). Certain calculations are performed by a third party.
- Scope 1: Emissions from employee rental/leased cars only; total 67 t CO2e in 2024. Calculations based on total mileage in leasing agreements, converted to litres and kWh using average fuel/electricity per km. Fuel emission factors from DEFRA (2024) and the Norwegian Environment Agency; electricity factor from IEA (2024). Hybrid vehicles use combined fuel and electricity factors; electricity for hybrids/EVs is reported under Scope 2.
- Scope 2: Indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heating, and cooling; reported using both location-based and market-based methods.
- Location-based results (2024): Total Scope 2 emissions 1,379 t CO2e; electricity is the primary source at 1,247 t CO2e. Data primarily from activity data; estimates used for smaller Norwegian locations (based on other offices’ consumption) and international representative offices (using Odyssee-Mure per-employee statistics). Emission factors are country/region-based from IEA (2024).

nodes.title: Market-based method
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.2.2 Market-based method
nodes.start_phrase: When using the market-based method, DNB’s total Scope 2 emissions were 384 t CO2e in 2024.
nodes.summary:
- The section explains DNB’s Scope 2 accounting under the market-based method for 2024, reporting total Scope 2 emissions of 384 t CO2e.
- Office electricity emissions are 0 t CO2e because DNB purchases guarantees of origin (GOs) covering 100% of its electricity consumption, making market-based emissions significantly lower than location-based results.
- A 2024 list shows 100% GO coverage across multiple countries; some GOs are bundled (Finland, UK, Sweden, Poland) and others unbundled (USA, Denmark, Latvia, Singapore, Chile, Luxembourg, China, Germany, Greece, Brazil, India, Spain, Australia, Switzerland).
- DNB does not buy GOs for electricity used by hybrid/electric cars or for district heating and cooling; these are calculated using the residual mix, which is typically higher than location-based factors due to Norway’s large export of GOs, implying more fossil-intensive electricity in the remaining mix.
- Consequently, emissions for these non-GO-covered energy uses are higher than under the location-based method.
- For Scope 3, financed emissions (category 15) are reported in CO2e, except for the shipping portfolio, which is reported in CO2 in line with IMO definitions.

nodes.title: Scope 3
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3 Scope 3
nodes.start_phrase: Financed emissions in Scope 3, category 15, are reported in CO2 equivalents (CO2e), with the exception of the emissions in DNB’s shipping portfolio, which are reported in CO2, as this is clearly defined by the IMO and in the Poseidon Principles.
nodes.summary:
- Scope 2 (market-based): DNB reports 384 t CO2e in 2024. Office electricity emissions are 0 t CO2e due to purchasing guarantees of origin (GOs) for 100% of electricity across multiple countries, using a mix of bundled and unbundled renewable GOs. Market-based emissions are therefore much lower than location-based.
- GO coverage details: 100% of office electricity in countries including the USA, Denmark, Finland, UK, Latvia, Singapore, Sweden, Chile, Luxembourg, Poland, China, Germany, Greece, Brazil, India, Spain, Australia, and Switzerland is covered by GOs (various bundled/unbundled types).
- Exclusions from GO purchases: No GOs are bought for electricity used by hybrid/electric cars or for district heating/cooling. Emissions for these uses are calculated with the residual mix (typically higher than location-based) because Norway exports large volumes of GOs, implying a more fossil-intensive remaining electricity mix in a market perspective.
- Scope 3 (Category 15 financed emissions): Reported mainly in CO2e; the shipping portfolio is reported in CO2 in line with IMO/Poseidon Principles. Financed emissions reflect DNB’s proportional share of client/company emissions; gas coverage varies by company, so CO2e is used at portfolio level and a gas-by-gas breakdown cannot be provided.
- Reporting delimitations: 
  - Loan portfolio coverage aligns with sectors in DNB’s transition plan.
  - Customer Scope 3 is not included except for the oil and gas sector and DNB Asset Management’s financed emissions, consistent with transition plan targets.
- Data quality: Of 25,515,575 t CO2e reported, 85% is based on actual data and 15% on estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2).
- Real estate methodology (mortgages, commercial real estate, housing cooperatives): Emission factors draw on 2023 statistics from Norwegian authorities and sources (NVE, Norwegian Environment Agency, Norsk Energi, CEMAsys, Statistics Norway, Norsk Fjernvarme’s fjernkontrollen.no). Calculations reflect a changing energy mix (district heating, electricity, oil, LPG/ethane, biofuels, natural gas), which can materially shift year to year and differs by portfolio type.
- Commercial real estate approach (PCAF-based): Financed emissions = attribution factor (loan drawn/last registered market value) × building emissions; building emissions = estimated energy use × emissions factor. Energy use is derived from:
  - EPC labels A–G via Enova’s rating (median thresholds) per building category (PCAF score 3.0).
  - CRREM national energy statistics (2020 baseline; Pathway to 2050):
    - With area data from Eiendomsverdi (PCAF 4.0): area × kWh/m2.
    - Without area data (PCAF 5.0): portfolio average area applied.
- Mortgages: Exposure is the outstanding loan amount on collateralized properties. If property type is missing, DNB assigns “row house” as a conservative assumption, which increases estimated energy consumption per m2.

nodes.title: Scope 3 - Introduction
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3 Scope 3
nodes.start_phrase: Financed emissions in Scope 3, category 15, are reported in CO2 equivalents (CO2e), with the exception of the emissions in DNB’s shipping portfolio, which are reported in CO2, as this is clearly defined by the IMO and in the Poseidon Principles.
nodes.summary: Overview of DNB Group’s Scope 3, category 15 financed emissions reporting (ESRS E1), stating portfolio-level emissions are reported in CO2e except shipping, which is in CO2 per IMO/Poseidon Principles. Financed emissions equal DNB’s proportional share of client/investee emissions; due to varying company GHG scopes and gases, DNB uses CO2e and cannot detail gases per company. Reporting delimitations: loan portfolio coverage limited to sectors in the transition plan; customers’ Scope 3 not reported except for the oil and gas sector and DAM’s financed emissions, aligned with transition plan targets. Total reported emissions are 25,515,575 tonnes CO2e, comprising 85% actual data and 15% estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2). For real estate portfolios (mortgages, commercial real estate, housing cooperatives), emissions factors use 2023 statistics from Norwegian authorities and sources (NVE, Norwegian Environment Agency, Norsk Energi, CEMAsys, Statistics Norway, fjernkontrollen.no), with an energy mix of district heating, electricity, oil, LPG/ethane, biofuels, and natural gas; year-to-year variability in the mix and carrier factors can materially change calculated financed emissions, and mixes differ between residential and commercial properties.

nodes.title: Commercial real estate
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3.1 Commercial real estate
nodes.start_phrase: The method for calculating absolute emissions from the commercial real estate portfolio is based on a methodology prepared by PCAF.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from DNB Group’s 2024 Annual Report (ESRS E1 – Climate change) referencing the Poseidon Principles and focusing on financed emissions methodology.
- Financed emissions approach: As a financial institution, DNB reports its share of client companies’ emissions, using CO2e at portfolio level due to varying scopes and gases reported by clients; cannot provide gas-by-gas detail per company.
- Scope and delimitations (Category 15 – Investments): 
  - Loan portfolio reporting limited to sectors covered by DNB’s transition plan.
  - Customers’ Scope 3 not reported, except for oil and gas and DNB Asset Management’s financed emissions, aligned with transition plan targets.
- Data quality: Total reported financed emissions are 25,515,575 tCO2e, with 85% actual data and 15% estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2).
- Real estate portfolios (mortgages, commercial real estate, housing cooperatives): 
  - Emission factors sourced from Norwegian authorities and databases (NVE, Environment Agency, Norsk Energi, CEMAsys, Statistics Norway, fjernkontrollen.no), using 2023 statistics.
  - Energy carriers include district heating, electricity, oil, LPG/ethane, biofuels, natural gas; annual changes in energy mix and factors can materially affect financed emissions; mixes differ between residential and commercial assets.
- Commercial real estate methodology (PCAF-aligned):
  - Financed emissions = attribution factor (loan amount drawn/market value; using latest registered value rather than origination) × building emissions.
  - Building emissions = estimated energy consumption × emissions factor.
  - Energy consumption data sources:
    - EPC labels A–G where available (PCAF score 3.0), using Enova’s rating scale and median thresholds per class and building category.
    - CRREM national energy statistics (2020 baseline) to align with a 2050 net-zero pathway, with two sub-cases:
      - Area from Eiendomsverdi available (PCAF score 4.0): m2 × estimated kWh/m2.
      - Area not available (PCAF score 5.0): use portfolio average area as a standard value.
- Mortgages methodology:
  - Uses outstanding loan amount to apportion exposure to property-related emissions.
  - If property type is missing, defaults to “row house” as a conservative assumption that increases estimated energy consumption.

nodes.title: Mortgages
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3.2 Mortgages
nodes.start_phrase: The mortgage portfolio covers the properties that DNB’s personal customers have provided as collateral for their mortgages.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Outlines DNB’s approach to measuring financed emissions under ESRS E1, referencing the Poseidon Principles and using CO2e as the portfolio-level metric due to varying company GHG scopes and gases.
- Boundary choices (Scope 3, category 15 – Investments):
  - Loan portfolio reporting limited to sectors covered by DNB’s transition plan.
  - Customer Scope 3 emissions are not reported except for the oil and gas sector and DNB Asset Management’s financed emissions, aligned with transition plan targets.
- Data quality and coverage: Reports 25,515,575 tonnes CO2e; 85% based on actual data and 15% on estimates (ESRS 2 BP-2). DNB cannot provide a detailed gas-level breakdown per company.
- Real estate portfolios (mortgages, commercial real estate, housing cooperatives):
  - Emission factors built from latest Norwegian sources (NVE, Environment Agency, Norsk Energi, CEMAsys, Statistics Norway, fjernkontrollen.no), reflecting an annually changing energy mix (district heating, electricity, oil, LPG/ethane, biofuels, natural gas). Differences in portfolio energy mixes drive year-to-year variation.
- Commercial real estate methodology:
  - PCAF-based attribution using loan-to-value (amount drawn/market value) multiplied by building emissions; last registered market value used (origination value unavailable).
  - Energy use per building from:
    - EPC labels A–G via Enova’s scale (PCAF score 3.0), using median between class thresholds.
    - CRREM national energy statistics (Pathway to 2050) with two data-quality paths:
      - Area from Eiendomsverdi (PCAF 4.0).
      - No area; use portfolio average area proxy (PCAF 5.0).
- Mortgages methodology:
  - Exposure based on outstanding loan amount tied to collateral properties.
  - Conservative assumptions: default property type “row house” if unknown; use primary-room area when available, else gross area; for interval-based area data, take the upper bound.
  - EPC-to-energy conversion via Enova: A at 95% of A threshold value; B–F as averages with preceding class; G at 115% of F. Data quality targeted at PCAF score ~4.0 using internal EPC-covered reference sets.
- Housing cooperatives methodology:
  - PCAF-based attribution: joint debt/value of underlying homes; single attribution factor per cooperative; last Eiendomsverdi market value used.
  - Three data-quality scenarios:
    - ≥50% units with EPC labels and area derivable (PCAF 3.0) using Enova’s scale.
    - <50% EPC coverage but at least one known unit area (PCAF 4.0); apply known EPC as proxy for whole cooperative and infer total area.
    - No EPC and no area (PCAF 5.0); estimate EPC and area from similar-data subsets by housing type.
  - Housing type rules: “flat” if specified; if unknown, assign “row house.” Apply Enova area correction using either average corrections by housing type or unit counts when available. Use average attribution factor when key values are missing.
- Motor vehicles portfolio:
  - Covers on-balance credit exposures from DNB Finans across geographies, primarily passenger cars and light commercial vehicles, with assumptions on available vehicle data noted.

nodes.title: Housing cooperatives
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3.3 Housing cooperatives
nodes.start_phrase: The sample for the calculations is DNB’s loans to housing cooperatives.
nodes.summary:
- Explains how Enova’s conversion table maps EPC labels to estimated energy delivered per m2: A set at 95% of the A threshold, B–F as the average of each label and the preceding one, and G at 115% of F.
- Describes DNB’s method to estimate kWh/m2 when property type and area are known, using averages from a portfolio with EPC coverage; contributes to an internal score and a total PCAF score of 4.0.
- States area selection rules: prefer primary rooms; if unavailable, use gross area; for interval data, use the upper bound for conservatism.
- Outlines PCAF-based financed emissions for housing cooperatives: emissions per building (estimated energy use × emissions factor) multiplied by an attribution factor; attribution is joint debt divided by the value of underlying homes; uses latest Eiendomsverdi market value when origination value is missing.
- Details three data-quality scenarios for housing cooperatives’ energy estimation:
  - ≥50% EPC coverage and some area data (PCAF 3.0): use Enova scale and median between class thresholds to derive kWh/m2 and total area.
  - <50% EPC coverage with minimal area data (PCAF 4.0): apply available EPC label(s) as proxy for the entire cooperative and extrapolate total area.
  - No EPC or area data (PCAF 5.0): estimate both EPC and area from the covered dataset within the same housing type.
- Specifies housing type handling: use “flat” if that is the only type in Eiendomsverdi; default to “row house” if unknown; acknowledges different Enova energy labels by type.
- Applies Enova’s area correction factor: estimate average correction by housing type when unit counts are unknown; when unit counts are known, apply correction per unit based on the Enova table; use an average attribution factor if property-specific values are missing.
- Introduces the motor vehicles portfolio scope: DNB Finans on-balance vehicle financing across geographies, primarily passenger cars and light commercial vehicles, with reporting assumptions noted.

nodes.title: Motor vehicles
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3.4 Motor vehicles
nodes.start_phrase: The motor vehicle sector includes DNB’s on-balance credit exposures associated with financing products for motor vehicles from DNB Finans, and covers customers in all geographical locations.
nodes.summary:
- Explains how DNB estimates building energy use from EPC labels using Enova’s conversion table: A = 95% of A-threshold kWh/m2; B–F = average of current and preceding label; G = 115% of F. When property type and area are known, DNB assigns kWh/m2 from a benchmarked internal portfolio with EPC coverage. Area preference is primary rooms, else gross area; upper bound of recorded interval is used for conservatism. Data quality contributes to PCAF scoring.

- Details financed-emissions methodology for housing cooperatives using PCAF: emissions per building = estimated energy consumption × emissions factor; financed share via an attribution factor (drawn amount/market value). If origination LTV is missing, latest Eiendomsverdi market value is used. Three data-quality tiers:
  - PCAF 3.0: ≥50% of units with EPC labels and at least one unit area known; Enova scale used to derive average kWh/m2.
  - PCAF 4.0: <50% EPC coverage but at least one unit area known; use available EPC labels as proxy for the entire cooperative.
  - PCAF 5.0: No EPC or area data; estimate both from the covered dataset by housing type.
  Housing type defaults to “flat” when only that is listed; otherwise “row house” if unknown. Applies Enova area correction factors, estimating by average per housing type when unit counts are unknown. Uses an average attribution factor when specific property values are missing.

- Describes motor-vehicle financed-emissions methods (DNB Finans portfolio; PCAF with Finance Norway adjustments), prioritized by data availability:
  - Method 1a: Actual fuel transactions × fuel-specific emissions factors; mileage from odometer deltas.
  - Method 1b: WLTP CO2 and actual mileage with period and attribution factors.
  - Method 2a: WLTP CO2 with statistically derived mileage, plus period and attribution factors.
  - Method 3a: No WLTP or mileage; use PCAF default 224 g CO2/km and national average mileage (11,883 km). Uses EU-average mileage for Danish/Finnish passenger cars and Nordic averages for vans; 2024 applied vehicle-, country-, and engine-specific emissions factors.

- Outlines upstream oil and gas financed-emissions calculation (PCAF with Finance Norway): emissions from audited reports or Rystad Energy; attribution factor = DNB loan commitment / enterprise value (debt + equity); portfolio emissions sum = customer emissions × attribution factor.

- Presents salmon farming financed-emissions approach (PCAF with Finance Norway): prefer customer-reported data; otherwise calculate Scope 1–3 using SINTEF emissions factors tied to production volumes and average customer intensity. Attribution factor for listed companies uses Bloomberg enterprise value; for unlisted, total debt + equity adjusted by replacing book value of licences with market value (from latest auction averages). Production volumes and financials sourced from company reports.

nodes.title: Oil and gas
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3.5 Oil and gas
nodes.start_phrase: For DNB’s upstream oil and gas portfolio, absolute financed emissions are calculated in accordance with the PCAF guidance, with the addition of the recommendations from Finance Norway for using the PCAF standard for Norwegian conditions.
nodes.summary:
- Describes DNB’s approach to calculating financed emissions using the PCAF methodology adapted with Finance Norway guidance, across motor vehicles, upstream oil and gas, and salmon farming.
- Motor vehicles:
  - Method 1a: Transaction-level actual fuel consumption multiplied by fuel-specific emission factors; mileage from last minus first valid odometer readings.
  - Method 1b: WLTP-based using actual mileage and vehicle CO2 data plus period and attribution factors.
  - Method 2a: WLTP-based without mileage; mileage estimated from local statistics plus period and attribution factors.
  - Method 3a: No WLTP or mileage; uses PCAF generic factors (224 g CO2/km) and average national mileage (11,883 km). For Denmark and Finland, applies EU average mileage for passenger cars and Nordic average for vans due to poor data.
  - 2024 uses differentiated emission factors by vehicle type, registration country, and engine type.
- Upstream oil and gas:
  - Financed emissions follow PCAF; emissions sourced from audited customer reports or Rystad Energy.
  - Attribution factor = DNB loan commitment / company value; company value = total debt + total equity (from audited accounts).
  - Portfolio emissions are the sum of customer emissions multiplied by attribution factors.
- Salmon farming:
  - Uses PCAF with Finance Norway adaptations; prioritizes customer-reported emissions.
  - When unavailable, calculates Scope 1–3 using SINTEF 2022 emissions factors and average intensity applied to reported production volumes.
  - Attribution factor based on drawn exposure:
    - Listed: divided by company value from Bloomberg.
    - Unlisted: divided by total debt + equity, adjusting license book values to market values (from latest auction averages).
  - Data on balance sheets and production volumes sourced from customer financial reports.
- Context: Content appears in the DNB Group Annual Report 2024, ESRS E1 Climate change section.

nodes.title: Salmon farming
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3.6 Salmon farming
nodes.start_phrase: For the salmon farming sector, DNB uses the PCAF methodology, with the addition of Finance Norway’s recommendations for using the PCAF standard for Norwegian conditions.
nodes.summary:
- Describes DNB’s approach to calculating financed emissions under the PCAF standard, adapted with Finance Norway guidance, within the ESRS E1 Climate Change context.
- Motor vehicles methodology:
  - Uses the most accurate available data per exposure (make, model, fuel type).
  - Method 1a: Calculates emissions from actual fuel volume per transaction using fuel-specific factors; mileage from reported odometer readings.
  - Method 1b: Uses WLTP CO2 values with actual mileage, plus period and attribution factors.
  - Method 2a: Uses WLTP CO2 values with estimated mileage from local statistics, plus period and attribution factors.
  - Method 3a: Fallback with no WLTP or mileage: PCAF default 224 g CO2/km and Norwegian average 11,883 km.
  - Applies EU average mileage for passenger cars and Nordic average for vans in Denmark and Finland due to poor mileage data; in 2024 used differentiated emission factors by vehicle type, country, and engine type.
- Oil and gas (upstream) methodology:
  - Calculates absolute financed emissions per PCAF with Finance Norway adaptations.
  - Emissions sourced from audited customer reports or Rystad Energy.
  - Attribution factor = DNB loan commitment / company value (total debt + equity from audited accounts).
  - Portfolio emissions are the sum of customer emissions multiplied by the attribution factor.
- Salmon farming methodology:
  - Applies PCAF with Finance Norway adaptations.
  - Uses customer-reported emissions when available; otherwise estimates Scope 1–3 using SINTEF (2022) emissions factors and average intensity tied to production volumes.
  - Attribution factor based on DNB’s drawn exposure:
    - Listed companies: divides by company value (from Bloomberg).
    - Unlisted: divides by total debt + equity, adjusted by replacing on-balance licence values with market values (average of last auction round).
  - Financial and production data sourced from customer reports reviewed by credit analysts.
- Notes WLTP as the standardized test for vehicle fuel consumption, CO2 emissions, and range.

nodes.title: Steel
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3.7 Steel
nodes.start_phrase: The steel sector includes DNB’s on-balance exposures towards customers in steel manufacturing in all geographical locations.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and methodology overview across sectors for DNB’s financed and operational emissions within the ESRS E1 Climate change context.
- Steel:
  - Covers on-balance exposures to steel manufacturing globally; excludes off-balance items.
  - Uses PCAF methodology adapted with Finance Norway’s guidance.
  - Prioritizes most accurate data per PCAF; for aluminium and steel customers in DNB’s transition plan, uses customer-reported emissions from the latest annual reports.
- Power generation:
  - Includes on-balance credit exposures globally; excludes off-balance.
  - Applies PCAF with Finance Norway recommendations and most accurate data per exposure.
  - Obtains reported emissions or production volumes from customers; uses extrapolation where data is missing to achieve full coverage.
- DNB Næringseiendom (real estate):
  - Monitors energy via Optima; calculations follow the GHG Protocol.
  - Location-based Scope 2 approach using Nordic electricity mix; guarantees of origin not factored.
  - Emission factors: electricity from CEMAsys; district energy and local heating/cooling from suppliers/Entro.
  - Data primarily from electronic meters; reports only buildings with full, comparable year-over-year data; excludes planning-phase assets, high-vacancy buildings, or those not owned for the full year.
- DNB Livsforsikring (life insurance):
  - Uses MSCI ESG Research data for portfolio companies’ Scope 1 and 2 emissions; Scope 3 excluded.
  - Financed emissions reporting covers ~65% of the portfolio.
  - For listed equities and bonds, ~85% data coverage; remaining 15% imputed using the average emissions of companies with available data.
- DNB Asset Management (DAM):
  - Uses MSCI ESG Research; high coverage for equities, lower for fixed income, especially Nordic FI.
  - Portfolio carbon footprint weighted by holdings; cash allocated proportionally across holdings.
  - For missing company data, uses MSCI modelled estimates; if neither reported nor estimated data exist, applies an average of companies with reported data.
- Shipping:
  - Includes Scope 1 emissions for vessels ≥5,000 gross tonnes (aligned with IMO reporting threshold); excludes off-balance exposures.
  - Calculates absolute financed emissions using ship-level data: fuel type, fuel volume during the period, and emissions factors per fuel type, sourced from customers or a designated third party.

nodes.title: Power generation
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3.8 Power generation
nodes.start_phrase: The figures include DNB’s on-balance credit exposures towards customers in all geographical locations.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of how DNB measures and reports financed emissions across key sectors and portfolios, focusing on on-balance exposures and sector-specific methodologies.
- Steel: Global on-balance exposures to steel manufacturing; PCAF methodology with Finance Norway adaptations; uses the most accurate data per exposure; for aluminium and steel customers under the transition plan, uses reported emissions from the latest annual reports.
- Power generation: Global on-balance credit exposures; PCAF + Finance Norway guidance; collects reported emissions or production volumes directly from customers; extrapolates where data are missing to achieve full coverage.
- DNB Næringseiendom (real estate): Tracks energy use via the Optima system; GHG Protocol-compliant, location-based CO2e using Nordic electricity mix (no guarantees of origin); emission factors from CEMAsys, energy suppliers, and Entro; direct electricity is the main Scope 2 source; data primarily from meters; reports only buildings with full, comparable annual data, excluding those in planning, with high vacancy, or not owned all year.
- DNB Livsforsikring (life insurance): Uses MSCI ESG Research for portfolio emissions based on Scope 1 and 2 only; financed emissions coverage ~65% of the portfolio; ~85% data coverage for shares and bonds; imputes missing 15% using the average of covered companies; Scope 3 excluded.
- DNB Asset Management: Uses MSCI ESG Research; high equity coverage, lower for fixed income (particularly Nordic); portfolio-weighted carbon footprint; cash allocated pro rata; uses MSCI modelled estimates when reported data are absent, and averages for firms lacking both reported and modelled data.
- Shipping: Includes Scope 1 emissions for vessels ≥5,000 GT (aligned with IMO threshold); off-balance exposures excluded; absolute financed emissions calculated per vessel using fuel type, fuel volume, and fuel-specific emission factors, sourced from customers or a third-party.

nodes.title: DNB Næringseiendom
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3.9 DNB Næringseiendom
nodes.start_phrase: DNB Næringseiendom monitors energy consumption through the Optima energy and environmental monitoring system.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: Partial sustainability report detailing how DNB measures and reports financed emissions across key sectors using PCAF methodology supplemented by Finance Norway guidance, prioritizing the most accurate data per exposure and focusing on on-balance sheet exposures.

- Steel (and aluminium under transition plans): Uses PCAF with Finance Norway recommendations; relies on customers’ latest reported emissions from annual reports; on-balance exposures only.

- Power generation: On-balance credit exposures included; PCAF plus Finance Norway guidance; emissions or production data obtained directly from customers; extrapolation used where data is missing to achieve full coverage.

- DNB Næringseiendom (commercial real estate): Energy use monitored via the Optima system; calculations follow GHG Protocol with location-based Scope 2; Nordic electricity mix used without guarantees of origin; emission factors from CEMAsys (electricity) and suppliers/Entro (district/local energy); primary data from meters; reporting limited to buildings with full, comparable annual data (excludes planning phase, high vacancy, or not owned for full year).

- DNB Livsforsikring: Measures portfolio companies’ emissions with MSCI ESG Research (Scope 1 and 2 only; Scope 3 excluded); financed emissions reporting covers ~65% of the portfolio; ~85% data coverage for equities/bonds; remaining 15% imputed using portfolio average emissions.

- DNB Asset Management (DAM): Uses MSCI ESG Research; higher coverage for equities than fixed income, with especially low Nordic fixed-income coverage; portfolio carbon footprint weighted by holdings, cash allocated proportionally; uses MSCI modelled estimates when reported data is unavailable; if neither reported nor modelled data exists, assigns average of companies with data.

- Shipping: Covers Scope 1 emissions for vessels ≥5,000 gross tonnes (aligned with IMO threshold); off-balance exposures excluded; financed emissions calculated using per-ship data on fuel type, fuel volumes, and fuel-specific emission factors.

nodes.title: DNB Livsforsikring
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3.10 DNB Livsforsikring
nodes.start_phrase: DNB Livsforsikring uses data from MSCI ESG Research to measure the greenhouse gas emissions of the companies in its portfolios.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of sectoral financed-emissions methodologies across DNB’s portfolios, focusing on on-balance exposures only and excluding off-balance items.
- Consistent application of PCAF methodology supplemented by Finance Norway’s guidance, using the highest-quality data available per exposure.
- Steel (and aluminium under the transition plan): use of customers’ latest reported emissions from annual reports.
- Power generation: inclusion of all on-balance credit exposures; collection of customer-reported emissions or production volumes; extrapolation applied where data is missing.
- DNB Næringseiendom (real estate): energy and emissions monitored via Optima; calculations follow the GHG Protocol using location-based Scope 2; Nordic electricity mix for direct electricity; emission factors from CEMAsys, energy suppliers, and Entro; reporting limited to buildings with full, comparable data and excludes those under planning, with high vacancy, or not owned for the full year.
- DNB Livsforsikring: portfolio emissions measured with MSCI ESG Research data (Scope 1 and 2 only); financed-emissions reporting covers ~65% of the portfolio; ~85% data coverage for shares/bonds; missing data filled by assigning the average emissions of companies with data.
- DNB Asset Management (DAM): uses MSCI ESG Research; high coverage for equities, lower for fixed income (especially Nordic); carbon footprint weighted by portfolio holdings with cash allocated proportionally; uses MSCI modelled estimates where companies lack reported data, and portfolio averages where neither reported nor estimated data exist.
- Shipping: Scope 1 emissions for vessels ≥5,000 gross tonnes (aligned with IMO threshold); excludes off-balance exposures; absolute financed emissions calculated from ship-level fuel type, fuel volume, and fuel-specific emission factors.

nodes.title: DNB Asset Management
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3.11 DNB Asset Management
nodes.start_phrase: DAM uses data from MSCI ESG Research to measure the greenhouse gas emissions of the companies in its portfolio.
nodes.summary:
- Document focus: How DNB measures and reports financed and operational greenhouse gas emissions across key portfolios under ESRS E1, including methodologies, data sources, scope, and data coverage/assumptions.
- Common approach: Prioritizes on-balance exposures; applies PCAF methodology with Finance Norway adaptations where relevant; uses the most accurate data available per exposure; relies on customer-reported data when possible and applies estimation/extrapolation for gaps.

- Steel:
  - Scope: On-balance exposures in steel manufacturing globally; off-balance excluded.
  - Method: PCAF + Finance Norway guidance.
  - Data: Customer-reported emissions from the latest annual reports; uses most accurate data per PCAF.

- Power generation:
  - Scope: On-balance credit exposures globally; off-balance excluded.
  - Method: PCAF + Finance Norway guidance.
  - Data: Customer-reported emissions or production volumes; extrapolation used where data are missing to achieve full coverage.

- DNB Næringseiendom (real estate):
  - Monitoring: Optima energy and environmental system.
  - Method: GHG Protocol; CO2e conversion; location-based Scope 2 using Nordic electricity mix (no guarantees of origin).
  - Emission factors: Electricity from CEMAsys; district heating/cooling and local heating/cooling from suppliers and Entro.
  - Data capture: Primarily electronic meter data.
  - Reporting boundary: Only buildings with full, comparable year-over-year data; excludes planning-phase assets, high-vacancy buildings, and assets not owned for the full year.

- DNB Livsforsikring:
  - Data source: MSCI ESG Research.
  - Scope: Financed emissions based on Scope 1 and 2 only (Scope 3 excluded).
  - Coverage: ~65% of total portfolio; ~85% for shares and bonds.
  - Estimation: For the remaining ~15%, assigns the portfolio average emissions of companies with data.

- DNB Asset Management (DAM):
  - Data source: MSCI ESG Research.
  - Coverage: High for equities; lower for fixed income, especially Nordic fixed income.
  - Method: Holdings-weighted portfolio carbon footprint; cash allocated proportionally.
  - Estimation: Uses MSCI modelled estimates where company data are missing; if neither reported nor modelled data exist, applies the average of companies with reported data.

- Shipping:
  - Scope: Scope 1 emissions for vessels ≥5,000 GT (aligned with IMO threshold); off-balance excluded.
  - Method: Absolute financed emissions calculated using ship-level data:
    - Fuel type
    - Fuel volume consumed
    - Emission factors per fuel type

nodes.title: Shipping
nodes.heading: 3.12.1.3.12 Shipping
nodes.start_phrase: The shipping portfolio includes Scope 1 emissions for vessels of 5 000 gross tonnes or more.
nodes.summary:
- Sector methodologies for financed emissions:
  - Steel: On-balance exposures only; PCAF methodology with Finance Norway adaptations; use most accurate data per exposure; for aluminium and steel clients in DNB’s transition plan, use customers’ reported emissions from latest annual reports.
  - Power generation: On-balance exposures only; PCAF with Finance Norway guidance; collect reported emissions/production directly from customers; extrapolate where data is missing to achieve full coverage.

- Real estate (DNB Næringseiendom):
  - Energy and emissions monitored via Optima; calculations follow GHG Protocol.
  - Location-based approach using Nordic electricity mix; emission factors from CEMAsys (electricity) and suppliers/Entro (district cooling/heating, local systems).
  - Direct electricity is the main Scope 2 source; metered electronic data.
  - Reporting limited to buildings with complete, comparable annual data; excludes planning-phase assets, high-vacancy buildings, and those not owned for the full year.

- Insurance (DNB Livsforsikring):
  - Uses MSCI ESG Research for portfolio emissions (Scope 1 and 2 only; excludes Scope 3).
  - Financed emissions reporting covers ~65% of portfolio; ~85% coverage for shares and bonds.
  - For remaining 15% with no data, assigns average emissions of covered companies.

- Asset management (DNB Asset Management):
  - Uses MSCI ESG Research; higher coverage for equities than fixed income, with low coverage in Nordic fixed income.
  - Portfolio carbon footprint is holdings-weighted; cash allocated proportionally.
  - Uses MSCI modelled estimates when company data is missing; if neither reported nor estimated data exist, applies portfolio average.

- Shipping portfolio:
  - Includes Scope 1 for vessels ≥5,000 GT (IMO threshold); off-balance exposures excluded.
  - Absolute financed emissions computed from fuel type/volume and standard emission factors (IMO/Poseidon Principles).
  - Attribution factor = DNB lending exposure / ship’s year-end market value; applied to ship emissions and aggregated across portfolio.

- Greenhouse gas intensity based on net revenue:
  - Defined as total tCO2e divided by net revenue (sum of net interest income and net other operating income; NOK 86,537 million in 2024).
  - 2024 intensity: 0.0003 tCO2e/NOK for both location- and market-based; no prior-year comparative provided.

- Climate credits:
  - Strategic focus on real-economy emissions reductions; credits considered for hard-to-abate residuals long term.
  - For own operations, credits purchased annually since 2014 for measured Scope 1 and selected Scope 3 (e.g., travel, waste); 7,088 tCO2e purchased in 2024 via klimate.co with rigorous due diligence.
  - Projects are 100% carbon storage: biosphere (ecosystem restoration, soil carbon) and geosphere (DACCS, mineralization).
  - Verified against Plan (46.5%), Gold Standard (34%), Artisanal C‑Sink (5%), Verra VCS (14%), EBC C‑Sink (0.5%); 99.6% outside Europe; credits annulled 2017–2024.
  - Intention to continue decarbonising operations to reduce reliance on credits.

nodes.title: Greenhouse gas intensity based on net income
nodes.heading: 3.12.2 Greenhouse gas intensity based on net income
nodes.start_phrase: The greenhouse gas intensity is calculated by dividing total greenhouse gas emissions in tonnes of CO2e by net revenue in NOK.
nodes.summary:
- Explains how financed emissions from DNB’s shipping portfolio are calculated: ship-level emissions are derived by multiplying fuel consumption by standard, fuel-specific emission factors (aligned with IMO and Poseidon Principles). DNB’s share is attributed by dividing its lending exposure by each ship’s year-end market value and multiplying by the ship’s emissions; results are aggregated across the portfolio to obtain total absolute financed emissions.
- Defines greenhouse gas intensity based on net revenue: total GHG emissions (tCO2e) divided by net revenue (NOK). For 2024, both location-based and market-based intensities are 0.0003 tCO2e/NOK; comparative data are not available. Net revenue equals Net interest income plus Net other operating income (NOK 86,537 million).
- Details DNB’s approach to climate credits under ESRS E1-7: prioritizes real-economy emissions reductions, viewing carbon credits as a long-term tool for residual emissions. For own operations, DNB has purchased credits for measured Scope 1 and upstream/own-operations Scope 3 emissions since 2014; in 2024 it bought 7,088 tCO2e of credits.
- Credits were sourced via klimate.co with rigorous due diligence (300+ data points) and are 100% carbon storage, focused on carbon removal in the biosphere (e.g., ecosystem restoration, soil carbon) and geosphere (e.g., DACCS, mineralization). Verification standards include Plan (46.5%), Gold Standard (34%), Verra VCS (14%), Artisanal C-Sink (5%), and EBC C-Sink (0.5%); 99.6% of projects are outside Europe. Credits were annulled during 2017–2024. DNB aims to continue decarbonizing operations to minimize reliance on credits.

nodes.title: Purchase of climate credits
nodes.heading: 3.12.3 Purchase of climate credits
nodes.start_phrase: Achieving the net-zero ambition will require that both DNB and its customers continue to increase the pace of emissions reduction associated with the real economy.
nodes.summary:
- Methodology for financed shipping emissions: Ship emissions are calculated by multiplying each fuel type consumed by its industry-standard emissions factor (as used by IMO and the Poseidon Principles).
- Attribution of financed emissions: DNB’s share of a ship’s emissions is determined by an attribution factor (DNB lending exposure divided by the ship’s last available year-end market value), applied to the ship’s emissions; summed across all ships to obtain total absolute financed emissions for the shipping portfolio.
- Greenhouse gas intensity metric: GHG intensity is total emissions (tCO2e) divided by net revenue (NOK).
- Reported GHG intensity: Both location-based and market-based emissions per net revenue are 0.0003 tCO2e/NOK for 2024; comparative figures are not available.
- Revenue basis: Net revenue equals Net interest income plus Net other operating income (NOK 86,537 million; per Group income statement).
- Carbon credits strategy: Primary focus is on enabling real-economy emissions reductions; credits are considered for hard-to-abate residual emissions over the long term.
- 2024 carbon credit purchases: DNB purchased 7,088 tCO2e in credits for measured direct and indirect emissions in own operations and upstream value chain (Scopes 1 and 3), continuing a practice since 2014.
- Vendor and due diligence: Credits bought from klimate.co, which assesses projects using 300+ data points on climate impact, additionality, integrity, and prospects.
- Nature of projects: 100% carbon storage via biosphere removals (e.g., ecosystem restoration, soil carbon) and geosphere removals (e.g., DACCS, mineralization).
- Standards and distribution: Projects verified under Plan (46.5%), Gold Standard (34%), Verra VCS (14%), Artisanal C-Sink (5%), EBC C-Sink (0.5%); 99.6% located outside Europe.
- Retirement of credits: Credits annulled over 2017–2024.
- Ongoing commitment: DNB aims to further decarbonise operations to avoid reliance on carbon credits.

structure.title: ESRS E3 Water and marine resources
structure.heading: 4 ESRS E3 Water and marine resources
structure.start_phrase: In the materiality analysis, extraction and use of marine resources was identified as a risk for DNB, as well as an area in which the Group has an indirect impact.
structure.summary:
- Focus and scope: ESRS E3 Water and marine resources, centered on the extraction and use of marine resources, strategy, and material impacts, risks and opportunities, aligned with ESRS 2 IRO-1 and SBM-3.
- Materiality and context: DNB identifies extraction/use of marine resources as a material risk and area of indirect impact, reflecting Norway’s economy where oil and gas, offshore, and seafood are key; seafood is a major exposure for DNB; one-fourth of Norway’s value creation comes from the sea.
- Impacts and risks: Potential negative impacts on marine ecosystems and biodiversity and on local communities dependent on marine resources; financial risks to clients from resource reduction/degradation or stricter regulation (loss of income, higher costs); reputational risks in oil and gas, fish farming, and other marine sectors; risks and impacts are relevant short, medium, and long term; DNB may have indirect negative impacts through financing and investments.
- Management approach (ESRS E3-1): Governing documents and methods to guide sustainable marine resource management, promote biodiversity, and reduce natural risk; principles integrated into credit processes, risk assessments, and expectation documents.
- Key policies:
  - Group policy for sustainability: Requires considering climate/environment, social responsibility, and governance across activities (products/services, advisory, investment/credit, operations, procurement), promoting sustainable marine resource management and biodiversity, and reducing natural risk.
  - Group instructions for sustainability in credit activities: Excludes financing for unregulated or harmful fishing (seabed-damaging gear, harmful techniques, endangered species), drift nets over 2.5 km, fish farming without permits; no financing for companies that materially harm legally protected habitats.
- Cross-references: Double materiality process under ESRS 2 General disclosures; Group policy disclosure referenced in ESRS E1 Climate change section.

nodes.title: Extraction and use of marine resources
nodes.heading: 4.1 Extraction and use of marine resources
nodes.start_phrase: In the materiality analysis, extraction and use of marine resources was identified as a risk for DNB, as well as an area in which the Group has an indirect impact.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on ESRS E3 Water and marine resources, specifically the extraction and use of marine resources, with links to ESRS 2 IRO-1 and SBM-3.
- Materiality assessment identifies extraction and use of marine resources as a key risk and area of indirect impact for DNB, reflecting Norway’s sea-based economy (oil and gas, offshore, seafood), with seafood a major exposure.
- Describes potential negative impacts on marine ecosystems, biodiversity, and local communities, and outlines financial and regulatory risks (reduced resources, stricter rules, income loss, higher costs) for financed companies, plus reputational risks in oil and gas, fish farming and other marine sectors.
- States that these impacts and risks are relevant across short, medium and long time horizons.
- Outlines management approach via governing documents under ESRS E3-1, aimed at sustainable marine resource management, promoting biodiversity, and reducing nature-related risk.
- Summarizes Group policy for sustainability: integrating environmental, social and governance considerations into products, advisory, sales, investment and credit decisions, production, procurement and operations; embedding principles into credit processes, risk assessments and expectation documents.
- Details credit instructions and exclusions: no financing for unregulated or harmful fishing (seabed-damaging gear, harmful techniques, endangered species, drift nets over 2.5 km), fish farming without required permits, or companies materially harming legally protected habitats.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 4.1.1 Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: In the materiality analysis, extraction and use of marine resources was identified as a risk for DNB, as well as an area in which the Group has an indirect impact.
nodes.summary:
- The section addresses ESRS E3 (Water and marine resources) with focus on extraction and use of marine resources, strategy, and material impacts, risks and opportunities, referencing ESRS 2 IRO-1 and SBM-3 and the double materiality assessment in ESRS 2 General disclosures.
- Materiality: DNB identifies extraction and use of marine resources as a material risk and area of indirect impact due to its exposure to Norway’s sea-based economy (oil and gas, offshore, seafood), with seafood a major banking exposure.

nodes.heading: 5.1 ESRS S1 Own workforce

- Scope and framework: ESRS S1 Own workforce, focusing on diversity, gender equality, and equal pay for work of equal value, linked to ESRS 2 SBM-3 on material impacts, risks, opportunities.

- Materiality: Diversity and equality identified as among the most material short‑term topics due to DNB’s direct impact and value‑creation opportunities.

nodes.title: Governing documents
nodes.heading: 5.1.1.2.1 Governing documents
nodes.start_phrase: DNB’s Code of Conduct, Group policy for sustainability and People Guide (the Employee Handbook) determine how the Group should work with diversity and equality.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: The section covers ESRS S1 for DNB’s own workforce (around 11,000 people), including permanent and temporary employees and hired consultants, across domestic and international operations.

- Materiality and strategy: Diversity, gender equality and equal pay for work of equal value are identified as short‑term, most material topics with significant impacts, risks and opportunities. A diverse and inclusive workforce is positioned as core to DNB’s ethical foundation and sustainable value creation, enhancing productivity, innovation, customer satisfaction, talent attraction and retention.

- Strategic priorities and actions: Focus on gender balance in management and increased multicultural representation. Measures include a multicultural diversity network, integrating diversity and inclusion in leadership programs, and embedding diversity considerations in hiring processes. The 2023 transition plan adds employee climate and transition competence building to support client advisory, linked to ESRS E1.

- Governance and policies (ESRS S1‑1, ESRS 2 MDR‑P): The Code of Conduct, Group policy for sustainability, and the People Guide set expectations for equality, non‑discrimination and inclusion. The Code bans discrimination and harassment on multiple grounds, applies group‑wide (including consultants, Board members), and is Board‑approved. Operational responsibility rests with executives and managers, who ensure compliance and training.

- Controls and monitoring: Ongoing internal control over working environment and HSE compliance; annual confirmation that employees have read the Code; monitoring of diversity and discrimination via employee surveys; stakeholder involvement in policy updates (audit, second‑line functions, unions, governance). Documents are accessible internally and publicly.

- Human rights commitments: Alignment with UN human rights instruments and ILO core conventions; risk‑based review of DNB’s own value chain for human and labour rights risks, with measures per OECD Guidelines. Note that the sustainability policy does not specifically cover child labour, human trafficking or forced/compulsory labour.

- People Guide and HR processes: Based on Norwegian law and aligned with UNGPs/OECD; provides guidance to prevent and handle discrimination/harassment; mandates active, systematic equality work; HR risk assessments with employee representatives; corrective measures where risks are found; biannual gender pay gap mapping.

- Reporting channels: Multiple whistleblowing avenues (electronic, management, safety representatives, HR) to safely raise concerns about human and labour rights.

- Intended outcomes: Better working environment, higher engagement and productivity, and strengthened capability to deliver the Group’s sustainability and transition ambitions.

- ESRS references cited: ESRS 2 SBM‑3; ESRS S1‑1 and S1‑4; cross‑reference to ESRS E1‑3 (Climate change) for competence building.

nodes.title: Interaction with own employees
nodes.heading: 5.1.1.3 Interaction with own employees
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has several processes where the management has a dialogue with the employees, including through trade unions.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: ESRS S1-2 (engagement with own workforce and worker representatives) and ESRS S1-3 (remediation processes and channels to raise concerns).
- Social dialogue and collective bargaining: DNB engages regularly with several trade unions; six unions represent over half of employees. Dialogue occurs via quarterly Group- and unit-level meetings and additional information/consultation meetings at multiple organizational levels. Decisions affecting employees are made within these forums, aligned with legislation, collective agreements, and internal practice. Responsibility sits with the Head of Governance and Strategy in HR, within the employer policy governance function.
- Effectiveness: No direct measurement system; low levels of conflict are used as a proxy for effective, balanced cooperation. Employee representatives are involved before decisions are made.
- Employee feedback and workplace climate: Annual working environment survey maps experiences of discrimination and unfair treatment, informing D&I strategy, goals, and measures, elevating the topic for discussion and providing guidance on actions and support. Managers are trained to detect and address discrimination and support vulnerable employees.
- D&I governance and networks: Dedicated D&I officers in every business area and Group unit ensure leadership support and integration of D&I in product and service development. Active employee-run networks (with HR support) cover equality, multicultural diversity, LGBT+, and an internal ODA network for women in technology, providing additional employee insights.
- Complaint and whistleblowing channels: Employees can report concerns via management, HR, safety representatives, or an external whistleblowing channel (varsling@dnb.no), with further details referenced under ESRS G1. Complaints are handled confidentially, respecting legal and agreed confidentiality. DNB promotes psychological safety to lower the threshold for speaking up.
- Case handling and remediation: Depending on case nature, HR engages appropriate resources (coaches, HR, legal, HSE), while internal audit or legal handle whistleblowing cases. Annual surveys map unfair treatment to guide preventive work and scope, with measures implemented as needed.
- Awareness and accessibility: Notification channels are communicated through internal webpages and information materials, with ongoing mapping to ensure visibility and use.

nodes.title: Notification channels
nodes.heading: 5.1.1.4 Notification channels
nodes.start_phrase: If an employee feels that they are being subjected to differential treatment or discrimination, or they experience other negative incidents, they can report this through different channels.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: ESRS S1 (Own workforce) covering engagement with employees and representatives, grievance/whistleblowing channels, and actions on material workforce impacts, risks, and opportunities.
- Social dialogue and collective bargaining: DNB maintains structured engagement with multiple trade unions (six in Norway, representing over half of employees) under collective agreements. Regular quarterly meetings occur at Group, business area, and unit levels, with additional information/consultation forums where decisions affecting employees are made in line with laws and agreements. Responsibility sits with HR’s head of governance and strategy within a central employer policy function.
- Effectiveness of engagement: No direct measurement framework, but low levels of conflict indicate effective, balanced cooperation. Employee representatives are consulted before decisions.
- Employee feedback and inclusion: Annual working environment surveys map experiences of discrimination and unfair treatment, informing D&I strategy, goals, and measures, and ensuring regular organisational discussion and guidance on reporting and support. Managers are trained to detect and address discrimination and support vulnerable employees.
- D&I governance and networks: Dedicated D&I officers in every business area/unit drive the agenda and embed D&I in products/services. Active employee-run networks (with HR support) include equality, multicultural diversity, LGBT+, and an internal ODA network for women in technology, providing insight into employee perspectives.
- Grievance and whistleblowing: Multiple confidential channels for reporting discrimination/unfair treatment (management, HR, safety reps, external whistleblowing channel). Emphasis on psychological safety and low reporting threshold. Cases are handled by appropriate functions (HR, legal, HSE, internal audit) and, when needed, external specialists; corrective measures may occur at individual and system levels.
- Awareness and training: Information on channels via intranet, materials, and surveys; mandatory annual Code of Conduct training covers how and why to report concerns. DNB monitors and follows up issues raised and collaborates with stakeholders to ensure channel effectiveness.
- Actions on material impacts and risks (2024): Updated D&I strategy (originally 2022) with new measures to increase women in management after a decline in levels 1–4; gender balance embedded in strategic job transitions. Requirements include: identifying top male and female finalists in management recruitment; targets of at least 50% women in leadership/talent programs and 40% women on successor lists; emphasis on gender balance when changing management team composition.
- Risk assessment and mitigation: Systematic 2024 risk assessments per Anti-Discrimination Act across recruitment, pay/conditions, promotions, development, facilitation, work–family balance, and risks of harassment/sexual harassment/gender-based violence; integrated into operational risk management. No new risks requiring additional measures beyond ongoing operations. Mitigation centers on Code of Conduct adherence, bias awareness, competence building, and regular training for managers and safety reps with clear escalation duties.
- Roles and accountability: Central HR ensures compliance with anti-discrimination protections and leads D&I measures; a dedicated subject-matter expert supports these topics; HR manages Group-level employer responsibilities.
- Additional 2024 initiatives: Strengthened the multicultural diversity network to build awareness and competence (e.g., celebrating diverse festivals/holidays).

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 5.1.1.5 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: Several measures have been implemented in the Group in connection with DNB’s work with diversity and equality and how it can affect employees positively by supporting equal opportunities.
nodes.summary:
- Reporting and conduct: Annual Code of Conduct training informs and encourages reporting of unacceptable circumstances; employee surveys check awareness of reporting channels. DNB monitors notifications, collaborates with stakeholders, and uses external specialists for complex discrimination cases; breaches may lead to individual and system-level corrective measures.

- ESRS S1-4 (Actions): Updated 2024 diversity and inclusion strategy (originally 2022) with new measures to lift women’s representation in management after a decline. Actions include:
  - Recruitment: identify the best qualified male and female candidates before final selection.
  - Talent/succession: target at least 50% female participation in leadership and talent programs and 40% women on successor lists; emphasize gender balance when reshaping management teams.
  - Risk management: systematic assessments of HR processes (recruitment, pay/conditions, promotions/development, facilitation, work–family balance) and risks of harassment/violence; 2024 assessments identified no additional required measures beyond ongoing work.
  - Mitigation: strengthen Code of Conduct compliance, address unconscious bias, regular manager and safety-rep training and escalation routines; central HR oversight with a dedicated expert.
  - Additional measures: strengthened multicultural diversity network (awareness, celebrations, role models), celebrations of International Women’s and Men’s Days, and two disability-focused digital courses with Stiftelsen VI.

- Measuring effectiveness: Ongoing evaluations of courses/events; employee surveys, risk assessments, and notification insights. Inclusion score target ≥5/6; Q4 2024 result 5.3 with 80% response rate. Results are externally processed and reported to Group Management and the Board. Legal limits on demographic data constrain identification of underrepresented groups. Premises follow local universal design/building regulations.

- ESRS S1-5 (Targets/metrics): No time-bound diversity/equality targets, but an ongoing 40/60 gender balance ambition at all management levels (1–4). Tracked quarterly across the Group (excluding managers on leave and a specified subsidiary), reported to the Board; metrics not externally validated beyond the auditor.
  - 2024 outcomes: Women at management levels 1–4 averaged 36.5% (down from 38.8% in 2023); Board 50.0% women; Group Management 41.7%.
  - Breakdown: Levels 1–2: 42.9% women (6/14); Level 3: 39.4% (41/104); Level 4: 35.6% (153/430).

- ESRS S1-6 (Workforce characteristics): As of 31 Dec 2024, total employees 11,515: 6,183 men, 5,332 women; “Other” and “Not reported” both 0. Figures may differ from financial note disclosures due to inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., employees on leave, AAP, certain subsidiaries).

nodes.title: Targets and tracking
nodes.heading: 5.1.1.6.1 Targets and tracking
nodes.start_phrase: DNB does not have any time-specific targets for the topics diversity and quality but has an express ambition of a 40/60 gender balance at every management level (1–4) at any given time.
nodes.summary:
- DNB’s DEI initiatives include showcasing multicultural role models, celebrating International Women’s and Men’s Days, and launching two disability-focused digital courses for employees with Stiftelsen VI. The Group follows building regulations in all countries for universal design.
- Effectiveness is monitored via ongoing course/event evaluations, employee surveys, risk assessments, and whistleblowing channels. Inclusion is tracked through an employee survey (target ≥5/6); Q4 2024 result was 5.3 with an 80% response rate. An external supplier processes survey data; results are reported to Group Management and the Board. Trend analysis flags negative changes for follow-up.
- Legal constraints limit collection/systematization of workforce demographic data, complicating identification of underrepresented groups and targeted quantitative tracking.
