nodes.title: ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users
nodes.heading: 5.2 ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users
nodes.start_phrase: In DNB, consumers and end-users are referred to as customers.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users with emphasis on data protection, linked to ESRS 2 SBM-3 on material impacts, risks, opportunities, and their interaction with strategy and business model.
- Context: DNB handles large volumes of personal data for ~2.4 million personal customers; improper processing poses significant short‑term, material risks to consumers/end-users and to DNB.
- Risk drivers and impacts: Digitalisation and AI increase data protection risk; non-compliance may lead to regulatory fines, reputational damage, customer and income loss, and remediation costs.
- Strategy and values: Data protection embedded in DNB’s strategy and core value “Do the right thing,” aiming to sustain high customer trust.
- Governance and policies (ESRS S4-1): Processing must be secure, transparent, and understandable; guided by the Code of Conduct and other governing documents to ensure compliance with statutory and internal rules.
- Controls and practices: Established governance model, processes and procedures for secure storage and handling of personal data; access management; internal controls; employee training; monitoring legal and regulatory changes; integration of data protection into technological solutions.
- Transparency and engagement: dnb.no provides information on data processing, customer rights, contact points, and complaint mechanisms; customer feedback is used to improve data protection practices.
- Overall: DNB prioritises managing data protection impacts, risks, and opportunities as an ongoing, integral part of operations to safeguard consumers/end-users and maintain regulatory compliance.

nodes.title: Data protection
nodes.heading: 5.2.1 Data protection
nodes.start_phrase: In DNB, consumers and end-users are referred to as customers.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users within DNB’s Sustainability Report, addressing data protection under ESRS 2 SBM-3 (material impacts, risks, opportunities) and ESRS S4-1 (policies).
- Scope and context: DNB treats consumers/end-users as customers and processes large volumes of personal data for ~2.4 million personal customers.
- Material risks and impacts: Improper data processing can breach data protection laws, trigger significant fines, cause reputational loss, and negatively impact customers; this is a material short-term risk intensified by digitalisation and the use of AI.
- Strategy and governance: “Do the right thing” is central to DNB’s strategy, embedding compliance with data protection laws. A group-wide governing model and governing documents guide daily compliance across business areas.
- Controls and practices: Ongoing compliance through employee training, internal controls and guidelines, access management, and monitoring of regulatory changes. Privacy-by-design is emphasized in technological solutions.
- Transparency and customer engagement: dnb.no provides information on personal data processing, customer rights, contact channels, and complaint mechanisms; customer feedback informs continuous improvement.
- Consequences of non-compliance: Potential loss of customers and income due to reputational damage, statutory fines, and remediation costs.
- Policy commitments (ESRS S4-1): All personal data processing must be secure, transparent, and understandable; the Code of Conduct requires adherence to legal and internal rules.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 5.2.1.1 Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: In DNB, consumers and end-users are referred to as customers.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users, focusing on data protection within DNB’s strategy and ESRS 2 SBM-3 (material impacts, risks, opportunities, and their interaction with the business model).
- Context: DNB treats consumers/end-users as customers and processes large volumes of personal data for ~2.4 million personal customers.
- Materiality and risk: Data protection is a short‑term material issue; improper processing can breach laws, trigger large fines, and cause reputational damage, posing risks to customers and DNB. Digitalisation and AI heighten these risks.
- Strategy and values: “Do the right thing” underpins compliance and trust; data protection requirements are embedded in governing documents and a group-wide governance model to ensure business area compliance.
- Controls and processes: Internal procedures for secure storage and management of personal data; access control; employee training; internal controls and guidelines; monitoring regulatory changes; integration of data protection into technological solutions.
- Customer transparency and engagement: dnb.no provides information on data processing, customer rights, contact points, and complaint channels; customer feedback is used to improve data protection practices.
- Consequences of non-compliance: Potential customer and income loss due to reputational harm, statutory fines, and remediation costs.
- Policies (ESRS S4-1): All personal data processing must be secure, transparent, and understandable; the Code of Conduct mandates adherence to legal and internal data protection requirements.

nodes.title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 5.2.1.1.1 Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: In DNB, consumers and end-users are referred to as customers.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and standards: ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users with links to ESRS 2 SBM-3 and ESRS S4-1, focused on data protection as a material topic for DNB’s customers (consumers and end-users).
- Material impacts, risks and opportunities: Handling large volumes of personal data for ~2.4 million customers; improper processing can cause legal breaches, fines, reputational loss, customer attrition and remediation costs; digitalisation and AI heighten data protection risks, making short‑term focus and long‑term risk management essential.
- Strategy and values: “Do the right thing” underpins compliance with data protection rules; maintaining customer trust is central; data protection integrated into technology solutions.
- Governance framework: Group-wide governing model for data protection with processes for secure storage, access control, internal controls, and monitoring legal changes; high priority on preventing breaches and safeguarding rights.
- Policies and documents (ESRS S4‑1): 
  - Code of Conduct (Board-approved) mandates lawful, transparent processing and immediate reporting of breaches.
  - Group Policy for Compliance (incl. GDPR adherence across jurisdictions).
  - Group Instructions for Personal Data Protection and a Global Framework for Personal Data Protection applying to all DNB entities.
  - Framework for the Data Protection Officer (DPO) function where appointed.
- Roles and responsibilities: Group EVPs accountable for compliance; all employees responsible for following rules; DPO monitors processing based on compliance and data subject risk; Compliance and Group Audit provide independent oversight.
- Training and awareness: Governing documents available in Norwegian/English; regular internal communication; mandatory e-learning on data protection with 92% employee completion in 2024; additional competence-building programs.
- Transparency and stakeholder communication: Privacy notices on dnb.no in relevant languages; customers informed via product terms; channels to ask questions or lodge complaints; ability to contact the DPO directly.
- Risk assessments and controls: Use of Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) for high-risk processing, with structured documentation ensuring accountability and verifiability; ongoing monitoring and control within each business area.
- Third-party expectations: Requirements for suppliers and partners via data processor agreements and third-party Code of Conduct.
- Human rights alignment: Commitment to internationally recognized human rights (UN declarations, covenants, ILO core conventions) and reference to OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises.

nodes.title: Governing documents
nodes.heading: 5.2.1.2 Governing documents
nodes.start_phrase: In DNB, all processing of personal data must be secure, transparent and understandable.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on building trust in DNB’s processing of personal data, with a duty for employees to report breaches of legal or internal rules; the Code of Conduct is Board-approved and public.
- Governance framework for data protection and compliance, including:
  - Group policy for compliance (GDPR and local laws).
  - Group instructions for personal data protection and a Global Framework for Personal Data Protection.
  - Framework for Data Protection Officer (DPO) function where required or adopted.
- Scope and applicability: covers all processing of personal data for customers, employees, and others across all DNB companies, including international operations, aligned with local laws.
- Clear roles and responsibilities:
  - Group EVPs accountable for compliance in their units.
  - All employees responsible for adhering to rules.
  - DPO monitors processing based on compliance and data subject risk.
  - Group Compliance and Group Audit provide independent oversight.
- Accessibility and training:
  - Governing documents available in Norwegian and English in the quality system.
  - Ongoing internal communications, guidelines on the intranet, and mandatory e-learning; 92% completion in 2024.
  - Additional courses and competence-building programs.
- Customer and partner transparency:
  - Privacy notice available online in multiple languages and embedded in product terms and agreements.
  - Expectations for suppliers and partners set via data processor agreements and a third-party code of conduct.
- Human rights alignment: commitments under UN human rights instruments and ILO core conventions.
- Risk management:
  - Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) for high-risk processing, with structured, quality-assured, and auditable documentation.
  - Obligation to report certain incidents to the Norwegian Data Protection Authority; 115 personal data breaches reported in 2024.
  - DPO monitors incidents and follow-ups with the Authority’s decisions.
- Complaints and whistleblowing mechanisms (ESRS S4-3):
  - Multiple channels: public notification email (varsling@dnb.no), online bank, customer service, direct DPO contact, and the right to complain to the Data Protection Authority.
  - DPO oversees complaint handling to protect rights and minimize negative impacts; multidisciplinary teams handle cases.
  - Strict confidentiality and access controls; options for anonymous contact.
  - External, independent management of the notification channel by NAVEX/GCS (EthicsPoint) ensuring confidentiality and no tracking.
  - Requirement that business partners provide anonymous, confidential whistleblowing channels.
  - While no explicit confidence assessments are made, incoming enquiries indicate awareness; visibility of channels is ensured and verified (including DPO info spot checks).
- Actions (ESRS S4-4):
  - Group-level measures and continuous, systematic efforts to minimize risks of personal data loss and maintain customer trust.

nodes.title: Complaints processing
nodes.heading: 5.2.1.3 Complaints processing
nodes.start_phrase: Customers can report breaches of the data protection rules and legislation through DNB’s public notification channel ( varsling@dnb.no ) or contact DNB about privacy rights or other data protection-related questions and complaints through the online bank or via the customer service centre.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on customer privacy and data protection compliance: DNB’s governance incorporates legal requirements, and the bank must report certain incidents to the Norwegian Data Protection Authority.
- Incident oversight: 115 personal data breaches were reported in 2024; the Data Protection Officer (DPO) monitors incidents and DNB’s follow-up on Authority decisions.
- Complaints and reporting channels (ESRS S4-3): Customers can report data protection breaches via a public notification channel (varsling@dnb.no), through online banking, customer service, or directly to the DPO by email/post; unsatisfied customers can complain to the Norwegian Data Protection Authority. Information is available on DNB’s data protection webpages.
- Complaint handling approach: The DPO oversees complaint processing to protect customer rights and minimize negative impacts; cases are handled through dialogue and cross-functional collaboration (privacy experts, product specialists, lawyers, managers).
- Confidentiality and access control: Customer data is protected by statutory and contractual confidentiality; access is limited to need-to-know. Anonymous contact with the DPO is possible, and the DPO has a statutory duty of confidentiality. Anonymous reporting via the notification channel is supported, with strict confidentiality and limited case access.
- External whistleblowing system: DNB uses NAVEX/GCS Compliance Services Europe and the EthicsPoint platform for the notification channel, ensuring independence, EU hosting, and enhanced privacy (no IP tracking, phone number storage, or call recording). Further details referenced under Corporate culture (ESRS G1-1).
- Expectations for partners: Business partners must have anonymous, confidential whistleblowing processes that protect whistleblowers.
- Awareness and effectiveness: While no formal assessment of customer confidence is conducted, incoming enquiries indicate familiarity with complaint mechanisms. DNB ensures visibility of channels across webpages, materials, agreements, and product terms; verification occurs via product/service approval and DPO spot checks for DPO contact info.
- Actions and effectiveness (ESRS S4-4): Group-level measures are in place to reduce risks of data mishandling, address customer inconveniences, and sustain trust, with ongoing, systematic improvement efforts.
- Context: Content forms part of the Sustainability Report, Social conditions, ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 5.2.1.4 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: To minimise the risk of personal data going astray and to be able to handle inconveniences to customers, DNB has implemented several measures at Group level.
nodes.summary:
- Commitment and obligations: DNB commits to respecting customer privacy and safeguarding personal data; it must report certain incidents to the Norwegian Data Protection Authority (NDPA). In 2024, DNB reported 115 personal data breaches. The Data Protection Officer (DPO) oversees incident handling and follow-up on NDPA decisions.
- Complaints and reporting channels (ESRS S4-3): Customers can raise data protection concerns via DNB’s public notification channel (varsling@dnb.no), online bank, customer service, or directly to the DPO by email/post; if unsatisfied, they can complain to the NDPA. Information is available on DNB’s privacy webpages.
- Confidentiality and access control: Customer data handling (including complaints) is subject to statutory and contractual confidentiality; only employees with a work-related need have access. The DPO has a statutory duty of confidentiality and can be contacted anonymously.
- Anonymous whistleblowing: Anonymous reports are possible via the notification channel; personal data is not registered. Cases are handled confidentially and restricted to case processors.
- Independent whistleblowing system: DNB uses NAVEX/GCS Compliance Services (EthicsPoint) in the EU to manage varsling@dnb.no, ensuring full confidentiality; the system is separate from DNB’s network and does not track IPs or store phone numbers/recordings. Business partners are required to maintain anonymous, confidential whistleblowing processes.
- Awareness and verification: While no explicit confidence assessment is conducted, incoming enquiries suggest customers know the channels. Availability of contact information is ensured via webpages, materials, agreements, and product terms, with verification through product/service approval processes and DPO spot checks.
- Actions to strengthen data protection (ESRS S4-4):
  - Transparency and information: Ongoing improvements to privacy notices (bank, subsidiaries, EU branches) begun in 2023 and continuing in 2025 to make information clearer and current.
  - Competence and culture: Annual data protection month, lectures with internal/external experts, interactive exercises, and a new internal data protection podcast launched in 2024, with more planned in 2025.
  - Accountability and internal guidelines: New operational privacy framework consolidating guidance and clarifying roles/responsibilities; new AI guidelines highlighting privacy considerations; applicable Group-wide.
  - Effectiveness and incident management: Compliance controls and internal audits assess effectiveness; incidents handled via Group instructions and a common non-compliance system with documented actions; DPO advises on protecting affected parties; customers are informed of high-risk breaches and may seek compensation, complain to NDPA, or pursue court claims.
  - Governance integration: Data protection is embedded in corporate governance, aligned with the Group compliance policy, operational incident management, and supplier-related security/risk management frameworks; NDPA supervises Norwegian companies.
- Organization and resources: Approximately 45 employees work full-time or near full-time on data protection across business areas and Group units, including a central operational privacy team and dedicated legal resources. The DPO acts independently, advises, monitors compliance, and serves as the point of contact for NDPA and data subjects; local DPOs support international offices.
- Metrics and targets (ESRS S4-5):
  - Policy approach: No specific numeric target; compliance with laws is mandated via the Code of Conduct and compliance policy. Compliance risk is managed by Group-wide criteria; practices include regulatory monitoring, personal data procedures, and employee training; ongoing controls, audits, and risk reporting inform continuous improvements.
  - Tracked metrics (externally verified):
    - Fines from NDPA related to GDPR breaches: None received in 2024 (confirmed by the Group Secretariat).
    - Number of non-compliance reports to NDPA (personal data breaches): Identified via a predefined report from the non-compliance system (2024 figure reported earlier as 115).
    - Percentage of employees completing four mandatory data protection courses: Tracked via the Motimate learning platform as of 31 December 2024 (excludes external consultants).

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 5.2.1.5 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: It follows from the Code of Conduct and the compliance policy that DNB must comply with all rules and legislation.
nodes.summary:
- Describes DNB’s data protection governance and resourcing: a distributed setup across all business areas and Group units, supported by a central enablement team and dedicated legal resources; around 45 employees work full-time (or nearly full-time) on data protection, with additional staff handling related tasks as part of broader roles.
- Explains the DPO function: an independent adviser who oversees compliance, organisation, training, and internal control, and serves as the contact point for the Norwegian Data Protection Authority (NDPA) and data subjects; the Group DPO role is led by DNB’s Norwegian DPO with a support team and local DPOs at international offices.
- Outlines policy and approach: compliance with laws per the Code of Conduct and compliance policy; no standalone data protection target—risk-based management using Group-wide materiality criteria; core practices include monitoring regulatory changes, defined procedures for personal data handling, and employee training; effectiveness assessed via controls, internal audits, and regular risk reporting, with continuous improvements to guidelines, technology, and training on an ongoing (non-year-specific) basis.
- Sets out metrics and assurance (inspired by GRI 418-1, verified by the external auditor): 
  1) Fines from the NDPA for GDPR breaches, tracked through Group Secretariat’s receipt of formal decisions (none received in 2024); 
  2) Number of breach notifications (non-compliance reports) sent to the NDPA, derived from a standardized report in the non-compliance system and quality-assured by data protection specialists; 
  3) Percentage of employees completing the four mandatory basic data protection courses, measured via the Motimate learning platform as of 31 December 2024 (excluding external consultants; figures not analyzed).

nodes.title: Targets and tracking
nodes.heading: 5.2.1.5.1 Targets and tracking
nodes.start_phrase: It follows from the Code of Conduct and the compliance policy that DNB must comply with all rules and legislation.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines how DNB organizes and governs data protection, the role of the Data Protection Officer (DPO), and the metrics it uses to monitor compliance under ESRS S4.

- Organization and resources: Data protection responsibilities are embedded across all business areas and Group units, with about 45 employees working full time or nearly full time on data protection. A central team supports operationalizing rules through Group-wide tools, solutions, and guidance, complemented by dedicated legal resources and additional staff with partial compliance duties.

- DPO function: The DPO acts as an independent adviser, overseeing compliance, organization, training, and internal control, and serves as the contact point for the Norwegian Data Protection Authority and all data subjects. The function is led by DNB’s Norwegian DPO with a dedicated team and supported by local DPOs at international offices.

- Policies, practices, and oversight: While no specific data protection target is set, the Code of Conduct and compliance policy require adherence to all laws, with compliance risk managed per Group-wide materiality criteria. Core practices include regulatory monitoring, procedures for handling personal data, and employee training. Effectiveness is assessed through controls, internal audits, and regular risk reporting to management, with continuous improvements implemented as needed rather than tied to a specific year.

- Metrics and verification (aligned with ESRS S4-5 and inspired by GRI 418-1), externally verified by the auditor:
  1) Fines from the Norwegian Data Protection Authority for GDPR breaches—tracked via Group Secretariat archiving of authority correspondence; confirmed no fine-imposing letters received in 2024.
  2) Number of non-compliance reports (personal data breach notifications) sent to the Authority—counted using a predefined report template from the Group’s non-compliance system, quality assured by data protection specialists.
  3) Percentage of employees completing four mandatory basic data protection courses—measured via the Motimate learning platform as of 31 December 2024; excludes external consultants and figures are unanalysed.

This content appears in DNB Group’s 2024 Annual Report under the Sustainability Report, Social conditions, ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users.

nodes.title: Access to quality information
nodes.heading: 5.2.2 Access to quality information
nodes.start_phrase: As a market leader in the Norwegian personal customer market, with about 2.4 million personal customers in different customer groups – from the young to the elderly – DNB can have a positive impact on customers’ financial choices by offering good advisory services and information, as well as by making information available to more people.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Access to quality information for consumers, framed under ESRS 2 SBM-3 (material impacts, risks, opportunities) and ESRS S4-1 (policies for consumers and end-users).
- Strategic context: As a Norwegian market leader with ~2.4 million personal customers, DNB aims to positively influence customers’ financial decisions through high-quality advice and accessible information; impact is material in the short, medium and long term.
- Risk and opportunity: Trust and reputation depend on accurate, unbiased, complete information; poor information can cause reputational damage, financial loss for DNB, and harm to customers’ finances and debt-servicing capacity.
- Management response: Systematic competence development for advisers to ensure responsible advisory services; delivery of tailored products and advice via a modern, multi-channel distribution network (online bank, mobile, customer service centres, branches).
- Inclusion and accessibility: Identification and mapping of vulnerable/special-needs customer groups (2023) using Statistics Norway data and external analyses; implementation of measures to improve access; work to meet universal design requirements for digital information to prevent discrimination.
- Governance framework: Guided by DNB’s Code of Conduct and Group sustainability policy, with ESRS cross-references to minimum disclosure requirements in other report sections.
- Conduct expectations: High-integrity, transparent, respectful customer service; robust complaints handling; communication that is open, honest, clear, timely and accurate.
- Ethical commitments: Respect for internationally recognised human rights and rights at work.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 5.2.2.1 Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: As a market leader in the Norwegian personal customer market, with about 2.4 million personal customers in different customer groups – from the young to the elderly – DNB can have a positive impact on customers’ financial choices by offering good advisory services and information, as well as by making information available to more people.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Access to quality information for consumers under ESRS S4 and ESRS 2 SBM-3, linking material impacts, risks, and opportunities to DNB’s strategy and business model.
- Strategic context: As Norway’s leading personal bank (≈2.4 million customers), DNB seeks to positively influence customers’ financial decisions through high-quality advisory services and broad information access; this positive impact is material in the short, medium, and long term.
- Risk perspective: Inaccurate, misleading, incomplete, or biased information can erode trust and reputation, lead to customer loss and financial impacts for DNB, and harm customers’ finances and debt-servicing capacity.
- Responses and programs: A systematic competence development program for advisers to ensure responsible, high-quality advice; customer-first strategy with advice and products tailored to needs.
- Channels and accessibility: Service delivered through online banking, mobile, customer service centers, and branches; emphasis on universal design for digital information to prevent discrimination and support customers with disabilities.
- Vulnerable customers: 2023 mapping of vulnerable groups using quantitative and qualitative analyses (Statistics Norway data and external insights); implementation of measures to improve access to advice and information for these groups.
- Governance framework: Code of Conduct and Group policy for sustainability guide conduct toward consumers and end-users, including standards for:
  - Customer service: integrity, accessibility, transparency, respectful treatment, and robust complaint handling.
  - Communication: open, honest, clear, timely, and accurate information.
- Commitments and references: Respect for internationally recognized human rights and labor rights; cross-references to related ESRS disclosures and governing documents.

nodes.title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 5.2.2.1.1 Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: As a market leader in the Norwegian personal customer market, with about 2.4 million personal customers in different customer groups – from the young to the elderly – DNB can have a positive impact on customers’ financial choices by offering good advisory services and information, as well as by making information available to more people.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of the section: Access to quality information for consumers/end-users within Strategy and Material impacts, risks and opportunities (ESRS 2 SBM-3; ESRS S4).
- DNB’s role and impact: As a Norwegian market leader with ~2.4 million personal customers, DNB can positively influence customers’ financial decisions through high-quality advice and information; impact is material in the short, medium and long term.
- Strategic priority and risk: “Customer comes first” strategy emphasizes trust and reputation; poor-quality information (inaccurate, misleading, incomplete, biased) poses reputational and financial risks for DNB and can harm customers’ finances and debt-servicing capacity.
- Capability building: Systematic competence development program ensures advisers provide responsible, high-quality financial advice.
- Service delivery model: Tailored products and advice offered through multiple channels—online bank, mobile, customer service centres and branches.
- Inclusion and accessibility: Vulnerable/special-needs customer groups mapped in 2023 using quantitative and qualitative analyses (Statistics Norway data and external insights); measures implemented to improve access; commitment to universal design of digital information to prevent discrimination, including for customers with disabilities.
- Governance and policies (ESRS S4-1): Customer advice and information practices are guided by DNB’s Code of Conduct and Group policy for sustainability, with cross-references to ESRS minimum disclosure requirements.
- Code of Conduct expectations: 
  - Customer service—professional, respectful, transparent, with robust complaints handling per established procedures.
  - Communication—open, honest, clear, timely and accurate.
- Human rights commitment: Sustainability policy requires respect for internationally recognised human rights and labour rights.

nodes.title: Governing documents
nodes.heading: 5.2.2.2 Governing documents
nodes.start_phrase: How DNB will work to offer good advisory services and information to personal customers is set out in the governing document DNB’s Code of Conduct and the Group policy for sustainability.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Access to quality information for consumers as a material topic under ESRS, tied to DNB’s strategy where “the customer comes first.”
- Materiality and risks: Accurate, timely, and unbiased information is critical to trust, reputation, and financial outcomes; poor information can harm customers’ finances and DNB’s reputation and profitability across short, medium, and long term.
- Strategy and delivery: Broad, needs-based advisory and product offering via online bank, mobile, customer service centres, and branches; systematic competence development for advisers to ensure responsible advice.
- Vulnerable customers and accessibility: 2023 mapping of vulnerable groups using Statistics Norway data and external analyses; measures to make advisory services and information accessible; commitment to universal design of digital information to include people with disabilities; targeted insight work including customers with non-Western backgrounds.
- Governance framework: Code of Conduct and Group Sustainability Policy guide customer treatment and communication (open, clear, honest, timely, correct), respect for human rights and worker rights; supporting guidelines and processes (e.g., Shelf Control, Activity Check) to protect consumer rights and ensure compliant marketing.
- Standards alignment: Practices assessed as consistent with OECD Guidelines (Consumer Interests) with emphasis on correct information, accessibility, complaints mechanisms, and legal compliance.
- Consumer engagement (ESRS S4-2): Proactive and reactive channels—ongoing customer contact, surveys, insight projects, and complaints—to identify impacts and opportunities; responsibility sits with the EVP of Personal Banking; effectiveness gauged via continuous customer satisfaction measurement and user testing.
- Complaints and remediation (ESRS S4-3): Multiple channels for raising concerns—online bank complaint form to DNB’s complaints department, mail (including anonymous by post), customer service/branches, DNB’s external notification channel, and external bodies (FinKN, Norwegian Anti-Discrimination Tribunal); no known 2024 cases to the Anti-Discrimination Tribunal.
- Oversight and processes: Clear procedures for handling complaints and feedback; customer-focused development of products, services, and information to enhance availability and quality.

nodes.title: Interaction with personal customers
nodes.heading: 5.2.2.3 Interaction with personal customers
nodes.start_phrase: DNB obtains or receives perspectives from personal customers on several levels, and these affect decisions or activities that focus on handling actual and potential impacts on customers, and contribute to identifying opportunities in various customer groups.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on open, clear, and honest communication with all target groups.
- Frameworks to protect consumer rights: Code of Conduct, sustainability policy, and specific guidelines, routines, and processes (e.g., Shelf Control, Activity Check, customer service routines).
- Alignment with OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises (Chapter VIII, Consumer Interests), focusing on correct and accessible information, disability adaptations, access to internal/external complaints mechanisms, and compliant marketing.
- Multiple reporting channels for personal customers: online forms, customer service, external notification channel, and external bodies (FinKN and the Norwegian Anti-Discrimination Tribunal); no 2024 cases reported to the Anti-Discrimination Tribunal related to information.
- ESRS S4-2 (Engagement): Proactive and reactive methods to gather customer perspectives (contact, surveys, insight work, complaints); integration into decisions and product/service development with strong advisory and accessibility focus. Responsibility spans relevant functions, with overall accountability held by the EVP Personal Banking. Effectiveness gauged via continuous customer satisfaction measurement and targeted insight, including mapping vulnerable/marginalised groups and an in-depth survey of people with a non-Western background. Ongoing work to meet universal design requirements for digital information through testing and user participation.
- ESRS S4-3 (Complaints and remediation): Clear channels to raise concerns and remediate negative impacts, including written card/bank complaints via online bank, post (with anonymous option), customer service, and branches; DNB’s notification channel; and guidance to external complaints bodies (FinKN and the Anti-Discrimination Tribunal).

nodes.title: Complaints processing
nodes.heading: 5.2.2.4 Complaints processing
nodes.start_phrase: Customers who are dissatisfied, experience negative incidents or want to raise concerns or needs can contact DNB through various channels and have the matter assessed.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines DNB’s commitment to open, clear, and honest communication with consumers, supported by the Code of Conduct, sustainability policy, and operational guidelines to protect consumer rights.
- It details processes (Shelf Control and Activity Check) and customer service routines designed to ensure accurate, accessible information, compliant marketing, and alignment with OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises (Consumer Interests).
- Multiple reporting and complaint mechanisms are available to personal customers: online forms, customer service, an external notification channel, and external bodies such as the Norwegian Financial Services Complaints Board (FinKN) and the Anti-Discrimination Tribunal; no related cases were reported to the Tribunal in 2024.
- Under ESRS S4-2, DNB engages consumers proactively (contact, surveys, insight work) and reactively (complaints) to manage impacts, with responsibility anchored in Personal Banking leadership; customer satisfaction is measured continuously, and targeted insight includes mapping vulnerable groups and improving universal design of digital services.
- Under ESRS S4-3, the complaints process includes clear channels (online, post, phone, in-branch), accessibility accommodations, and defined timelines (initiation within three business days; responses within 15 days, up to 35 in extraordinary cases); remediation and compensation may occur when significant negative impacts are found, especially where external bodies uphold complaints.
- Oversight and learning include regular reporting of notification cases to Group Management and the Board, quarterly FinKN updates to Personal Banking management, customer satisfaction surveys after complaints, and continuous process improvements based on feedback; complaint volumes are reported to the Financial Supervisory Authority of Norway.
- Under ESRS S4-4, actions to enhance advisory quality and information accessibility include strengthening Shelf Control with a 2024 compliance risk guide (security, marketing, greenwashing), adviser training on cultural diversity (2024–2025), capability building for supporting customers with financial difficulties (completed 2024 and embedded in onboarding), and awareness initiatives such as #huninvesterer (#girlsinvest).

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 5.2.2.5 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: DNB has implemented several measures to offer good advisory services and information, and to make this information available to more people.
nodes.summary:
- Remediation and compensation: DNB remedies or contributes to remedying significant negative customer impacts, including compensating personal customers for financial losses from misinformation when external complaints bodies uphold their cases.
- Complaints handling and accessibility: Multiple channels (including a notification channel in Norwegian and English, via phone or in writing) are available to all personal customers; DNB aims to resolve issues at first contact, starts processing within three business days, sends a preliminary reply within 15 business days if unresolved (up to 35 days in extraordinary cases). Support is provided for customers facing language or disability barriers; non-digital customers may need to sign and return forms.
- External complaints and oversight: Public, no-cost external complaints bodies are available; DNB monitors cases across channels and reports complaint volumes to Finanstilsynet via the card and bank complaints channel (for all cases, not only information/advisory). Status of notification cases is regularly reported to Group Management and the Board; Personal Banking management receives quarterly updates on FinKN cases.
- Measuring effectiveness and learning: While no explicit effectiveness assessment of channels is made, usage indicates awareness. Customer satisfaction surveys (including for card and bank complaints) capture scores and feedback; insights are reviewed continuously and shared internally to improve processes and advisor learning.
- Actions to improve advice and information (ESRS S4-4): Key controls include Shelf Control and Activity Check to ensure relevant, high-quality products, services, and communications; a 2024 compliance risk guide enhances assessments of security, marketing, and greenwashing risks.
- Advisor competence and training: Training on cultural diversity (initiated 2024, completes 2025); competency building for handling customers with financial problems (completed 2024 and embedded in mandatory onboarding); a 2024 training program following the Sbanken acquisition to guide brand choice; ongoing basic and role-specific training with internal tools to ensure consistent, accurate information.
- Customer initiatives and outcomes: Focus on young customers via targeted communications and the Ung-milliarden mortgage campaign; surveys show 30% of customers aged 18–33 rated advice 5–6/6 in Q4 2024 vs 25% overall. #huninvesterer (#girlsinvest) continues with high reach—57% of Norwegians aware (≈2.5m adults) and 45% of those aware have taken steps to improve their finances.
- Error handling and prevention: Internal feedback loops from complaints to product/business areas; example correction in 2024 where Sbanken’s website provided incorrect fee information—fees were reversed after complaints. Guidelines, routines, and the Shelf Control/Activity Check processes aim to prevent misleading or incomplete information.
- Internal support structures: Cross-functional units, subject matter managers, and dedicated referral functions support advisors in delivering accurate advice and routing customers to the right expertise.
- Scope and assurance: Measures largely pertain to Personal Banking in Norway; effectiveness is reviewed via internal/external audits, stakeholder feedback, and surveys.
- Metrics and targets (ESRS S4-5): No single overarching target; DNB relies on established processes to ensure information quality, monitors complaint volumes (including FinKN cases), and uses customer satisfaction insights to drive continuous improvements to guidelines, governance documents, and training without a fixed-year target.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 5.2.2.6 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: No overriding target has been set for this topic, but several processes have been established to ensure that the information that is given to customers is of good quality and is up to date.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines DNB Group’s approach to consumer and end-user matters under ESRS S4, focusing on metrics, targets, and continuous improvement. Key points include:
- A dedicated unit directs personal customers to advisers with the right expertise.
- No single overarching target is set for ESRS S4-5; instead, established processes ensure customer information is accurate, high-quality, and current (details referenced under Actions, ESRS S4-4).
- Performance is monitored through customer complaints (card and bank) and cases escalated to FinKN, with further details under Complaints processing (ESRS S4-3).
- Customer satisfaction surveys provide insight into the effectiveness of measures.
- Insights drive ongoing enhancements such as updates to internal guidelines, revisions to governing documents, and employee training.
- This is a continuous effort without a fixed target year, embedded within the DNB Group Annual Report 2024 Sustainability report (Social conditions, ESRS S4).

nodes.title: Targets and tracking
nodes.heading: 5.2.2.6.1 Targets and tracking
nodes.start_phrase: No overriding target has been set for this topic, but several processes have been established to ensure that the information that is given to customers is of good quality and is up to date.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from DNB Group’s 2024 Annual Report, Sustainability Report—Social conditions, ESRS S4 (Consumers and end-users).
- Customer advisory setup: A dedicated unit routes personal customers with specific thematic needs to advisers with appropriate expertise.
- ESRS S4-5 (Metrics and targets): No single overarching target; instead, established processes ensure customer information is accurate, high quality, and up to date (with related procedures detailed under Actions, ESRS S4-4).
- Monitoring and feedback: DNB tracks customer-reported card and bank complaints, cases escalated to FinKN, and conducts customer satisfaction surveys to gauge effectiveness (with complaints handling detailed under ESRS S4-3).
- Continuous improvement: Insights drive updates to internal guidelines, revisions to governing documents, and employee training; work is ongoing and not tied to a specific target year.

nodes.title: Cyber security
nodes.heading: 5.3 Cyber security
nodes.start_phrase: Financial institutions like DNB are continuously exposed to cyber attacks.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Cyber security as a company-specific, material topic for DNB under ESRS 2 (SBM-3 and MDR-P), despite not being covered by topical ESRS standards.
- Risk context: Financial institutions face continuous cyber threats from actors seeking data theft, system sabotage, and financial gain.
- Strategic relevance: Cyber security is integral to DNB’s strategy and business model, aligned with its ambition to support a safe digital economy.
- Potential impacts: Attacks can disrupt stable operations, payments, and critical banking services; harm profitability, reputation, and customer trust; and have broad negative effects on customers, employees, partners, and society.
- Data and system protection: Emphasis on confidentiality, integrity, and availability—preventing unauthorized access, alteration, deletion, or loss, and ensuring information is accurate and accessible.
- Financial and regulatory consequences: Possible large fines, customer churn, and reduced societal trust. The risk is identified in the downstream value chain and is especially relevant in the short term.
- Governance framework: Managed through DNB’s Board-approved governance principles; objectives based on regulatory requirements, supervisory expectations, contractual obligations, the threat landscape, and risk appetite; aligned with internationally recognized security practices.
- Management objectives: Prevent, detect, handle, and avoid recurrence of security incidents.
- Supporting policies:
  - Group policy for security: Defines roles, responsibilities, security management, and objectives (excludes HSE), and is publicly available on dnb.no.
  - Group policy for information technology (IT policy): Sets principles for IT governance to ensure high-quality, state-of-the-art services, clarify roles and responsibilities, and support business processes and future growth.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 5.3.1 Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: Financial institutions like DNB are continuously exposed to cyber attacks.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Cyber security as a company-specific, material topic for DNB, not covered by topical ESRS but addressed under ESRS 2 (SBM-3 and MDR-P).
- Strategic integration: Core to DNB’s strategy and business model, aligned with its ambition to enable a safe digital economy.
- Risk landscape: Continuous exposure to cyber attacks from actors seeking data theft, system sabotage, and financial gain.
- Potential impacts: Operational disruptions (including payments and critical banking services), data integrity and availability risks, and negative effects on customers, employees, partners, and society; financial penalties, customer churn, reputational damage, and loss of trust.
- Value chain and time horizon: Material risk identified in the downstream value chain; most acute in the short term to ensure future viability.
- Governance and objectives: Board-approved governance principles guide security; objectives based on regulatory requirements, supervisory expectations, contractual obligations, threat landscape, group goals, and risk appetite; grounded in internationally accepted practices.
- Management approach: Prevent, detect, manage, and prevent recurrence of security incidents.
- Key policies:
  - Group Policy for Security: Defines roles, responsibilities, management approach, and objectives for security; excludes HSE; publicly available on dnb.no.
  - Group Policy for Information Technology: Sets principles for IT management and governance, ensures high-quality IT delivery, supports adoption of new technology for state-of-the-art services and growth, and clarifies IT roles and responsibilities supporting business processes.

nodes.title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 5.3.1.1 Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: Financial institutions like DNB are continuously exposed to cyber attacks.
nodes.summary:
- Positions cyber security as a company-specific, material topic for DNB under ESRS 2 SBM-3 and MDR-P, despite not being covered by topical ESRS standards.
- Explains DNB’s exposure to cyber attacks and dependence on stable IT systems and robust internal processes to safeguard operations and customers.
- Describes threat actors’ motives (data theft, system sabotage, financial gain) and the potential consequences: operational disruptions (including payments and critical services), impacts on customers, employees, partners, and society, as well as fines, customer churn, reputational damage, and loss of trust.
- Frames cyber security as integral to DNB’s strategy and business model, aligned with its ambition to enable a safe digital economy.
- Specifies security objectives centered on protecting confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information; ensuring accuracy and timeliness; and preventing, detecting, managing, and avoiding recurrence of incidents.
- Identifies the negative impact and risk primarily in the downstream value chain and as a short-term priority for viability.
- Outlines governance: Board-approved governance principles; objectives grounded in regulatory requirements and expectations across operating countries, contractual obligations, the current threat landscape, the Group’s goals and risk appetite, and internationally accepted security practices; documents available in DNB’s internal quality system.
- Lists key governing policies:
  - Group Policy for Security: defines roles, responsibilities, and management approach to security; sets overall objectives; excludes HSE; publicly available on dnb.no.
  - Group Policy for Information Technology: sets principles for IT governance and delivery to ensure high-quality, state-of-the-art services and support future growth; clarifies roles and responsibilities for IT management and delivery; supports business processes.

nodes.title: Management of material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 5.3.2 Management of material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The overarching governing document for managing material impacts, risks and opportunities relating to cyber security in the Group is DNB’s governance principles, which have been approved by the Board of DNB Bank ASA.
nodes.summary:
- Cyber security is identified as a company-specific, material topic for DNB under ESRS 2 (SBM-3), even though it is not covered by topical ESRS standards.
- It is integral to DNB’s strategy and business model, aligned with its ambition to enable a safe digital economy.
- DNB faces continuous cyber threats from actors seeking to steal information, sabotage systems, or gain financially, posing risks to confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data.
- Potential impacts include operational disruptions (e.g., payments and critical services), harm to customers, employees, partners, and society, as well as financial penalties, customer churn, reputational damage, and reduced trust.
- The negative impacts are identified particularly in the downstream value chain and are most acute in the short term, requiring immediate focus to ensure future viability.
- Governance is anchored in Board-approved governance principles; security objectives are based on regulatory requirements, authority expectations, contractual obligations, the threat landscape, and DNB’s goals and risk appetite, and follow internationally accepted practices.
- The aim is to prevent, detect, manage, and avoid recurrence of security incidents.
- Key governing documents include:
  - Group policy for security: defines roles, responsibilities, management approach, and overall objectives (excludes HSE) and is publicly available on dnb.no.
  - Group policy for information technology (IT policy): sets IT governance principles, ensures high-quality IT delivery, supports innovation and future growth, and clarifies roles and responsibilities for IT management and delivery.

nodes.title: Governing documents
nodes.heading: 5.3.2.1 Governing documents
nodes.start_phrase: The overarching governing document for managing material impacts, risks and opportunities relating to cyber security in the Group is DNB’s governance principles, which have been approved by the Board of DNB Bank ASA.
nodes.summary:
- Topic and materiality: Cyber security is identified as a company-specific, material topic for DNB under ESRS 2 (SBM-3, MDR-P, MDR-A), even though it is not covered by topical ESRS standards. As a financial institution, DNB faces continuous cyber threats that can disrupt operations, impact customers, employees, and society, and harm profitability, reputation, and trust.
- Strategic integration: Cyber security is integral to DNB’s strategy and business model, aligned with its ambition to support a safe digital economy. Objectives focus on protecting information and IT systems (confidentiality, integrity, availability), preventing, detecting, managing, and avoiding recurrence of incidents.
- Impact scope and time horizon: The primary negative impacts and risks are in the downstream value chain, with highest relevance in the short term due to immediate operational and customer-facing implications (e.g., payment execution and critical services).
- Governance framework: An overarching governance principles document approved by the Board sets direction for managing cyber-related impacts, risks, and opportunities. Security objectives are based on regulatory expectations in operating jurisdictions, contractual obligations, threat landscape, goals, and risk appetite, and reflect internationally accepted practices.
- Policies and instructions:
  - Group policy for security: Defines roles, responsibilities, and overall security management (publicly available on dnb.no).
  - Group IT policy: Sets principles for IT governance and delivery to ensure high-quality, modern services.
  - Group instructions for cyber security: Requirements to prevent, detect, and respond to attacks; protects information processed for customers and third parties.
  - Group instructions for security governance: Describes systematic security governance to achieve and maintain acceptable security levels.
  - Group instructions for business continuity: Requirements for crisis management, IT backup and recovery, outsourcing arrangements, and emergency preparedness.
  - All documents are available in Norwegian and English to all employees, apply across the DNB Group (including international operations), and are subordinate to applicable laws and binding rules.
- Roles and accountability: The CEO is responsible for day-to-day security, conducts annual assessments with Group Management, and reports to the Board. The Group EVP of Technology & Services oversees comprehensive security governance. The CSO leads Group Security, sets objectives, and reports to the CEO and Board. Group EVPs own risks in their areas, must involve the CSO/CISO, and report risks and non-compliance; IT-responsible EVPs implement IT management requirements.
- Standards adopted: DNB has adopted the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 for risk management and bases security requirements and controls on NIST SP 800-53.
- Actions and resources (2024 focus): Continuous monitoring and updating of security measures to enhance digital resilience. Key 2024 action included strengthening security governance by updating governing documents with clear linkage to control-level requirements; an overarching cyber security roadmap concluded in 2024, while other measures continue on an ongoing basis.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 5.3.2.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: Managing the negative impacts that can arise from cyber attacks and data breaches requires continuous monitoring and updating of security measures.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasizes the critical role of cybersecurity for DNB’s customers and Norwegian society, outlining comprehensive governance through group-level instructions and policies.
- Details three core governing documents:
  - Group instructions for cyber security (prevent, detect, respond; protect digital information and IT systems, including customer/third-party data).
  - Group instructions for security governance (systematic security management to maintain acceptable security levels).
  - Group instructions for business continuity (framework for continuity and crisis management, IT backup/outsourcing/recovery plans, emergency organization).
- Clarifies scope and accessibility: policies apply to all DNB entities, employees (permanent and temporary), and international operations; documents are available internally in Norwegian and English; the Group Security policy is public. External laws take precedence in case of conflicts, with duties to notify the document owner.
- Defines governance and accountability:
  - CEO accountable for day-to-day security; annual assessment with Group Management and reporting to the Board.
  - Group EVP Technology & Services responsible for comprehensive security governance and information to management/Board.
  - CSO leads Group Security, sets objectives, and reports security levels.
  - Group EVPs own risks in their areas, must involve CSO/CISO, report risks/non-compliance, and ensure IT management adherence where applicable.
- Adopts recognized frameworks: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 for risk management and NIST SP 800-53 for adaptable security and privacy controls.
- Outlines 2024 actions (ESRS 2 MDR-A):
  - Strengthened security governance by updating governing documents and linking them to control-level requirements; established assurance controls and improved operationalization for better risk/compliance insight.
  - Advanced regulatory compliance with DORA and NYDFS cybersecurity rules, reducing compliance risk.
  - Shifted toward data-driven security reporting, including quarterly reporting of cyber resilience.
  - Built security culture via awareness and training: quarterly phishing simulations, corporate travel safety, AI security guidance, an interactive cyber exercise during Safety Month, and enhanced training for designated security roles (Local/Regional Security Officers and Security Champions). 2025 focus is deeper integration of security in processes, products, and services; participation and course completion tracked.
  - Elevated security within the updated technology strategy; progressed standardization of security architecture; made requirements more accessible and controls more data-driven.
  - Concluded the three-year cybersecurity roadmap in Q1 2024, meeting goals to reduce cyber risk, increase maturity, and strengthen operational resilience; integrated aims into OKRs; began developing a new roadmap to align with group and technology strategies, operational from H1 2025.
  - Increased transparency through the “Financial security in an uncertain world” report (Jan 2024), covering threats, trends, and incidents in cyber/physical/personnel security, fraud, AML, and sanctions; next edition due Feb 2025.
- References material impacts, risks, and opportunities for cybersecurity across the value chain (ESRS 2 SBM-3).
- Lists metrics and targets (ESRS 2 MDR-M) used to track security objectives, reported internally and externally:
  - Percentage of employees completing annual mandatory information security training.
  - Percentage of new employees completing basic information security training.
  - Notes common methodology/assumptions and that metrics are not externally validated.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 5.3.3 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: In order to document target attainment in relation to the security objectives, there is a selection of metrics that are tracked and reported on, internally and externally, on an ongoing basis.
nodes.summary:
- Establishment and operationalisation of assurance controls to ensure an appropriate security level, with better visibility into security and compliance risks.
- 2024 regulatory compliance efforts, notably implementing requirements from the EU’s DORA and New York State’s 23 NYCRR 500 to strengthen compliance and reduce risk.
- Shift toward data-driven IT security reporting, including quarterly reporting on cyber resilience.
- Strengthening security culture through awareness and training: quarterly phishing simulations, corporate travel safety guidance, AI security awareness, an interactive cyber exercise during Safety Month, and continued development of three security roles (Local Security Officers, Regional Security Officer, Security Champions).
- Emphasis for 2025 on deeper integration of security into processes, products, and services; training effectiveness measured by participation and course completion.
- Security elevated within the updated technology strategy; adoption of a standardized security architecture and more accessible, data-driven security requirements and controls to simplify implementation.
- Completion of a three-year cyber security roadmap (approved by the Board in Q1 2024) that reduced cyber risk, increased security maturity, and enhanced operational resilience; objectives embedded into OKRs; development of a new roadmap aligned with the Group and technology strategies to be operational in H1 2025.
- Publication of “Financial security in an uncertain world” in January 2024, covering threats, trends, and incidents across cyber, physical, personnel security, fraud, AML, and sanctions; next edition planned for February 2025.
- Metrics and targets (ESRS 2): tracking training completion and incident management; data sourced directly from learning and security platforms without external assurance.
- Training results for 2024: 85% of all employees completed mandatory annual security training; 98% of new employees completed basic security training.
- Cyber incident monitoring and reporting: 24/7 logging and detection, quarterly reporting, and centralized analysis by the Cyber Defence Center; total incidents roughly flat (20,357 in 2024 vs. 20,208 in 2023) with a reduction in high-severity potential incidents (from 11 to 3); no serious impact on customers or the Group.
- Governance and objectives (ESRS 2 MDR-T): overarching security objectives aligned with NIST CSF 2.0 and NIST SP 800-53; objectives include maintaining an appropriate security level, integrating and prioritizing security, promoting transparency and culture, and continuous evaluation; alignment with regulatory expectations (including Finanstilsynet feedback) to safeguard confidentiality, integrity, availability, business continuity, and stakeholder trust.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets - Introduction
nodes.heading: 5.3.3 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: In order to document target attainment in relation to the security objectives, there is a selection of metrics that are tracked and reported on, internally and externally, on an ongoing basis.
nodes.summary: DNB Group’s ESRS 2 MDR-M/MDR-T disclosure details metrics and tracking for information security targets, focusing on employee training completion and cyber incident monitoring. Two training KPIs—percentage of all employees completing the annual mandatory course and percentage of new employees completing basic security training—use data pulled directly from the Motimate platform (Safe and Secure – Focus 2024; Safe and Secure – Basic training), as of 31 December 2024, and are not externally validated; results were 85% and 98%, respectively. A third metric tracks cyber security incidents via continuous 24/7 security monitoring and logging, with incidents identified through automated alarms and reports, severity assessed against a classification model, quarterly reporting, and data retrieved by the internal Cyber Defence Center; this metric is not externally assured. In 2024, attempted attacks and IT security incidents totaled 20,357 (vs. 20,208 in 2023), while incidents with serious potential to harm fell from 11 to 3, with no serious consequences for customers or the Group, reflecting ongoing efforts to strengthen operational resilience and remedy vulnerabilities.

nodes.title: Targets and tracking
nodes.heading: 5.3.3.1 Targets and tracking
nodes.start_phrase: In DNB, overarching security objectives have been set to achieve a comprehensive and systematic approach to cyber security.
nodes.summary:
- Annual mandatory cyber security training delivered via the Motimate platform:
  - 2024 package: “Safe and Secure – Focus 2024”; new hires receive “Safe and Secure – Basic training.”
  - Completion rates: 85% of employees completed the annual training; 98% of new employees completed basic training by 31 Dec 2024.
  - Data sourced directly from the learning platform; topics adjusted to evolving competence needs; additional role- and topic-specific awareness activities conducted.

- Cyber security incident monitoring and management:
  - Continuous 24/7 security monitoring and logging; IT managers/platform owners ensure deployment of relevant tools.
  - Data flows from security tools to a central logging platform; detection/alerts integrated with incident management platforms.
  - Incidents registered via automated alerts and reports from employees/consultants/external parties; severity assessed using a classification model.
  - Quarterly incident reporting; data retrieved by the internal Cyber Defence Center; metrics not externally assured.

- Incident outcomes and resilience:
  - Attempted attacks and IT security incidents remained stable: 20,208 (2023) vs 20,357 (2024).
  - Serious-potential incidents declined from 11 (2023) to 3 (2024).
  - No incidents in 2024 had serious consequences for customers or the Group.
  - Ongoing improvements in operational resilience and vulnerability remediation.

- Governance, objectives, and frameworks (ESRS 2 MDR-T context):
  - Overarching security objectives guide a systematic approach; not result- or time-specific; unchanged in 2024.
  - Objectives aligned with regulatory requirements, authority expectations (incl. Finanstilsynet feedback), Group targets, and risk appetite.
  - Framework alignment: NIST CSF 2.0; structure based on NIST SP 800-53.
  - Stated objectives: maintain an appropriate, managed security level; integrate security into operations; prioritise security work; promote transparency and a strong security culture; continuously evaluate the security level.
  - Purpose: better risk prioritisation, effective controls/metrics, protection of confidentiality/integrity/availability, business continuity, and stakeholder trust.

- Assurance, oversight, and continuous improvement:
  - Controls and internal audits assess effectiveness and policy compliance; operational risk reported to management levels.
  - Actions include process/procedure updates, technology and digital defence enhancements, and further employee training; work is continuous, not year-bound.
  - Annual independent CSO “Status of Security” report evaluates 11 areas across three maturity levels; reviewed by Group Management and the Board.
  - Operational assurance controls provide insight into compliance and inform risk assessments.

- Transparency and stakeholder engagement:
  - Publication of “Financial security in an uncertain world.”
  - Collaboration with Digital Norway to invite corporate customers to the national cyber security exercise “Hele Norge øver” at DNB customer offices.

- Contextual navigation cues indicate linkage to ESRS S4 (Consumers and end-users) and forthcoming Governance information topics (ESRS G1 Business conduct, corporate culture, corruption/bribery, financial crime, financial infrastructure and stability).

nodes.title: ESRS G1 Business conduct
nodes.heading: 6.1 ESRS G1 Business conduct
nodes.start_phrase: A good corporate culture is crucial for maintaining trust in DNB.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on ESRS G1 Business conduct with emphasis on corporate culture as a material impact, risk, and opportunity linked to strategy and the business model (ESRS 2 SBM-3).
- Corporate culture is deemed short-term material: unethical conduct can lead to financial losses and reputational harm; a strong culture underpins trust in DNB.
- Culture influences strategy, governance, and daily operations; it affects employees and external stakeholders, shaping workplace quality and the Group’s market standing.
- Consequences of weak culture include customer loss, lower ratings, and higher financing costs; a strong culture enhances resilience and reputation.
- Measures in place include internal policies, processes, training programs, and a whistleblowing channel to detect and report misconduct against internal guidelines and the Code of Conduct.
- Governance oversight by the Board and Group Management is referenced under ESRS 2 GOV-1 (detailed in the general disclosures).
- The Code of Conduct is the top-level governing document guiding employee behavior; it covers sustainability, whistleblowing, conflicts of interest, insider information, and anti-corruption, aiming to protect stakeholders, reduce business conduct risks, support a healthy work environment, and safeguard the Group’s reputation.
