nodes.title: Governing documents
nodes.heading: 6.1.1.2.2 Governing documents
nodes.start_phrase: DNB’s Code of Conduct (ethical principles) sets out expectations, obligations and requirements for how employees in the Group should act.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: ESRS G1 Business conduct, emphasizing corporate culture, governance, and ethical business practices within DNB’s strategy and business model.
- Materiality and strategy: Corporate culture identified as a short‑term material topic due to risks of unethical conduct causing financial loss and reputational harm; strong culture supports trust, stakeholder relations, and operational resilience.
- Governance and oversight: Board of Directors and Group Management oversee business conduct (ESRS 2 GOV-1); managers expected to act as role models, foster open dialogue on ethics, and ensure compliance with governing documents.
- Policies and standards: The Code of Conduct is the Group’s top-level policy setting behavioral expectations across sustainability, whistleblowing, conflicts of interest, insider information, anti‑corruption, AML/sanctions, data protection, and security; all employees must comply, complete annual digital training, and face consequences for violations.
- Culture initiatives: New mission and values established with the refreshed strategy; embedded via performance reviews, quarterly tracking, employee surveys, internal communications, and targeted training.
- Whistleblowing framework: Multiple confidential channels for employees and external stakeholders, including an external option (BDO); supports anonymous two‑way communication; clear procedures, roles, and confidentiality safeguards; initial assessments within 48 hours (internal) or 7 days (external); semiannual reporting to Group Management and Board; investigations conducted by Group Audit Special Investigations for independence.
- Legal compliance and protections: Adherence to Norway’s Working Environment Act (anti‑retaliation) and the EU Whistleblower Protection Directive; commitment to non‑retaliation and provision of independent support resources for reporters.
- Actions and resources (ESRS 2 MDR-A): Annual corporate governance cycle with a dedicated ethics month; mandatory competence requirements (e.g., Code of Conduct, duty of confidentiality, conflicts of interest); communications to embed new values; PULS survey gauges how values are reflected in daily work.
- Metrics and targets (ESRS 2 MDR-T): No quantitative targets yet due to topic nature; consideration of setting such targets for 2025.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 6.1.1.3 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: DNB has implemented measures to contribute to sound corporate culture, business conduct and governance.
nodes.summary:
- Compliance and framework: DNB aligns with the EU Whistleblower Protection Directive (EU) 2019/1937 in countries where implemented, establishing a whistleblowing channel for employees and third parties with options for anonymity and two-way anonymous communication. Notifications are handled confidentially with strict access controls.

- Case handling and timelines: Internal fraud/irregularity cases are governed by Group instructions detailing immediate action criteria, notification protocols, and review within 48 hours to assess content and plan next steps (typically same or next business day). External notifications have a seven-day deadline.

- Independence and oversight: Whistleblowing cases are processed by Group Audit Special Investigations under Group Audit, which reports formally to the Board and operatively to Group Management, ensuring objective and independent handling.

- Protection and support: Zero tolerance for retaliation against good-faith reporters, including those who first raise issues with managers. Employees have access to independent support (employee and safety representatives, and occupational health services).

- Training and responsibilities: Managers must inform staff about whistleblowing procedures. Annual mandatory training (via Motimate) covers the whistleblowing channel, Code of Conduct, duty of confidentiality, and conflicts of interest. All employees are responsible for understanding and adhering to the Code and maintaining high ethical standards.

- Actions to strengthen culture (ESRS 2 MDR-A): An annual corporate governance cycle highlights monthly focus areas, with one month dedicated to ethics and conduct. Communication initiatives are planned to embed new corporate values. The PULS working environment survey assesses how well values are reflected in daily work (scored 1–6).

- Metrics and targets (ESRS 2 MDR-T): No measurable, result-oriented targets have been set for this topic due to its nature; DNB will evaluate setting such targets for 2025 and how to track effectiveness.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 6.1.1.4 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: DNB has not set any measurable, result-oriented targets for this material topic due to the nature of the topic.
nodes.summary:
- Compliance with EU Whistleblower Protection Directive (EU) 2019/1937 across DNB’s EU operations.
- Establishment of a whistleblowing channel open to employees and third parties, allowing anonymous, two-way communication; no personal data collected for anonymous reports; strict confidentiality in case handling.
- Clear investigation procedures for internal fraud/irregularities, including immediate action criteria, notification protocols, and review timelines (internal cases assessed and planned within 48 hours—typically same or next business day; external notifications within seven days).
- Objective, independent case processing by Group Audit Special Investigations, organized under Group Audit, which reports to the Board and operates under Group Management.
- Strong anti-retaliation stance for good-faith reporters; availability of independent support (employee and safety representatives, occupational health service).
- Manager responsibility to communicate whistleblowing procedures; mandatory annual training via Motimate; organization-wide expectation to know and live by the Code of Conduct and high ethical standards.
- ESRS 2 MDR-A: Actions and resources to strengthen corporate culture and governance, including an annual corporate governance cycle with a monthly focus on priority topics; one dedicated month for ethics and conduct, reinforcing mandatory courses (Code of Conduct, confidentiality, conflicts of interest).
- Ongoing initiatives to embed new corporate values, supported by communication measures and the PULS employee survey (H2 2024 question on values reflected in daily work).
- Emphasis on managerial role modeling to promote sound governance and conduct.
- ESRS 2 MDR-T: No measurable, result-oriented targets set yet for this topic; DNB will assess appropriateness and potential target-setting for 2025.

nodes.title: Targets and tracking
nodes.heading: 6.1.1.4.1 Targets and tracking
nodes.start_phrase: DNB has not set any measurable, result-oriented targets for this material topic due to the nature of the topic.
nodes.summary:
- DNB aligns with the EU Whistleblower Protection Directive (EU) 2019/1937 across relevant EU countries and has established a whistleblowing channel open to employees and third parties, enabling anonymous, two-way, confidential reporting with no personal data captured for anonymous submissions.
- Case handling is governed by Group instructions for internal fraud and irregularities, with internal cases reviewed within 48 hours (typically same or next business day) and external notifications acknowledged within seven days; investigations are conducted independently by Group Audit Special Investigations, which sits under Group Audit and reports to the Board and Group Management.
- The bank commits to a no-retaliation policy for good-faith reports and offers independent support through employee representatives, safety representatives, and the company health service; managers must inform staff about procedures, and annual whistleblowing training is delivered via the Motimate platform.
- All employees are required to know and adhere to the Code of Conduct, take ethical responsibility, and ensure decisions align with it.
- Actions to strengthen culture, conduct, and governance include an annual corporate governance cycle with monthly focus topics, a dedicated month for ethics and conduct, mandatory courses (Code of Conduct, confidentiality, conflicts of interest), and communication initiatives to embed new values; the PULS survey gauges how values are reflected in daily work.
- Managers are expected to act as role models for sound governance, culture, and conduct.
- DNB has not yet set measurable targets for this topic but will consider doing so for 2025; culture is monitored through thrice-yearly employee surveys covering strategy, values, management, engagement, inclusion, and unwanted conduct, with follow-up at Group and unit levels and measures defined as needed.
- An annual performance process sets goals for both performance and conduct, emphasizing manager-employee dialogue; training and guidance are provided via internal communications and digital courses.
- Remuneration supports strategic goals and risk appetite; variable pay depends on compliance with the Code of Conduct and balances financial and non-financial targets. Violations of rules, the Code, or risk appetite typically result in no bonus.
- No baseline period is set for measuring progress, but DNB generally receives strong external ratings on culture, conduct, and governance risk.

nodes.title: Corruption and bribery
nodes.heading: 6.1.2 Corruption and bribery
nodes.start_phrase: DNB has identified corruption and bribery as material risks that can affect the Group’s own operations.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Corruption and bribery risks within DNB’s own operations, especially where employees interact with external parties, under ESRS 2 SBM-3 and ESRS G1-1.
- Strategic importance: Ethical corporate culture is emphasized to maintain trust among customers, stakeholders and society; topic is most material in the short term.
- Potential impacts: Reputational damage, loss of trust, fines, financial losses, share price decline, higher cost of capital, and reduced access to capital.
- Ongoing management: Continuous prevention and detection efforts to protect financial stability and reputation and to mitigate losses for the Group, investors and stakeholders.
- Key measures: A Group-wide anti-bribery and corruption (ABC) programme aligned with national and international laws; regular risk assessments; employee training; internal control mechanisms to monitor and report suspicious activities.
- Policy framework: Zero tolerance for corruption in the Code of Conduct and Group anti-corruption instructions; a global anti-corruption framework requiring top-level commitment, risk assessments, documented routines and processes, customer and other due diligence, communication and training, and control and follow-up.
- Governance and accountability: The Group EVP for Group Compliance holds ultimate responsibility for implementation; the Group Compliance unit monitors adherence and maintains the anti-corruption framework.
- Documentation and awareness: Governing documents are available in the internal quality system; all employees must be familiar with them and report suspicions of corruption.
- Related references: Minimum disclosure requirements (ESRS 2 MDR-P) for the Code of Conduct are cross-referenced (ESRS S1-1); Code of Conduct is further detailed in the conflicts of interest policy and whistleblowing instructions.

nodes.start_phrase: According to the Code of Conduct, DNB has zero tolerance for all forms of corruption, and the Group must actively prevent and detect corruption by ensuring that all employees are familiar with and follow established rules and routines, as well as by reporting any suspicion of corruption.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: DNB’s approach to corruption and bribery under ESRS G1 Business conduct (ESRS 2 SBM-3, G1-1, G1-3, G1-4, MDR-A/MDR-P).
- Materiality and strategy: Corruption and bribery are identified as material, near‑term risks, especially where employees interact with external parties. Potential impacts include reputational damage, fines, financial losses, share price decline, and higher capital costs. DNB emphasizes a strong ethical culture and continuous prevention/detection to protect financial stability and trust.
- Governance and accountability: Zero‑tolerance set out in the Code of Conduct, Group anti‑corruption instructions, and a global anti‑corruption (ABC) framework requiring top‑level commitment, risk assessments, due diligence (customer and other), communication, training, controls, and follow‑up. The Group EVP for Group Compliance is responsible for implementation; Group Compliance (second line) monitors and reports to Management and the Board; Group Audit (third line) independently investigates and reports to the Board. Whistleblowing and conflicts‑of‑interest policies support the framework. All governing documents are accessible internally and managers must ensure staff understanding and training.
- Prevention and detection: Units must tailor procedures based on ABC risk assessments across their value chains. Suspicion is handled via incident management and whistleblowing channels. Training is risk‑based with three competence levels: mandatory annual digital courses for all employees, plus enhanced/dilemma training and topical seminars for higher‑risk roles. High‑risk functions include direct customer contact, procurement, contract awarding, and hiring. Training also covers the Board and Group Management. Course completion is tracked.
- 2024 actions: Updated governing documents; introduced a gifts and business entertainment register for transparency and documentation; adopted a more quantitative methodology for company‑specific risk assessments. All measures implemented and applicable to all employees.
- Metrics/outcomes: No convictions or fines for breaches of anti‑corruption or anti‑bribery legislation in 2024.

nodes.title: Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.2.2 Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery
nodes.start_phrase: The Code of Conduct, the Group instructions for anti-bribery and the Group’s anti-corruption framework describe what corruption is and provide guidance for employees on how to prevent and detect it.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on DNB’s governance of anti-corruption and bribery under ESRS G1 (Business conduct), with references to whistleblowing channels detailed in Corporate culture (ESRS G1-1).
- Manager responsibilities: ensure employees understand governing documents, adopt a proactive compliance mindset, and complete role-adapted training.
- ESRS G1-3 framework: Code of Conduct, anti-bribery instructions, and a global anti-corruption framework define corruption and guide prevention/detection.
- Unit-level implementation: each unit must build procedures and processes based on ABC (anti-bribery and corruption) risk assessments across value chains; controls and training support the program.
- Reporting and investigation: suspicions are handled via incident management and whistleblowing; Group Audit (third line) investigates notifications and can use external resources; Compliance (second line) reports to Group Management and the Board; Group Audit is independent and reports to the Board.
- Training program: documents accessible to all; annual mandatory digital training for all employees; three risk/competence levels with risk-based depth; additional targeted training (e.g., dilemma training, seminars) for higher-risk roles; coverage includes customer-facing, procurement, contract awarding, hiring, as well as the Board and Group Management.
- 2024 actions: updated governing documents; introduced a gifts and business entertainment register for transparency; adopted a more quantitative, company-specific risk assessment methodology; measures implemented group-wide.
- Metrics/outcomes (G1-4): no convictions or fines for breaches of anti-corruption/anti-bribery laws in 2024.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.3 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: The Group’s governing documents were updated in 2024.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Extract from DNB Group’s 2024 Annual Report, ESRS G1 Business conduct, covering Corporate culture (whistleblowing channel referenced) and ESRS G1-3 Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery, plus ESRS 2 MDR-A Actions and resources and G1-4 Metrics.
- Governance and lines of defence: Compliance is the second line, reporting to Group Management and the Board; Group Audit is the independent third line, investigates corruption/bribery notifications and reports to the Board; external resources may be used when needed.
- Policies and frameworks: The Code of Conduct, Group instructions for anti-bribery, and the global anti-corruption framework define corruption and guide prevention/detection; documents are accessible in the quality system and mandatory for all employees to know, with annual tracking of training completion.
- Risk-based approach and procedures: Each unit must create procedures based on ABC risk assessments across value chains; controls are in place; suspicions are handled via incident management and whistleblowing channels (details cross-referenced under Corporate culture, ESRS G1-1).
- Training and competence: Three risk-based competence levels determine scope and intensity of training; annual mandatory digital training for all on the framework and corruption risk; enhanced, dilemma-based and topical training for higher-risk roles; coverage includes high-risk functions (customer-facing, procurement, contract awarding, hiring) and extends to the Board and Group Management.
- 2024 actions (ESRS 2 MDR-A): Updated governing documents; introduced a gifts and business entertainment register to improve documentation and transparency; adopted a more quantitative, company-specific risk assessment methodology; measures implemented and applicable to all employees.
- Metrics and outcomes (G1-4): No convictions or fines for breaches of anti-corruption or anti-bribery legislation in 2024.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.5 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: The Group was not convicted of any breaches of the anti-corruption or anti-bribery legislation in 2024, and has consequently not been fined.
nodes.summary:
- Overview and cross-reference to the Group’s whistleblowing channels under Corporate culture (ESRS G1-1) within ESRS G1 Business conduct.
- Management responsibilities: ensure employee awareness of governing documents, proactive compliance, and completion of mandatory training.
- Anti-corruption governance: Code of Conduct, Group instructions for anti-bribery, and a global anti-corruption framework guiding prevention and detection; each unit must tailor procedures based on ABC risk assessments in their value chains; incidents handled via incident procedures and whistleblowing, with external resources available when needed.
- Three lines of defence: Compliance as the second line reporting to Group Management and the Board; Group Audit as an independent third line investigating corruption/bribery notifications and reporting to the Board.
- Training approach: governing instructions accessible to all; annual tracking of course completion; risk-based, tiered competence model with three levels; mandatory annual digital training for all employees; enhanced training (dilemmas, seminars) for higher-risk roles; coverage includes high-risk functions (customer-facing, procurement, contracting, hiring) and extends to the Board and Group Management team.
- 2024 actions (ESRS 2 MDR-A): updated governing documents; introduced a gifts and business entertainment register for transparent documentation; adopted a more quantitative, company-specific risk assessment methodology; measures implemented for all employees.
- Metrics (G1-4): no convictions or fines for breaches of anti-corruption or anti-bribery laws in 2024.

nodes.title: Confirmed incidents of corruption or bribery in 2024

nodes.title: Targets and tracking
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.5.2 Targets and tracking
nodes.start_phrase: No measurable and result-oriented targets have been set in relation to corruption and bribery.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Tracking effectiveness of anti-corruption and anti-bribery measures under ESRS 2 MDR-T (incl. MDR-M) and disclosures on political influence (ESRS G1-5).
- Targets: No measurable, result-oriented targets set for corruption/bribery; effectiveness monitored primarily through training metrics.
- Training program:
  - Mandatory annual digital anti-corruption course for all employees and confirmation of having read and understood the Code of Conduct.
  - Course includes case studies to help detect corruption and requires familiarity with related governing documents.
  - Risk-based approach: training depth varies by role risk; higher-risk roles receive additional “dilemma training.”
  - Risk assessment conducted via unit-level ABC risk assessments aligned with the Group’s inherent risk assessment.
- Performance metrics:
  - 93% of employees completed the KNOW:RISK anti-corruption course (as at 31 December 2024).
  - 100% of Board members completed the KNOW:RISK course (on the reporting date).
- Objective: Reduce corruption risk and protect the Group’s reputation and financial stability.
- Political influence (G1-5): As of 2024, no members of the Board or Group Management held comparable positions in public administration (including supervisory authorities) in the two years prior to appointment.

nodes.title: Political influence
nodes.heading: 6.1.2.6 Political influence
nodes.start_phrase: As at 2024, no members of the Group’s administrative, management and control bodies, in DNB the Board and the Group Management team, have had comparable positions in public administration (including supervisory authorities) during the last two years before appointment.
nodes.summary:
- The section addresses ESRS 2 MDR-T on tracking the effectiveness of anti-corruption policies and actions. While no measurable, result-oriented targets for corruption and bribery have been set, the Group monitors effectiveness through training-related metrics.
- All employees must annually complete a short digital anti-corruption course (KNOW:RISK) and confirm they have read and understood the Code of Conduct; the course includes detection guidance and case studies, and employees must be familiar with related governing documents.
- Training is risk-based: positions are assessed via ABC risk assessments, and higher-risk roles receive additional training such as dilemma training.
- 2024 completion rates: 93% of employees and 100% of Board members completed the KNOW:RISK anti-corruption course.
- Under Political Influence (ESRS G1-5), in 2024 no members of the Board or Group Management held comparable positions in public administration (including supervisory authorities) within the two years prior to their appointment.

nodes.title: Financial crime
nodes.heading: 6.1.3 Financial crime
nodes.start_phrase: Financial crime, which includes fraud, money laundering and sanctions violations, poses a serious societal problem and a threat to our welfare system, while also undermining a healthy business sector.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Financial crime (fraud, money laundering, sanctions violations) as a company-specific, material topic for DNB under ESRS 2 SBM-3 and MDR-P, linked to ESRS G1 Business conduct, despite not being covered by topical ESRS standards.
- Context and significance: Financial crime is a major societal issue undermining welfare and business integrity. As Norway’s largest financial institution, DNB has a key role in limiting financial losses and safeguarding the financial system for customers, investors and society.
- Impacts and risks: Potential negative impacts include customer harm and financial risk to DNB through fraud losses, investigation/prosecution costs, fines and compensation claims. Positive impact arises from DNB’s systemic role in preventing and detecting financial crime.
- Time horizon and operations: Risks and impacts are tied to DNB’s own operations, especially the need for safe, secure digital systems; they are considered short term and critical for ongoing viability.
- Ongoing threat environment: Persistent threats (fraud, money laundering, sanctions evasion) require continuous monitoring and updates to security measures.
- Governance and management approach:
  - Code of Conduct: Commitment to actively prevent and detect money laundering and terrorist financing through compliance with rules and internal procedures.
  - Handling of external fraud: Governing document covering detection and prevention of external data fraud; Group Security sets processing rules and investigates cases.
  - Anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT): Governing document outlining required controls and roles; Group AML Manager oversees procedures.
  - International sanctions: Group-wide sanctions compliance program to prevent violations and misuse; defines required controls and roles.
- Accountability and oversight: Governing documents are accessible to all employees via the internal quality system; business area and unit managers are responsible for implementation and compliance; risk and compliance reporting occurs periodically to provide the Board of Directors with status and relevant updates.
- Source context: Extract from DNB Group Annual Report 2024, Sustainability Report, Governance information.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 6.1.3.1 Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: Financial crime, which includes fraud, money laundering and sanctions violations, poses a serious societal problem and a threat to our welfare system, while also undermining a healthy business sector.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines DNB’s approach to financial crime as a material, company-specific sustainability topic under ESRS 2 SBM-3 and MDR-P, even though it is not covered by topical ESRS standards. It defines financial crime (fraud, money laundering, sanctions violations) as a persistent societal and business risk with potential negative impacts on customers and DNB’s financial results (losses, investigation costs, fines, claims), while highlighting DNB’s positive role in safeguarding the financial system. The risks and impacts are closely tied to DNB’s own operations and secure digital systems, requiring continuous monitoring and short‑term, immediate action to ensure future viability. Management is driven by governing documents: the Code of Conduct for AML/CFT; a Handling of external fraud policy (led by Group Security); an AML/CFT policy (with a Group AML Manager responsible for oversight); and an International sanctions policy detailing a Group-wide compliance program and expected controls. These documents are accessible in the internal quality system, apply to all employees, and are implemented by business area and unit managers under DNB’s governance model. Risk management and compliance are reported periodically, providing the DNB Bank ASA Board with status and oversight.

nodes.title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 6.1.3.1.1 Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: Financial crime, which includes fraud, money laundering and sanctions violations, poses a serious societal problem and a threat to our welfare system, while also undermining a healthy business sector.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Financial crime (fraud, money laundering, sanctions violations) as a material topic for DNB, despite not being covered by topical ESRS standards.
- Context and impacts: Significant societal and financial sector risks; negative impacts include customer harm, fraud losses, investigation costs, fines, and compensation claims. Positive impact stems from DNB’s role in safeguarding a secure financial system benefiting customers, investors, and society.
- Risk horizon: Impacts and risks arise primarily from DNB’s own operations and secure digital systems; considered short term but critical for long-term viability due to persistent, evolving threats requiring continuous monitoring and security updates.
- Strategy and governance (ESRS 2 SBM-3; ESRS 2 MDR-P; ESRS G1):
  - Code of Conduct: Commitment to actively prevent and detect money laundering and terrorist financing.
  - Governing documents:
    - Handling of external fraud: Detect and prevent external data fraud; Group Security division sets processing rules and investigates cases.
    - Anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT): Defines expected controls, roles, and oversight; Group AML Manager accountable for follow-up.
    - International sanctions: Group-wide sanctions compliance program to prevent violations and circumvention; outlines controls and roles.
- Implementation and oversight: Policies available to all employees via the internal quality system; business area and unit managers responsible for compliance and implementation under DNB’s governance model.
- Reporting: Periodic risk and compliance reporting provides the DNB Bank ASA Board with status and relevant updates.

nodes.title: Managing impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 6.1.3.2 Managing impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: According to the Code of Conduct, DNB will actively prevent and detect money laundering and terrorist financing by following established rules and internal procedures for anti-money laundering and combatting the financing of terrorism.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines DNB’s treatment of financial crime—fraud, money laundering and sanctions violations—as a material topic under ESRS 2 (SBM-3 and MDR-P), even though it is not covered by topical ESRS standards. It explains the societal and business impacts, noting both negative effects (customer harm, financial losses, investigation costs, fines and claims) and positive contributions via DNB’s role in safeguarding the financial system. Threats are persistent and require continuous monitoring and secure digital systems, with a short-term focus deemed critical for the Group’s ongoing viability. Management is governed by the Code of Conduct and three key Group-wide policies: Handling of external fraud (led by Group Security for detection, prevention and investigations), Anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing (defining controls and roles; overseen by the Group AML Manager), and International sanctions (a sanctions compliance program specifying controls and responsibilities). These governing documents apply to all employees, are accessible in the internal quality system, and are implemented by business-area managers under DNB’s governance model. Risk and compliance are reported periodically, providing the Board of Directors with status and oversight; the topic is positioned within ESRS G1 Business conduct.

nodes.title: Governing documents
nodes.heading: 6.1.3.2.1 Governing documents
nodes.start_phrase: According to the Code of Conduct, DNB will actively prevent and detect money laundering and terrorist financing by following established rules and internal procedures for anti-money laundering and combatting the financing of terrorism.
nodes.summary:
- Topic and materiality: Financial crime (fraud, money laundering, sanctions violations) is not a topical ESRS standard but is deemed a material topic for DNB due to its societal impact and DNB’s role as Norway’s largest financial institution.
- Impacts, risks, opportunities: Financial crime can harm customers and create financial risks for DNB (fraud losses, investigation costs, fines, compensation claims). DNB can also have a positive impact by safeguarding the financial system for customers, investors, and society. Threats are persistent, requiring continuous monitoring and security updates. Impacts and risks stem from DNB’s own operations and secure digital systems, with a short‑term focus critical to future viability.
- Governance and policies (ESRS 2 MDR-P): 
  - Code of Conduct commits to preventing and detecting money laundering and terrorist financing.
  - Handling of external fraud policy covers detection and prevention of external data fraud; Group Security leads investigations and rules.
  - AML/CFT governing document sets expected controls and roles; Group AML Manager oversees procedures.
  - International sanctions governing document defines the sanctions compliance program and control expectations.
  - Documents are accessible in the internal quality system, apply to all employees; business area/unit managers ensure implementation. Periodic risk and compliance reporting informs the Board. Cross-reference to Code of Conduct disclosures under ESRS S1-1.
- Actions and resources in 2024 (ESRS 2 MDR-A):
  - Updated Global AML Framework to ensure compliance, consistency across Norway and international operations, and guidance on laws and regulatory expectations; Group Compliance owns the document and conducts regulatory monitoring via RegChange in BWise.
  - Updated Group-wide inherent money laundering/terrorist financing risk assessment (DNB ML‑TF IRA) to guide local risk assessments, resource allocation, customer risk classification, and due diligence; enhances business-wide awareness and compliance with national/international requirements.
  - Updated Group-wide sanctions risk assessment to inform entity-level assessments, strengthen controls, identify new mitigating measures, and raise awareness of sanctions exposure, using insights from DNB operations, peers, and external sources.
  - Developed a new, standardized, more quantitative methodology for business-specific risk assessments across AML, anti-corruption, and sanctions to align with regulatory expectations and ensure clear linkage between risk assessments and controls.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 6.1.3.3 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: Managing the negative impacts and risks that can arise from fraud and money laundering requires continuous monitoring and updating of security measures.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from DNB Group’s 2024 Annual Report (ESRS G1 Business conduct), noting where ESRS 2 MDR-P Code of Conduct disclosures are located, and focusing on ESRS 2 MDR-A (actions/resources) and ESRS 2 MDR-M (metrics) related to financial crime risk.
- 2024 actions to manage fraud, money laundering, terrorist financing, and sanctions risks:
  - Updated governing documents, including DNB’s Global AML Framework, to ensure consistent compliance across Norway and internationally; Group Compliance owns the framework and performs regulatory monitoring via RegChange in BWise.
  - Updated Group-wide inherent ML/TF risk assessment (DNB ML-TF IRA) to guide local risk assessments, resource allocation, customer risk classification, and due diligence across units and branches.
  - Updated Group-wide sanctions risk assessment to strengthen identification of required controls, harmonize practices, and reflect new insights from operations, peers, and external sources.
  - Developed a new, standardized, more quantitative methodology for business-specific risk assessments covering AML, anti-corruption, and sanctions, linking risk assessments to customer risk classification and transaction monitoring (Coverage Assessment). Risk is defined as threats exploiting DNB vulnerabilities; aims to improve efficiency, consistency, and compliance.
  - Measures apply to all employees, are ongoing and not time-limited; AML/CFT instructions are publicly available at dnb.no.
- Metrics and tracking of effectiveness:
  - Number of fraud cases handled in the alarm management system (calendar year).
  - Number of unique customers affected by fraud (annual).
  - Number of fraud incidents reported to the Norwegian police (annual; one report may cover many cases).
  - Total value of attempted fraud against customers and the Group that DNB stopped (annual).
  - Number of cases reported to Økokrim’s FIU (ongoing; all suspicious transactions are reported unless suspicion is disproven).
  - Number of frozen and reported transactions under sanctions rules and sanctioned-party lists (ongoing; all customers and transactions screened).
  - Percentage of employees completing annual AML/CTF training (mandatory).
- Collaboration: Continuous cooperation with the financial industry, Økokrim, and other authorities to protect customers and society from financial crime.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 6.1.3.4 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: To track the effectiveness of governing documents and goals and targets relating to financial crime, DNB monitors and reports on a selection of metrics on an ongoing basis, both internally and externally.
nodes.summary:
- DNB has adopted a new, externally aligned financial-crime risk methodology that defines risk as a threat’s ability to exploit DNB’s vulnerabilities, increases emphasis on DNB’s exposure, and improves consistency across customer risk classification, enterprise risk assessments, and transaction monitoring scenario coverage (via the Coverage Assessment tool). This is intended to enhance efficiency, risk management, and compliance.
- Anti-money laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CTF) measures are continuous, apply to all employees, and are supported by publicly available Group instructions (dnb.no).
- Under ESRS 2 MDR-M, DNB tracks and reports metrics to assess effectiveness, working closely with the financial industry, Økokrim, and authorities. Metrics include:
  - Number of fraud cases handled in the alarm management system.
  - Number of unique customers affected by fraud.
  - Fraud cases reported to the Norwegian police.
  - Total value of attempted fraud stopped.
  - Suspicious matters reported to Økokrim’s FIU (ongoing, when suspicion is not disproven).
  - Frozen/reported transactions under sanctions rules and lists.
  - Share of employees completing annual AML/CTF training.
- Metrics are supported by monitoring systems, technology investments, cooperation with authorities, and employee training; statutory auditor assurance is the only validation performed.
- 2024 outcomes vs 2023 indicate increased activity and prevention: more fraud cases (12,038 vs 9,723), more customers affected (5,729 vs 5,010), more police reports (47 vs 38), higher value of attempted fraud stopped (NOK 2,137m vs 1,543m), more FIU reports (3,478 vs 2,563), more sanctions-related freezes/reports (15 vs 4); AML/CTF training completion slightly decreased (92% vs 94%).
- Under ESRS 2 MDR-T, DNB has set no measurable result-oriented targets for financial crime; effectiveness is pursued by:
  - Knowing customers, partners, and suppliers (KYC).
  - Monitoring account transactions.
  - Understanding, managing, and assessing risks.
  - Taking a holistic, cross-functional approach.
- DNB conducts annual Board-approved Group-wide inherent risk assessments for ML/TF and sanctions violations, and publishes threats, advice, and related reports on its website to support transparency and continuous improvement.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets - Introduction
nodes.heading: 6.1.3.4 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: To track the effectiveness of governing documents and goals and targets relating to financial crime, DNB monitors and reports on a selection of metrics on an ongoing basis, both internally and externally.
nodes.summary: DNB Group outlines ESRS 2 MDR-M and MDR-T metrics to track the effectiveness of its financial crime governance, working with the financial industry, Økokrim, and other authorities to protect customers and society against fraud. Defined metrics include: number of fraud cases handled in the alarm management system, unique customers affected, cases reported to the Norwegian police, total value of attempted fraud stopped, cases reported to Økokrim’s FIU (ongoing), number of frozen/reported transactions under sanctions rules (ongoing; all customers/transactions screened), and the percentage of employees completing mandatory AML/CFT training. Only statutory auditor assurance has been performed on these metrics. The 2024 results versus 2023 are: cases against customers 12,038 (9,723); customers affected 5,729 (5,010); police reports 47 (38); attempted fraud stopped NOK 2,137m (1,543m); FIU reports 3,478 (2,563); sanctions-related frozen/reported transactions 15 (4); AML/CFT training completion 92% (94%). DNB highlights continued investment in technology, monitoring and security system improvements, cooperation with public authorities, and internal training to combat financial crime.

nodes.title: Targets and tracking
nodes.heading: 6.1.3.4.1 Targets and tracking
nodes.start_phrase: No measurable and result-oriented targets have been set in relation to financial crime.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on DNB’s efforts to combat financial crime, emphasizing mandatory employee training in anti‑money laundering (AML) and counter‑terrorist financing (CTF), individual responsibility, and continuous improvement of monitoring and security systems.
- Commitment to investing in new technology, cooperating with public authorities, and strengthening internal capabilities to reduce fraud risk and support a secure digital economy.
- Metrics for 2024 (with 2023 comparisons) used to track effectiveness:
  - Cases against customers: 12,038 (9,723 in 2023)
  - Customers affected by fraud: 5,729 (5,010)
  - Fraud cases reported to Norwegian police: 47 (38)
  - Attempted fraud value stopped: NOK 2,137 million (NOK 1,543 million)
  - Cases reported to Økokrim’s FIU: 3,478 (2,563)
  - Sanctions-related frozen/reported transactions: 15 (4)
  - Employees completing annual AML/CTF training: 92% (94%)
- Only validation of these metrics is assurance by the statutory auditor.
- Under ESRS 2 MDR-T (tracking effectiveness), DNB states it has not set measurable, result-oriented targets for financial crime yet.
- Key elements of effective financial crime work outlined: knowing customers/partners/suppliers (KYC), monitoring account transactions, understanding and managing group risks, and taking a holistic, cross‑business approach.
- Effectiveness is tracked via annual, Board‑approved Group-wide inherent risk assessments for ML/TF and sanctions violations, with ongoing risk identification and public transparency through published advice, threat assessments, and related reports.

nodes.title: Financial infrastructure and financial stability
nodes.heading: 6.1.4 Financial infrastructure and financial stability
nodes.start_phrase: As a systemically important financial institution in Norway 1, DNB plays a critical role in maintaining financial stability in the Norwegian economy.
nodes.summary:
- DNB’s designation as a systemically important financial institution in Norway and its critical role in safeguarding national financial stability and essential public services.
- Strategic emphasis on a stable, secure digital economy, with continuous focus on operational stability, risk management, and crisis management to protect customers, profitability, and societal trust.
- Identification of key risks from system disruptions and downtime (financial loss, increased costs, reputational damage), and mitigation through action plans, restoration procedures, and defined risk limits.
- Materiality conclusion: financial infrastructure and stability is a short-term, highly relevant company-specific topic not covered by topical ESRS standards but material for DNB.
- Governance and policy framework: a Board-approved Group risk appetite principles document that sets risk governance and tolerance (including operational risk/stability), ensures effective risk identification, handling, monitoring, and reporting, and is accessible to all employees.
- Scope and accountability: the principles apply across all DNB operations and to business partners acting on DNB’s behalf; Group Risk Management develops the principles.
- Oversight structure: second-line coordinators for each risk dimension monitor adherence, initiate follow-up, and implement action plans upon breaches, supporting the first line of defence in maintaining stability.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 6.1.4.1 Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: As a systemically important financial institution in Norway 1, DNB plays a critical role in maintaining financial stability in the Norwegian economy.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: DNB’s role as a systemically important financial institution in Norway and its responsibility for safeguarding financial infrastructure and stability, especially in a digital economy.
- Materiality and strategy: The topic is identified as highly material in the short term under ESRS 2 SBM-3, despite not being covered by topical ESRS standards. DNB prioritizes operational stability, risk management, and crisis management to sustain its own viability and societal financial health.
- Risks and impacts: Operational disruptions (e.g., system downtime, payment service outages) pose financial risks (lost income, higher costs) and reputational risks, potentially undermining customer trust and broader financial system confidence.
- Actions and recovery: DNB maintains action plans to ensure financial stability, restore operations after disruptions, and define acceptable risk limits.
- Governance and policies (ESRS 2 MDR-P): A Board-approved, Group-wide risk appetite framework sets governance and control requirements for all operations and relevant business partners. It covers operational risk and stability, supports effective risk identification, monitoring, reporting, and alignment with risk tolerance, and is accessible via the internal quality system.
- Risk oversight structure: Group Risk Management develops the risk appetite principles. Coordinators in the second line of defence are assigned per risk dimension to oversee implementation, initiate follow-up, and trigger action plans when limits are breached, supporting the first line of defence.

nodes.title: Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 6.1.4.1.1 Material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: As a systemically important financial institution in Norway 1, DNB plays a critical role in maintaining financial stability in the Norwegian economy.
nodes.summary:
- Company-specific topic: Financial infrastructure and financial stability, framed under ESRS 2 SBM-3 and ESRS 2 MDR-P; not covered by topical ESRS but deemed material for DNB.
- Role and context: DNB is designated a systemically important financial institution in Norway, with a critical role in sustaining national financial stability and essential public services.
- Strategy: Focus on securing a stable and safe digital economy through robust action plans, risk management, and crisis management to ensure operational stability and resilience.
- Risks and impacts: System disruptions and downtime (e.g., payment services) pose financial risks (lost income, higher costs) and reputational risks (loss of customer trust), with societal implications; maintaining stability underpins trust in the broader financial system.
- Time horizon: Assessed as most relevant in the short term to ensure future viability.
- Governance and policies: Board-approved Group Principles for Risk Appetite serve as the overarching governance document for risk control, including operational risk and operational stability; aims for effective risk identification, handling, monitoring, and reporting, and alignment with the Group’s risk tolerance; accessible to employees via the internal quality system.
- Scope: Principles apply across all DNB operations globally and to business partners acting on DNB’s behalf.
- Responsibilities and oversight: Group Risk Management develops the principles; a second-line coordinator is assigned per risk dimension to monitor adherence, trigger follow-up, and implement action plans if limits are breached; structure supports the first line of defence.

nodes.title: Management of material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: 6.1.4.2 Management of material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: In order to maintain financial stability, it is important that DNB works to manage risk that can affect the financial infrastructure, and thus stability.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Financial infrastructure and stability as a company-specific, short-term material topic for DNB, tied to ESRS 2 SBM-3 and ESRS 2 MDR-P, though not covered by topical ESRS standards.
- Systemic role: DNB is designated a systemically important financial institution in Norway and plays a critical role in safeguarding overall financial stability and the digital economy.
- Strategic objective: Ensure a stable and secure digital economy through continuous operational stability, risk management, and crisis management to maintain customer trust and societal confidence.
- Risk context: Disruptions (e.g., system downtime, especially in payment services) pose financial risks (lost income, higher costs) and reputational risks.
- Action readiness: Maintains action and recovery plans to restore operations during disruptions and sets clear limits for acceptable risk.
- Governance framework: A Board-approved Group-wide risk appetite document governs risk identification, handling, monitoring, and reporting, including operational risk and stability, ensuring activities align with risk tolerance; accessible via the internal quality system.
- Scope and accountability: Principles apply across all geographies, customer groups, and units, including business partners acting on DNB’s behalf.
- Roles and lines of defence: Group Risk Management develops the risk appetite principles; coordinators in the second line of defence are assigned per risk dimension to ensure implementation, monitor breaches, and trigger follow-up and action plans.

nodes.title: Governing documents
nodes.heading: 6.1.4.2.1 Governing documents
nodes.start_phrase: In order to maintain financial stability, it is important that DNB works to manage risk that can affect the financial infrastructure, and thus stability.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: DNB’s role in safeguarding financial infrastructure and stability as a systemically important financial institution in Norway; company-specific, short‑term material topic under ESRS 2 SBM‑3, not covered by topical ESRS but deemed material for DNB.

- Strategic intent: Ensure a stable, secure digital economy to protect DNB’s viability and broader financial health; continuous emphasis on operational stability, risk management, and crisis management to maintain trust and reduce disruptions (e.g., payment downtime) that carry financial and reputational risks.

- Governance and policies (ESRS 2 MDR‑P):
  - Group-wide Risk Appetite Principles approved by the Board, covering operational risk and stability; designed for effective risk identification, handling, monitoring, and reporting.
  - Applicability across all DNB operations and relevant partners; developed by Group Risk Management.
  - Second-line coordinators per risk dimension oversee adherence and trigger action plans if limits are breached; first line accountable for execution.
  - Regular reporting: quarterly to the Board; monthly to Group Management.
  - Internal stakeholder consultation on significant document updates; documents accessible via the internal quality system.

- Capabilities and criticality management:
  - Group instructions define a capability model and a Group-wide criticality scale (72-hour perspective) to prioritize and coordinate during crises.
  - Distinguishes critical, significant, and other capabilities; identifies those critical for society (financial stability) versus DNB-critical.
  - Governance: Group EVP Technology & Services owns the models; strategic ownership of critical capabilities at Group EVP level in business areas/units.
  - Annual assessments and business impact analyses required; policies apply to all employees and Group entities, including international operations.

- Business continuity and cyber security:
  - Group instructions for business continuity set requirements for managing serious disruptions; related cyber security details referenced under ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users.

- Actions and resources (ESRS 2 MDR‑A):
  - Preventive measures: regular risk assessments, robust internal controls, and continuous monitoring of external threats; ongoing effort to reduce vulnerabilities and sustain operations during crises.
  - Recovery plan and crisis management aligned with BRRD II, integrated into risk and capital management; covers DNB Bank ASA and subsidiaries across geographies.
  - Key components: risk assessments, crisis management plans, and communication plans.
  - Acknowledges local regulatory/cultural constraints; mapped and mitigated (e.g., increasing asset liquidity to enable efficient crisis disposals).

- Outcomes sought: Minimize incident probability, protect profitability and reputation, preserve customer trust, and contribute to overall financial system stability.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 6.1.4.2.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: In order to prevent the potential negative impact and the risk that may arise if DNB does not maintain stable operations and the financial infrastructure, and to ensure the customers’ trust in the financial system, DNB carries out a number of preventive measures.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and oversight of risk: Managers are accountable for adhering to risk principles and tolerances; risk appetite status is reported quarterly to the Board and monthly to Group Management. Updates to governing documents involve internal stakeholder consultation to ensure interests are safeguarded.
- Capabilities and criticality framework: Group instructions define capabilities (e.g., payment services, IT operations), classify them as critical, significant, or other, and guide crisis prioritization. Critical capabilities may be critical to society (financial stability) or DNB-critical. A Group-wide criticality scale (72-hour perspective) supports identification and coordination of critical capabilities and functions to maintain stability during crises.
- Roles and responsibilities: The Group EVP for Technology & Services owns the capability and criticality assessment models. Strategic ownership of critical capabilities sits with Group EVPs, who must conduct at least annual assessments and business impact analyses. Instructions apply to all employees and entities, including international operations, with documents available in the internal quality system.
- Business continuity: Group instructions outline requirements to manage serious disruptions, with links to cyber security practices.
- Actions and resources (ESRS 2 MDR-A): Preventive measures include ongoing risk assessments, robust internal controls, and monitoring of external threats. DNB’s recovery plan and crisis management, aligned with BRRD II, are integral to risk and capital management and apply Group-wide, with adaptations for local regulations and cultural differences. Measures include increasing asset liquidity and integrating critical sub-suppliers into risk and crisis plans, acknowledging limits on oversight of their full value chains.
- Continuous improvement and 2024 initiatives: DNB aims to strengthen emergency preparedness in collaboration with regulators, updating procedures and expanding stress testing to assess robustness and identify improvements. In 2024, DNB merged central crisis management and recovery teams to streamline decisions, advanced resolution planning via a major internal exercise and FMI emergency plans, and introduced quantitative analysis of interdependencies among recovery options to assess feasibility and synergies.
- Stakeholders affected: Regulators (financial stability oversight), customers (deposit and investment protection), and taxpayers (potential public support in crises).
- Metrics and targets (ESRS 2 MDR-T): No single CSRD-style target; stability ensured through regulatory risk management. Processes track risk appetite and breaches across risk types, including operational risk and IT stability. DNB monitors customer-impacting IT incidents by counting days with moderate/significant incidents and categorizing them green/yellow/red, with red indicating a significant operational incident based on user experience.

nodes.title: Actions - Introduction
nodes.heading: 6.1.4.2.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: In order to prevent the potential negative impact and the risk that may arise if DNB does not maintain stable operations and the financial infrastructure, and to ensure the customers’ trust in the financial system, DNB carries out a number of preventive measures.
nodes.summary: Overview of DNB Group’s preventive actions and resources to manage material sustainability risks tied to operational stability and financial infrastructure, emphasizing continuous risk assessments, robust internal controls, and external threat monitoring. Details a Group-wide recovery plan and crisis management framework aligned with BRRD II and integrated into risk and capital management, covering DNB Bank ASA and all subsidiaries across geographies with risk, crisis, and communication plans. Notes constraints from local regulations and cultural differences, mapped operational obstacles, measures such as increasing asset liquidity for efficient crisis disposals, and inclusion of critical sub-suppliers despite limited control over their full value chains. Describes plans to enhance emergency preparedness with regulators by updating procedures, ensuring legal/best-practice compliance, and expanding stress-testing to assess robustness, identify weaknesses, and define remediation. Mentions several Group-wide resilience measures implemented in 2024.

nodes.title: Changed the governance structure for the recovery plan
nodes.heading: 6.1.4.2.2.1 Changed the governance structure for the recovery plan
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, DNB improved the efficiency of its crisis management by merging the central crisis management team and the recovery team into a single unit.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on strengthening DNB’s emergency preparedness and crisis management, including expanded stress testing to evaluate robustness, identify weaknesses, and define improvement measures.
- Inclusion of critical sub-suppliers in risk assessments and crisis plans, while noting limits to DNB’s control over sub-suppliers’ full value chains.
- 2024 governance change: merger of the central crisis management team and the recovery team to streamline decision-making and ensure consistency across the Group.
- Enhanced resolution planning: major internal crisis exercise, evaluation of the crisis framework, and new emergency preparedness plans for Financial Market Infrastructures to safeguard critical services and financial stability.
- Quantitative analysis of interconnections and dependencies among recovery options to assess overall recovery capacity, feasibility, synergies, and constraints.
- Stakeholder considerations: regulatory oversight for financial stability, customer expectations for protection of deposits/investments, and potential taxpayer exposure in severe crises.
- Metrics and monitoring per ESRS 2 (MDR-T/MDR-M): no single overriding CSRD target due to the risk-management nature and regulatory requirements; continuous processes to maintain stability via ongoing risk appetite monitoring across risk types, including operational and IT risk.
- IT stability tracking: monitoring days with moderate/significant customer-impacting incidents, color-coded (green/yellow/red); “red” days indicate significant operational incidents based on user experience.

nodes.title: Updated the description of DNB’s efforts within resolution planning
nodes.heading: 6.1.4.2.2.2 Updated the description of DNB’s efforts within resolution planning
nodes.start_phrase: DNB continued to develop its crisis management capabilities in 2024, with a focus on operational preparedness and emergency preparedness planning.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on strengthening DNB’s emergency preparedness and financial stability through enhanced recovery planning, crisis management, and closer collaboration with regulators.
- Recognition of limited control over critical sub-suppliers’ broader value chains, while including them in risk assessments and crisis plans.
- Expansion of stress testing to assess robustness, identify weaknesses, and guide improvement measures in crisis management.
- 2024 governance change: merger of the central crisis management team and the recovery team to streamline decision-making and ensure consistency across the Group.
- Enhancements to resolution planning, including a major internal crisis exercise, framework evaluation, and new emergency preparedness plans for Financial Market Infrastructures to ensure continuity of critical services.
- Introduction of a quantitative analysis of interconnections and dependencies among recovery options to evaluate overall recovery capacity, feasibility, and potential synergies.
- Stakeholder considerations: regulatory oversight for financial stability, customer protection of deposits/investments, and potential taxpayer exposure in severe crises.
- Metrics and targets (ESRS 2 MDR-T): no single CSRD “overriding target” due to the risk-management nature and regulatory framework; instead, continuous processes to maintain stability.
- Ongoing monitoring of risk appetite and limit breaches across risk types, with particular emphasis on operational and IT risk.
- IT stability objective: minimize critical incidents; track days with moderate/significant customer-impacting IT events and classify them green/yellow/red, with “red” indicating a significant operational incident based on user experience.

nodes.title: Quantified the effect of connections and dependencies on DNB’s total recovery capacity
nodes.heading: 6.1.4.2.2.3 Quantified the effect of connections and dependencies on DNB’s total recovery capacity
nodes.start_phrase: One of the main measures in the 2024 recovery plan was inclusion of a general quantitative analysis of connections and dependencies between different recovery alternatives and how these affect DNB’s overall recovery capacity.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on strengthening DNB’s crisis management and recovery capabilities to maintain financial stability and infrastructure, including integration of critical sub-suppliers in risk and crisis planning despite limited control over their broader value chains.
- Commitment to enhance emergency preparedness through collaboration with regulators, updating procedures and guidelines to align with laws and best practices, and expanding stress testing to assess robustness, identify weaknesses, and define improvement measures.
- 2024 organizational changes include merging the central crisis management team with the recovery team to streamline and harmonize decision-making across the Group.
- Ongoing development of resolution planning and operational preparedness, including a major internal crisis exercise and the establishment of emergency preparedness plans for Financial Market Infrastructures to secure continuity of critical services.
- Introduction of a quantitative analysis of interconnections and dependencies among recovery options to evaluate overall recovery capacity, feasibility, effectiveness, and potential synergies.
- Recognition of key stakeholders—regulators, customers, and taxpayers—and the importance of credible plans to protect deposits and maintain financial stability in crisis scenarios.
- Under ESRS-related disclosures, no single overarching CSRD target is set for financial stability due to its nature as a risk management domain subject to strict regulation; instead, stability is managed via established processes and risk appetite frameworks.
- Continuous monitoring of risk appetite across risk types, with a particular emphasis on operational and IT risk; tracking IT stability through the number of days with moderate or significant customer-impacting incidents, categorized green/yellow/red based on internal criteria, with “red” signifying significant operational incidents as experienced by users.

nodes.title: Metrics and targets
nodes.heading: 6.1.4.3 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: No overriding target in accordance with the disclosure requirements in the CSRD has been set to ensure that DNB maintains financial stability and its financial infrastructure because this is largely a matter of risk management.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on strengthening DNB’s crisis management and recovery planning to maintain financial stability and infrastructure, including assessing critical sub-suppliers in risk and crisis plans while acknowledging limited control over their full value chains.
- Collaboration with regulators to refine internal crisis management frameworks, update procedures and guidelines for compliance, and expand stress-testing to evaluate robustness, identify weaknesses, and define improvement measures.
- 2024 Group-wide enhancements:
  - Merged central crisis management and recovery teams to streamline and align decision-making.
  - Advanced resolution planning, ran a major internal crisis exercise, and evaluated the crisis framework.
  - Developed emergency preparedness plans for Financial Market Infrastructures (FMIs) to ensure continuity of critical services.
  - Introduced quantitative analysis of interconnections and dependencies among recovery options to assess overall recovery capacity, feasibility, and potential synergies.
- Stakeholder impact: addresses expectations of regulators (system stability), customers (protection of deposits/investments), and taxpayers (potential government intervention risk).
- Metrics and targets (ESRS/CSRD context):
  - No single overriding target due to the risk-management nature and regulatory requirements.
  - Stability managed via continuous monitoring of risk appetite, limit breaches, and operational risk (including IT stability).
  - IT performance tracked by counting days with moderate/significant customer-impacting incidents, color-coded green/yellow/red; “red” denotes a significant user-impact operational incident.
- Overall objective: continuous improvement to reinforce trust, resilience, and DNB’s ability to withstand and manage crises.

nodes.title: Targets and tracking
nodes.heading: 6.1.4.3.1 Targets and tracking
nodes.start_phrase: No overriding target in accordance with the disclosure requirements in the CSRD has been set to ensure that DNB maintains financial stability and its financial infrastructure because this is largely a matter of risk management.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on DNB’s crisis management and recovery planning: strengthening emergency preparedness, infrastructure stability, and collaboration with regulators; evaluating and updating procedures and guidelines; expanding stress testing to assess robustness and identify weaknesses and improvement areas.
- Limits to control over critical sub-suppliers’ full value chains acknowledged and incorporated into risk and crisis planning.
- 2024 Group-wide measures:
  - Merged central crisis management and recovery teams to streamline governance and decision-making.
  - Advanced resolution planning: ran a major internal crisis exercise, reviewed the crisis framework, and developed emergency plans for Financial Market Infrastructures to secure critical services.
  - Introduced quantitative analysis of interconnections and dependencies among recovery options to improve feasibility and effectiveness assessments and identify synergies.
- Stakeholder considerations: regulatory oversight for financial stability, customer protection expectations, and potential taxpayer exposure in crisis scenarios.
- Metrics and targets (ESRS 2 MDR-T):
  - No single overarching CSRD target due to the risk management nature and strict regulation; instead, continuous monitoring of risk appetite across risk types, including operational/IT risk.
  - IT stability tracked via “coloured days” (green/yellow/red) based on incident severity and customer impact; metrics verified by the statutory auditor.
  - 2024 outcomes: 4 red days (down from 7 in 2023) and 9 yellow days (down from 12).
  - Recovery plan includes early-warning metrics and predefined actions under a clear governance structure involving Group Management and the Board; plans reviewed annually by Norwegian and international regulators; sensitive details not disclosed per ESRS 1 §7.7.
- EU Taxonomy disclosures:
  - Mixed-group KPI overview shows average taxonomy-aligned ratios of approximately 4.8% (turnover-based) and 4.8% (Capex-based), with non-financial activities showing 0% alignment.
  - Asset manager KPIs: taxonomy-aligned investments represent about 2.3% (turnover-based) and 2.7% (capex-based) of assets covered; coverage ratio ~99%; most assets are not taxonomy-eligible; detailed breakdowns provided by geography, counterparty type, and environmental objective.
  - Environmental objective alignment primarily in climate change mitigation (including small shares of transitional and enabling activities); minimal to no alignment reported for other objectives (adaptation, pollution, biodiversity, water, circular economy except a small share).

- Asset managers’ KPI (Annex IV):

- Credit institutions’ KPIs (Annex VI):
  - Main KPI (GAR stock, 31 Dec 2024):

structure.heading: 2.11 0. KPIs of insurance and reinsurance undertakings
structure.start_phrase: The weighted average value of all the investments of insurance or reinsurance undertakings that are directed at funding, or are associated with Taxonomy-aligned economic activities, with following weights for investments in undertakings per below:
structure.summary:
- Scope and purpose: EU Taxonomy KPIs for insurance and reinsurance investments (Annex X) with standard Article 8 templates (Annex XII), excluding sovereign exposures; focus on Taxonomy eligibility/alignment, counterparty breakdowns, and nuclear/fossil gas-related activities.

- Asset base and coverage:
  - Assets covered by KPI: 161,929 NOK million; coverage ratio 89.4% of total investments (ex-sovereigns).
  - Derivatives: (2,431) NOK million, representing (1.5)% of assets covered.

- Taxonomy eligibility and alignment (overall):
  - Non-eligible investments: 136,923 NOK million (84.6% of assets covered).
  - Eligible but not aligned: 18,872 NOK million (11.7%).
  - Taxonomy-aligned (weighted average of investments): 5,202 NOK million (turnover-based) and 4,738 NOK million (capex-based), equal to 3.2% and 2.9% of assets covered.
  - Investments (ex unit-linked) that are aligned: 2,022 NOK million (turnover-based) and 1,795 NOK million (capex-based); equals 1.2% and 1.1% of assets covered.

- Environmental objective split (aligned):
  - Climate change mitigation: 3.1% (turnover), 2.7% (capex), incl. transitional 0.3% and enabling 0.9–1.0%.
  - All other objectives (adaptation, water, circular economy, pollution, biodiversity): 0%.

- Counterparty and geography breakdown (amounts and proportions over assets covered):
  - Exposures subject to Articles 19a/29a (EU):
    - Non-financial: 7,643 NOK million; 4.7% of assets.
    - Financial: 40,881 NOK million; 25.2% of assets.
  - Exposures not subject to 19a/29a:
    - Non-financial: 34 NOK million; 0%.
    - Financial: 15,335 NOK million; 9.5%.
  - Non-EU not subject to 19a/29a:
    - Non-financial: 1,962 NOK million; 1.2%.
    - Financial: 17,155 NOK million; 10.6%.
  - Other counterparties and assets: 81,349 NOK million; 50.2%.

- Aligned exposure details:
  - To undertakings subject to 19a/29a:
    - Non-financial: 1,031 NOK million (turnover), 1,345 NOK million (capex) → 0.6% and 0.8% of assets.
    - Financial: 194 NOK million (turnover), 765 NOK million (capex) → 0.7% and 0.5%.
  - To other counterparties/assets: 2,977 NOK million (turnover), 2,627 NOK million (capex) → 1.8% and 1.6%.

- Unit-linked exclusion: Separate reporting for investments other than those where life insurance policyholders bear investment risk.

- Nuclear and fossil gas-related activities (Template 1): The undertaking has exposures to all listed nuclear activities (R&D, new build, operation/safety upgrades) and fossil gaseous fuel activities (power generation, CHP, and heat generation) — all marked YES.

- Article 8 standard templates (Templates 2–3, Total GAR assets, stock – Turnover):
  - Denominator (aligned activities): Total 144,246 NOK million (5.16%); includes 43 NOK million under Section 4.28 and remainder under “other taxonomy-aligned activities.”
  - Numerator (aligned activities): Total 144,246 NOK million (100% of numerator); includes 41 NOK million under Section 4.28 and remainder under “other taxonomy-aligned activities.”

- Template 1 – Nuclear and fossil gas related activities: The undertaking confirms “YES” exposures/activities across:
  - R&D, demonstration and deployment of innovative nuclear electricity generation with minimal fuel-cycle waste.
  - Construction and safe operation of new nuclear installations (including district heating/industrial uses such as hydrogen) and safety upgrades.
  - Safe operation of existing nuclear installations (including district heating/industrial hydrogen) and safety upgrades.
  - Construction/operation of electricity generation using fossil gaseous fuels.
  - Construction, refurbishment, and operation of combined heat/cool and power using fossil gaseous fuels.
  - Construction, refurbishment, and operation of heat generation using fossil gaseous fuels.

- Template 2 – Taxonomy-aligned economic activities (denominator):
  - Breakdown by Delegated Regulation 2021/2139 Sections 4.26–4.31 shows mostly zero amounts; Section 4.28 records NOK 43 (with 0.00% share shown in the template’s percentage columns).
  - “Other taxonomy-aligned economic activities” account for the bulk: NOK ~144,203 (CCM+CCA), with NOK ~144,199 in CCM and ~NOK 3 in CCA.
  - Total applicable KPI denominator: NOK ~144,246, representing 5.16%.

- Template 3 – Taxonomy-aligned economic activities (numerator):
  - Small amounts in specific sections: NOK 1 (Section 4.27) and NOK 41 (Section 4.28); all others zero.
  - “Other taxonomy-aligned economic activities” comprise virtually all of the numerator: NOK ~144,204 (99.97%).

structure.summary:
This excerpt from DNB Group’s 2024 Annual Report (EU Taxonomy section) presents Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures for capex, structured in three templates:

- Template 1 confirms the undertaking carries out, funds, or has exposures to all listed nuclear and fossil gas-related activities: nuclear R&D and deployment; construction and safe operation of new and existing nuclear installations (including safety upgrades and industrial heat/hydrogen uses); and construction/refurbishment/operation of electricity, CHP, and heat generation facilities using fossil gaseous fuels. All six categories are marked “YES.”

- Template 2 (denominator) and Template 3 (numerator) report amounts and proportions of taxonomy-aligned economic activities under Delegated Regulation 2021/2139 (Sections 4.26–4.31, covering nuclear and fossil gas activities) and “other taxonomy-aligned activities,” in NOK million and percentages, mapped to climate objectives (CCM, CCA, or both).
  - Nuclear/gas sections show negligible amounts: Section 4.27 is NOK 29m in the denominator (NOK 23m in the numerator), Section 4.28 is NOK 13m in both; Sections 4.26 and 4.29–4.31 are NOK 0.
  - “Other taxonomy-aligned economic activities” dominate: NOK 144,536m in both denominator and numerator.
  - Totals: NOK 144,577m taxonomy-aligned capex included in the KPI. In the denominator this equals 5.17% of total applicable GAR assets; in the numerator, composition is 99.98% “other taxonomy-aligned,” with nuclear/gas shares rounding to 0.00–0.02%.

Overall, the disclosure indicates the bank has exposures to nuclear and fossil gas activities but the taxonomy-aligned capex captured in the KPI is overwhelmingly in other taxonomy-aligned activities, with nuclear/gas contributions immaterial in percentage terms.
